### Summary of the book of Iamblichus.

*Porphyry <note>Porphyry of Tyre (c. 234–305 AD) was a student of Plotinus and a major Neoplatonist philosopher.</note>, who among the Platonists is called "the Philosopher" because of his excellence, sent a long letter to Egypt to Anebo the priest, full of various and serious questions looking toward all parts of philosophy, especially toward God, as well as angels, spirits <term>dæmones: in Neoplatonism, these are intermediary spirits between gods and humans, not necessarily evil</term>, and souls; toward providence, toward fate, prophecies, magic, miracles, sacrifices, and vows. Iamblichus, his student, responded to Porphyry's questions. Indeed, he introduces the Egyptian priest Abammon as the one responding to Porphyry on behalf of Anebo, his own disciple, to whom Porphyry sent the letter. Therefore, of this entire inquiry and truly divine response—as if I were still too much occupied with Plotinus <note>Ficino was famously translating the massive "Enneads" of Plotinus during this period</note>—I have translated almost not the individual words, but the meanings, so that it should not be thought a wonder if the speech seems fragmented in places, especially among the principles of the argument themselves, where the loss of words is of less importance. From now on, the context of the words will also appear more continuous. I was indeed forced at times to insert into it some words for the sake of either continuity or understanding. Moreover, the cause of this swifter edition was Pierleoni <note>Piero Leoni da Spoleto (died 1492), the personal physician to Lorenzo de' Medici and a close friend of Ficino</note>, a man most desirous of all secret things. Truly, that which I admire above all is that he always seems to strive for what he already possesses. For by a certain divinity of intellect, he understands the secrets of the Philosophers, both of the Greeks and the "Barbarians" <note>In this context, "Barbarians" refers to non-Greek ancient cultures, such as the Egyptians, Chaldeans, and Persians, whom the Neoplatonists respected as sources of ancient wisdom</note>, even those not yet read.*

<summary>Marsilio Ficino introduces the "Reply of Abammon" (Iamblichus's On the Mysteries), explaining that it was written to answer Porphyry’s skeptical questions about religion and magic. Ficino also notes his own translation method—focusing on the "sense" rather than literal words—and credits his friend Piero Leoni for encouraging the project.</summary>
<keywords>Porphyry, Iamblichus, Abammon, Piero Leoni, translation theory, Neoplatonism, Egyptian priesthood, spirits, providence</keywords>

->*On the knowledge of divine things.*<-

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'A' at the beginning of the text, featuring ornate foliage and vine patterns within a square frame.</image-desc>
EGYPTIAN writers, believing that all things were discovered by Mercury <term>Mercurius: the Roman name for the Greek Hermes, here identified as Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Egyptian sage and father of writing and philosophy</term>, dedicated their books to Mercury. Mercury presides over wisdom and eloquence. Pythagoras, Plato, Democritus, Eudoxus, and many others visited the Egyptian priests. The teachings of this book belong to the Assyrians and Egyptians, and come from the columns of Mercury <note>According to legend, the ancient wisdom of the Egyptians was inscribed on stone pillars or columns to preserve it for future generations</note>. Pythagoras and Plato learned philosophy from the columns of Mercury in Egypt. The columns of Mercury are full of teachings. Before any use of reason, there is a naturally implanted notion of the gods; indeed, there is a certain touch of divinity that is better than mere knowledge, from which is stirred the natural desire for the good, as well as reasoning and judgment. The essential knowledge of divine things is perpetual to the soul; however, this is not truly the same as the "knowledge" <note>original: cognitio; Ficino distinguishes between intellectual study and a direct mystical experience</note> by which we enjoy God. For in [ordinary] knowledge there is "otherness" <note>original: alteritas; in Neoplatonic philosophy, this refers to the separation between the person who knows and the object being known</note>, but [in this divine state there is] a certain contact...

<summary>This page introduces the Egyptian and "Hermetic" origins of Iamblichus's work, asserting that great Greek philosophers like Plato and Pythagoras drew their wisdom from Egyptian pillars. It also describes a "touch of divinity" that exists in the human soul prior to rational thought.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of how the soul relates to the divine. # IAMBLICHUS

[essential knowledge is] essential and simple. For we cannot reach unity itself, unless by something most unified <note>original: vnitissimo; referring to the highest, most singular part of the human spirit</note>, and by a unity of the mind which stands above the specific properties of the soul and the intellect.

The unity of the gods itself unites souls to itself from eternity through their own unities, according to a contact so intimate and effective that it appears to be a continuity. The divine intellect gives being to the soul through its own essential act of understanding. Therefore, the "being" of the soul is a certain kind of understanding—specifically, an understanding of God, upon whom it depends.

Our true being consists in knowing God, because the principal being of the soul is its intellect, in which being and the understanding of divine things are the same thing in a perpetual act. From that principal being, however, the discursive <term>discurrentes: reasoning that moves step-by-step from one idea to another, as opposed to the instant "intellectual" grasp of truth</term> powers of the soul are derived. 

After the gods, we place demons, heroes, and pure souls: these three orders are the attendants <note>original: pedissequi; literally "foot-followers," those spirits who follow in the retinue of a specific deity</note> of the gods. We cannot reach these attendants of the gods—demons, heroes, or pure spirits—through the usual wanderings of human reason. Instead, it is necessary to rise up to an essential and eternal intelligence. 

Just as the gods are always reached by an innate notion, so too the divine powers that attend the gods are first reached only when the soul has laid aside its shifting mode of cognition. This shifting mode belongs to the rational power, which [is shaped] by intellect and intelligence...

<summary>This page explores the metaphysical bond between the human soul and the divine, arguing that the soul's truest essence is a perpetual act of understanding God. It also introduces the spiritual hierarchy of demons, heroes, and pure souls that serve as intermediaries between humanity and the gods.</summary>

<keywords>Neoplatonism, Unity of Mind, Divine Intellect, Hierarchy of Spirits, Demons, Heroes, Marsilio Ficino, Iamblichus, Discursive Reason</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of how the soul relates to the divine. # ON THE MYSTERIES

...is perfected, which they call the **acquired intellect** <term>intellectum adeptum: in Neoplatonic philosophy, this is the state where the human mind has fully realized its potential and is actually possessing divine truth</term>. For the first knowledge consists in the active intellect. Since knowledge occurs through **conformity** <note>original: adæquationem; the principle that the knower must become like the thing known</note>, it follows that we reach even the smallest eternal and immovable things by a notion that is itself eternal, immovable, and simple. 

The knowledge by which we know **separate substances** <term>substantias separatas: beings that exist independently of physical bodies, such as gods, angels, or demons</term> is of a different kind than the knowledge by which we know other things. The knowledge of divine things was always in the soul through a simple **intuition** <note>original: intuitum; a direct "looking upon" or immediate grasp of truth without step-by-step logic</note> or contact. 

Some people think they will reach these separate beings through a certain method of opposition—namely, that material things are mobile, localized, and subject to suffering, and therefore separate beings must be immobile, and so on. In this way, one certainly learns what they are *not*; but what they truly *are* is known by the conformity of our knowledge to that which is naturally present in the soul through the intellect. This is acquired in the **rational power** <note>original: rationali potentia</note> through a specific kind of study—not so much a study of comparison and guesswork, but rather through the duty of **separation** and **purification** <note>original: separationis, & purificationis; the process of stripping away material distractions to let the soul's inner light see clearly</note>. 

There was also a method of logical division: for instance, that "gods and divine things are either temporal or eternal." Since they are not temporal, they must be eternal. Yet even this mode of reasoning, because of its own "mobility" <note>the way the human mind moves from one logical point to another</note>, does not truly suit those beings who are themselves immovable.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of divine beings. # IAMBLICHUS

...from a genus that is in itself indeterminate, and a defining difference. For those **substances** <term>substantiae: the fundamental realities or beings that exist independently, like the gods or the soul</term> are complete species in every respect, existing in a determined and complete act. If **separate substances** <term>substantiae separabiles: non-physical beings, such as angels or pure intellects, that exist apart from matter</term>, being simple, do not differ among themselves by specific differences under the same genus, then they do not differ by individual differences under the same species. Therefore, each one is like a single genus or a species existing by itself. 

They differ, however, by their own nature, by the order of their ranks, and by how they relate differently to the **First One** <note>original: ad primum; referring to the "One," the ultimate source of all existence in Neoplatonic thought</note>. **Intelligences** <term>Intelligentiæ: pure, divine minds that contemplate truth directly without needing to reason it out</term> do not agree or differ among themselves through a shared category or any such differences, for they are most simple. Instead, they differ only insofar as they are related to the First One by the same or different ratios; some are arranged in the higher ranks of perfection, while others are in the subsequent ones. 

The differences between things in their actions and **passions** <note>original: passionibus; here meaning "undergoing" or being acted upon, rather than human emotions</note> must always be traced back to differences in their inherent properties, and these in turn to differences in their **essences** <term>essentiarum: the very core "whatness" or nature of a thing</term>. One must never rest upon the secondary effects, but must always advance toward the primary causes. 

Neither in substances superior to our soul, nor in the soul itself, is there any passive motion; rather, the whole is an **effective act**. The movement of the soul, by which it moves itself, is not divided into a "mover" and a "thing moved," or into "moving" and "being moved," but is an essential act proceeding temporal-

# ON THE MYSTERIES

->**a 5**<-

...ly. **Accidental properties** <term>accidentia: traits that a thing may or may not have while remaining itself, like being "tall" or "warm"</term> apply to composite things and to forms that exist within a subject, but they do not belong to immaterial forms. Whatever exists within **separate forms** <note>original: formis separabilibus; these are forms that exist independently of physical matter, such as divine intellects</note> is being itself, and is essential by a certain preeminence and perhaps equality. Neither is any accident or secondary consequence found there. 

Movements and actions differ because of the differences in their natures, not the other way around. If we were to say that there is only one **genus** <term>genus: a general category or class of things</term> of separate beings, we would throw **theology** <note>original: theologiam; here referring to the study of the divine hierarchy and the nature of the gods</note> into confusion. **Separate substances** <term>substantiae separabiles: non-physical beings that exist apart from matter</term> do not meet in a single common category in which they are distinguished by specific differences; instead, they are distinguished by their own selves and by their order of ranks, insofar as they are related to the **First One** <note>The "First One" refers to the ultimate source of all existence in Neoplatonic philosophy</note> through various degrees of perfection. However, those beings that are related to the First and the Last in a more similar way share more in common with one another. 

**The Good** is twofold: that which is above **essence** <term>essentia: the fundamental nature or "is-ness" of a thing</term>, and that which exists according to essence. Essence is the property of all the gods. But the Good itself is above essence and is called the cause of good—that is, the principle of essential good. Accordingly, the ranks of the gods are distinguished from one another based on their degrees of essence. In the lowest **rational souls**, essential good is not present as it is in the gods; instead, they possess a participation in the good according to intellectual beauty, and this beauty dwells within them immutably.

<summary>This page explains that divine beings lack non-essential 'accidents' and are instead defined by their proximity to the ultimate Good. It distinguishes between the 'Good' that exists above all being and the 'Good' that constitutes the essence of the gods.</summary>

<keywords>immaterial forms, accidents, essence, hierarchy of the gods, the Good, rational souls, Neoplatonism, divine substances</keywords>

### *On the Order of the Higher Beings.*

Our souls are counted among the classes of divine beings. **Heroes** <note>In this context, heroes are not just brave men, but a specific class of semi-divine beings ranking above humans but below demons</note> are greater than men, and therefore **demons** <term>dæmones: in Neoplatonism, these are not "evil" spirits, but intermediary "power-brokers" or "guiding spirits" that link the human and divine realms</term> are much mightier. The first of the divine beings is the **Good** itself and the gods following it. The last are the particular rational souls. Between these two extremes are two intermediaries: namely, the heroes, who are near the souls, and the demons, who are near the gods—just as air and water exist between fire and earth. 

Although heroes surpass us in power, virtue, beauty, and magnitude, they nevertheless agree much with our soul and its manner of life. Demons are superior to heroes and serve as the ministers of the gods, acting as the assistants to the "architects" in the **worldly workmanship** <note>original: opificio mundano; this refers to the creation and maintenance of the physical cosmos</note>. Whatever is ineffable and hidden within the gods, the demons express and reveal. 

Demons and heroes adapt the universal, simple, and unmoving gifts of the gods to lower beings. They reconcile all things and are the authors of the **harmonic consensus** and the **mutual compassion** <note>original: compassionis; in a philosophical sense, this refers to "sympathy," the Neoplatonic idea that all parts of the universe are interconnected and vibrate in harmony with one another</note> of all things. They translate divine things to us and, in equal measure, lead our things back to the divine. Furthermore, they arrange the degrees of the gifts given by the higher beings and oversee the preparation of those who receive them. The diverse kinds of divine beings differ among themselves through a threefold mode of properties: namely, in what pertains to their **essences**, their **virtues**, and their **actions**. ### ON THE MYSTERIES

->**11**<-

The characteristic of the gods is **unity**, a remaining within themselves, the immovable cause of all motions, and a superior **providence** <note>original: prouidentia; in this philosophy, providence is the "overflowing" care the higher beings have for the lower, without the higher being affected or changed by those they help</note> which has nothing in common with those things for which it provides. This specific property is preserved in them according to their **essence** <term>essentia: the fundamental "whatness" or nature of a thing</term>, their power, and their activity.

The characteristic of **Souls** is a leaning toward multiplicity and motion, a joining with the gods, and a capacity to receive something from others. They are filled by a vital motion and must harmonize everywhere with all things—some remaining stable and others flowing—tempering everything within themselves and through themselves. This property is preserved in them according to their essence, power, and activity.

The characteristics of **demons** are to contain within themselves the gifts of the gods, though in a lower way than the gods do. However, under the form and reason of these gifts, they contain the conditions of lower things; that is to say, they are multiplied, yet mixed in a unified way—though they also remain unmixed. Finally, they are moved, but in a stable manner. 

**Heroes**, on the contrary, possess unity, identity, stability, and excellence while existing under the condition of multiplicity, motion, and mixture. 

Demons and heroes are closest to the extremes: the former to the gods, the latter to souls. The differences between demons and heroes lie chiefly in this: that heroes sometimes lean more toward particular and changeable things than demons do. These two intermediaries—namely, demons,

### *How the actions of the superior beings are distinguished from one another.*

Gods occupy the highest rank of all beings, while souls occupy the lowest. Gods are capable of all things, united in a single instant; souls, on the contrary, are capable of neither all things, nor in an instant, nor are they united. Gods act upon and care for all things without being "inclined" <note>original: *non inclinati*; in Neoplatonic thought, to be "inclined" means to be pulled down or distracted by the material world. The gods help the world without losing their high status</note> toward them; souls act with a certain inclination and turning [toward the material]. 

Gods are the primary causes; souls depend perpetually upon the gods' will. Gods, with the swiftest vigor, grasp their innermost ends together with their beginnings <note>This refers to the gods being outside of time; they see the start and the finish of a thing as one simultaneous event</note>; souls proceed from one thing to another, traveling from the imperfect to the perfect. 

Gods cannot be grasped by any measure or form; souls are held back and overcome by inclination, by habit, and by impulse. They are touched by a longing for lesser things and by a familiarity with them, and from this they contract certain qualities <note>i.e., the soul takes on the "flavor" or characteristics of the physical world it inhabits</note>.

### *On the Intellect and the Soul.*

The **Intellect** <term>Intellectus: also known as *Nous*, this is the divine "Craftsman" or the level of reality containing the eternal patterns of all things</term>, the maker of all things, is always present most fully to all the gods through a single act remaining within itself. The Soul is a participant in the intellect, but in a more divisible and multiform way.

Likewise, the Gods possess an order derived from higher causes, as well as beauty itself—or rather, the very cause of both order and beauty. The **Soul**, however, possesses an order and an intellectual beauty <note>original: *intellectualisq; pulchritudo*; in Neoplatonism, this refers to beauty that belongs to the realm of the Mind or 'Nous' rather than the senses</note> of its own. 

Furthermore, in the Gods there is a measure that is powerful over all things; but the Soul defines that measure and acts through it only upon specific things. **Demons** <note>original: *daemones*; in this context, these are not "demons" in the modern sense, but intermediary spirits that link humanity to the divine</note> and **heroes** <note>semi-divine beings or elevated human spirits</note>, acting as intermediaries between the Gods and Souls, are composed of a fitting proportion relative to both the highest and lowest beings. They are made of the properties of both Souls and Gods, which we have described in the preceding sections. 

Therefore, if you wish to grasp the nature <note>original: *speciem*</note> of the Gods, consider the properties of the lowest rational Soul and attribute their opposites, in absolute perfection, to the Gods. If it pleases you to define the nature of a **demon**, compose it from both, while attributing more of the divine to it; finally, if you seek the nature of a **hero**, compose it from both, but introduce more of the qualities and conditions of the Soul. 

The author <note>Iamblichus</note> finds fault with **Porphyry** <note>Iamblichus's teacher and intellectual rival</note> for distinguishing these separate beings according to their relationship to bodies—namely, defining the Gods by their relationship to **etheric bodies** <note>the stars and heavenly fire</note>, demons to **aerial bodies**, and souls to **terrestrial bodies** <note>earthly bodies</note>. This is because primary things and causes should clearly not be defined by secondary things and their effects. Incorporeal <note>non-physical</note> substances are not *within* bodies; rather, they lead them from the outside, and they give something to the bodies without receiving anything in return.

### *On the Anger of the Gods.*

When we turn ourselves away from the beneficial care of the gods, as if turning away from the light of the sun, we are immediately in darkness, and God is then said to be "angry" with us. Therefore, to appease the "anger" of the gods is simply to return to them by means of supplication. Appeasement of this kind does not bring any **passion** <note>original: *passionem*; in this context, it refers to an emotional change or a state of being affected by something external. The author argues that God is "impassible," meaning He does not feel anger as humans do.</note> to God; instead, it frees the soul from its own former passions. The gods and divine daemons, when humbly adored and worshiped, repel many evils that would otherwise occur naturally.

### *On the Necessity and Liberty of the Gods.*

It is necessary that the gods exist exactly as they are—not because of a necessity forced upon them from the outside, but because of a necessity that is natural to them and which is the best state for them. Therefore, their state is most voluntary, for they would never wish to be any other way even if offered a choice. Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher and student of Plotinus who often questioned the mechanics of theurgy.</note> and many other philosophers say that the gods are "pure intellects," while daemons are either intellects themselves or "participations in intellect," some of which are **associated with the soul** <note>original: *animales*; referring to beings that possess *anima* (soul) or are intermediate between pure mind and physical matter.</note>. But Iamblichus objects that the specific nature of daemons is not correctly defined in this way. For even souls are intellect...

### *On the difference between the Gods and Daemons according to the Greeks and the most devout.*

Gods are not rightly defined according to the rationale of intellect itself, but according to unity, and goodness, and the **intelligible object** <term>original: *intelligibilis obiecti*; an entity or truth that can be grasped only by the mind, not by the senses</term>.

Porphyry <note>A scholar and critic of ritual practices who often debated with Iamblichus.</note> suspects that pure and **separate substances** <term>original: *separatis substantiis*; beings that exist independently of physical matter</term> have no relationship to sensible things <note>Physical things perceived by the senses.</note>, nor do they hear prayers. Nevertheless, the principal worship must be offered to these separate substances. In this worship, the highest part of the soul is awakened and joined to the highest things; the supreme beings encompass and know all our affairs within their unity, and they embrace the actions of religious prayers within themselves. They do not depart from themselves, but remaining fixed within themselves, they are fully present to the intention of those who pray. Indeed, it is fitting to supplicate most humbly. For acknowledging our own lowliness, if we are compared to the higher beings, causes us to pray most earnestly, to turn ourselves entirely toward them, and through constant habit, to become like them. Prayers sent from the divine, in which a divine power dwells, are especially beneficial. These things are said against Porphyry, who thinks we should specifically worship the **worldly gods** <note>original: *mundanos deos*; gods or powers associated with the physical cosmos and the movement of the stars.</note>, because

Pure intellects <term>original: *intellectus puri*; minds or consciousnesses that exist without being tied to a body</term> know sensible things <note>Physical objects perceived through the five senses.</note> without the need for sensory perception.

### *Again, on Supplications.*

Porphyry <note>A philosopher and student of Plotinus who questioned the efficacy of religious rituals.</note> claims that certain material objects are used in supplications, and therefore they are only used for those gods who are animate beings <note>In this context, gods who are associated with the physical world or have a "soul" like living creatures.</note>. Iamblichus responds that within these material objects, beyond their physical qualities, there also lie hidden incorporeal and divine **principles, forms, and measures** <term>original: *rationes, species, & mensuras*; the underlying spiritual logic and structure of things</term>, through which the things offered are made suitable for the gods. Indeed, whenever something is brought forward that is in any way agreeable to and like the gods, the gods are soon present; they join with us, bestow their gifts, and hear our prayers. Even a small degree of harmony between our world and the gods is enough for us to draw grace from them. For they are always most ready to do this because of their natural goodness and wondrous power. For a truly powerful cause acts upon matter, or upon that which has been prepared. Porphyry distinguishes **daemons** <note>In ancient Neoplatonism, *daemones* were intermediary spirits, neither fully human nor fully divine, who acted as messengers or guardians.</note> from gods by this: he claims the former are incorporeal, while the latter are corporeal. Iamblichus says that their true substances and properties cannot be distinguished by such simple definitions.

<summary>This page features Iamblichus’s defense of the use of material objects in prayer and ritual, arguing that even physical matter contains divine principles that allow for a connection with the gods. He also begins to challenge Porphyry's definitions of gods and intermediary spirits (daemons).</summary>
<keywords>Iamblichus, Porphyry, supplication, prayer, material offerings, daemons, divine nature, Neoplatonism</keywords>

### *On the difference between gods and demons, and concerning celestial beings.*

Celestial gods can be called incorporeal <note>original: *incorporei*; existing without a physical body or material substance</note>, since no hindrance from physical bodies affects their superior activity or the happiness of their lives. But insofar as the gods strive toward the **One** itself <term>original: *ipsum vnum*; in Neoplatonist thought, the ultimate, simple source of all reality from which everything else flows</term>, their bodies naturally strive toward that same goal. These gods do not "contain" souls as if they were cages, but rather they are most excellently contained *by* those souls.

The celestial body is most closely related to incorporeal things because of its simple, undivided, and constant nature, and its single action—that is, its circular motion—as well as its innate life and light. In the heavens, there is no fusion of soul and body into a single third nature <note>Unlike humans, who are seen as a composite of two different things, the heavens are perfectly unified.</note>; instead, the body is drawn entirely toward the nature of the soul. It is, as it were, a kind of visible soul. Perhaps the heaven is light itself without matter and without dimension <note>original: *sine dimensione*; without the physical bulk or measurable thickness associated with earthly objects</note>. Dimension appears there only because of the soul's vast and ample presence. 

Hence, the heaven is the soul of heaven adapting itself to human eyes and to perishable things; that great circle we see is the revolution of the soul, and the light is its intellect. Just as in the lowest of bodies, form becomes material <note>On earth, the "idea" or "form" of a thing is buried in heavy matter.</note>, so in the highest realm, matter becomes "formal" <note>In the heavens, the substance is so refined it behaves like pure spirit or thought.</note>; it is an **animated body** rather than a "corporeal soul," if indeed there is any matter in heaven at all. Just as the highest air becomes fiery, so the celestial fire becomes...

### *On the closeness of celestial bodies to incorporeal forms.*

The celestial gods, having their origin in the intelligible world <term>original: *mundus intelligibilis*; the realm of pure thought and Forms, which exists beyond the reach of the physical senses</term>, while they contemplate the Ideas of themselves, move the heavens by this very act of intelligence and by a will that is exceedingly effective and perpetual. And therefore they rule without labor, which is clearly apparent from the always-constant order of the stars. Being thus disposed, the gods are joined to the separate, immaterial forms rather than to physical bodies. 

Their governance over the heavens cannot distract the gods from the focus of their intelligence, since they rule all the more powerfully and easily the more attentively they speculate upon that higher realm; for from the latter proceeds the former. This same thing would also happen to our own living beings if they were to contemplate their own cause, from which even the faculty of growth <note>original: *vegetandi facultas*; the basic biological power of nutrition and life-sustenance</note> originates.

### *Confirmation of the above.*

The divine Mind <term>original: *Mens divina* or *Nous*; in Neoplatonism, the second principle of reality and the seat of the eternal Forms</term>, through its Ideas, procreates the souls of the celestial gods, and through them the celestial bodies, and it retains both as perpetually joined to itself. The worldly gods <note>original: *dii mundani*; gods who oversee the physical cosmos</note>,...

He argues that the physical heavens are a direct result of the gods contemplating eternal Ideas, ensuring that their governance of the world never distracts them from their divine focus.</summary>

In natural composite things <note>physical objects made of many different elements or parts</note>, unity is accidental, depending on higher things, and is overcome by multiplicity. In separable forms <note>immaterial forms that can exist apart from matter</note>, unity overcomes multiplicity, and in the gods it overcomes it to such a degree that their very being is a certain unity—I say "a certain" unity, because the first principle <note>the One, the ultimate source of all existence in Neoplatonic thought</note> is itself unity in its simplest form. Since, therefore, unity so prevails within the gods from the inside, it rightfully overflows from the higher gods into those that follow, so that these latter consist in the unity of the former. By this unity—which is, as it were, common to all—everyone is one by a certain act, just as bodies are one among themselves by a certain material potentiality. ### *On Providence, Gods, and Daemons.*

The providence <note>the protective care and divine direction of the universe</note> of the gods is universal, whereas that of daemons <term>original: *dæmonum*; in this context, intermediary spirits that bridge the gap between gods and mortals, not necessarily "demons" in the modern evil sense</term> is particular. The First God <note>The supreme, transcendent source of all</note> gives all things to all. The gods who follow bestow certain things upon everyone. Daemons and souls, however, give only to certain beings and only certain things. There are invisible gods, and there are also gods visible in the heavens <note>referring to the stars and planets</note>, and there are also daemons. The gods visible in the heavens exist in a state of union with the hidden <term>original: *occultos*; transcendent or invisible</term> gods. Daemons, however, are far removed from them; while the gods are pure contemplators, daemons are more actively occupied in the realm of action. For this reason, they are also far removed from the visible gods. Likewise, the essence, power, and universal providence of both types of gods extend through all things; but the nature of daemons is a particular providence focused on specific matters and provinces <term>original: *prouincias*; specific domains or spheres of influence</term>. Furthermore, the gods so greatly surpass their bodies, and those bodies are so obedient to them, that the gods are said to be "separated" from their bodies. Daemons, on the contrary—

### *How Daemons, Heroes, and Souls Differ.*

There are in the gods generative <note>The power to produce or create life and matter</note> and creative powers, and there are also life-giving <term>original: *vivificae*; the specific power of bestowing and maintaining life</term> powers, which are contained more sublimely in those gods who come first. The first powers are more widely diffused than the second. The second are defined by the first: daemons <note>In Neoplatonism, daemons are not "demons" in the modern sense, but intermediary spirits who act as messengers and executors of the divine will</note> arise after a long progression of these powers, at the point where they are already divided into many parts; heroes are defined by the second—that is, the life-giving powers—before they reach the very end. For at the end of these powers, souls arise. 

Therefore, the duty of daemons is craftsmanship <term>original: *opificium*; the work of a craftsman or architect</term> concerning mundane <note>Belonging to the physical, material world</note> natures, to pass through and simultaneously perfect individual things, and to bind souls to bodies. But the role of heroes is to give life, to reason, to guard souls, and to release them from bodies. The duty of daemons is broader than that of heroes: the former work more around the universe as a whole, while the latter work rather around individual souls. We do not say that souls are created by them, but that they receive something from daemons and heroes, and add many things from themselves besides, and begin their own...

### *How Daemons, Heroes, and Souls Differ.*

**All** the higher beings, when invoked, come into view, but some appear under different forms and with different powers. The souls of the stars also move the sight in certain new ways. The visions of the **Gods** appear uniform and most simple; those of **archangels** are somewhat less uniform or simple. Those of **angels** are even less so; those of **daemons** are already varied; those of the **principalities** <note>original: *principatuum*; these are the "Archons" or cosmic rulers in Iamblichus's system</note> are more varied, but in a marvelous order of variety. Those of **heroes** are almost similar to these [daemons]; those of the **rulers** <note>original: *principes*; referring to the sublunary or material archons</note> are very varied and little ordered. Those of **individual souls**, of course, take all forms. Since the higher beings are different in their natures and actions, and appear to each individual according to their own mode, they deservedly appear in different ways to different people.

The **Gods** come into view in a way that is quite overwhelming <note>original: *insalutares*; literally "not-to-be-greeted," meaning their majesty is so transcendent it is unapproachable or even crushing to human senses</note>; **archangels** are terrifying and yet gentle at the same time; **angels** are milder; **daemons** are to be feared; **heroes** are less to be revered; **principalities** are astonishing; **rulers** are harmful and hostile; **souls** are similar to heroes, though inferior.

The images of the **Gods** appear entirely immutable. In magnitude, form, figure, and action, those of **archangels** and **angels** are gradually less immutable, but remain close to the Gods. Those of **daemons** are indeed mutable in magnitude and form, for they appear differently at different times, yet are recognized as the same beings. The images of the **principalities** are immutable; those of **heroes** are much like those of daemons; those of the **rulers** appear in many forms...

When **souls** appear, if they are pure souls established within the angelic order, they call the observer upward, provide salvation to the mind, and offer sacred hope and the sacred gifts for which one prays. **Impure souls**, however, twist the observer back toward generation <note>original: *generationem*; the cycle of physical birth, decay, and rebirth</note>; they frustrate hope by taking away its fruits, and they fill the soul of those who behold them with passions.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of spiritual beings encountered in theurgy. ### ON THE MYSTERIES.

An **angel**, or a good **daemon** <note>original: *daemon bonus*; in this Neoplatonic context, a 'daemon' is a mediating spirit, not necessarily an evil one</note>, teaches man when they appear what their essence truly is and of what sort it is, speaking nothing beyond or short of the truth. For just as light naturally and constantly follows the sun, so truth follows God and His attendants—especially since they are perfect and full; they neither need nor are they able to claim for themselves more than what they are. 

When a mistake is made in **theurgy** <term>theurgia: from the Greek 'theos' (god) and 'ergon' (work); the practice of rituals intended to invoke the presence of or unite with the divine</term>—that is, the divine and priestly faculty—then it is not the good divinities which were desired, but inferior and evil ones that encounter us under the guise of good ones. For evil spirits often transform themselves into the likeness of good ones, and they come boastfully, claiming for themselves more than what they are. Truly, where a corrupted first beginning arises, much falsehood proceeds from that perversity. 

It is necessary for priests to examine the appearances of spirits by the rule of the whole [sacred] order, and to remember that boastful arrogance is in no way characteristic of true and good spirits. They must also take care that there is never a departure from the sacred rite. But if, through some error, certain insolent spirits suddenly arrive during an apparition, it is not right to judge the common and entire nature and condition of the divinities based on the condition of these [impostors]. For indeed, in every class of being, the primary principles begin first from themselves and provide for themselves exactly what they offer to others; this occurs in their essence, their life, and their motion. Similarly, the higher beings, who offer truth to all, first declare the truth about themselves and especially reveal their own **essence** <term>essentia: the fundamental "being" or inner nature of a thing that makes it what it is</term> to our contemplations.

Therefore, they rightly demonstrate to the priests the fire that is to be seen in its own right and in its own proper form. For it is not the nature of heat to make things cold, nor of light to darken or hide things; nor is it possible for anything that acts according to its essence to ever do the opposite of what it is. A **phantasm** <note>original: *phantasma*; a deceptive or empty image</note>—that is, a likeness sent by something without possessing its actual nature, appearing only like a reflection in a mirror—vainly leads the mind of the viewer astray and deceives it. It pretends to be something while possessing nothing of that thing's true nature. Falsehood is therefore the result of this, and it in no way belongs to any true essence.

Consequently, falsehood does not belong to the gods. They and their attendants reveal images of themselves that are not thin or empty, but natural and true. They are not mirror-like or vain images (as I mentioned); for why would they send such things? # ON THE MYSTERIES.

...any utility. For what utility can be found in a combination of lies and deception? Finally, they <note>Referring to the gods or higher beings</note> do not send such things because their nature would somehow project an **idol** <term>idolum: here meaning a deceptive image or a hollow "double" of a real thing</term> from itself. Indeed, an essence that is firm and consistent within itself—and is thus the cause of essence and truth for all other things—never sends out a deceptive or misleading imitation of itself into another. Such an imitation would be a thing that claims to be something while possessing nothing of that thing’s true nature. 

Therefore, neither the gods nor their followers <note>original: *sequaces*; referring to the "retinue" of attendants like angels or archangels that accompany a god</note> transform their nature into any **simulacra** <term>simulacra: deceptive images or masks that look like the real thing but lack its substance</term>, nor do they produce these images from themselves to be sent elsewhere. Instead, they illuminate and demonstrate their true forms within the true character of the soul. 

Note how similar this is to the idea that in our **homeland** <note>original: *in patria*; referring to the celestial or divine realm from which the soul originates</note>, the blessed mind sees the divine essence not through a created image (which would be entirely lacking compared to the original), but through that very same essence. It is like one who sees light by means of light, within light—not like one who perceives heat through light, or who sees a body reflected in a mirror. **Separate substances** <term>substantiæ separatæ: a term for beings that exist entirely without physical matter, such as pure intellects or divine spirits</term> share no common genus with one another. 

Likewise, gods, angels, and good demons do not appear in a phantasmal way, but in a way that is entirely their own and true. However, evil spirits appear in a phantasmal and deceptive manner. It is not right to judge the way the good beings shape the soul by their presence based on the conditions under which these evil spirits appear to us.

Porphyry says that the knowledge of divine matters is a sacred thing, but ignorance, however... <note>original: *Porphyrius*; the catchword "vero" at the bottom of the page indicates the sentence continues: "ignorance, however, is..."</note>

### On the power of the Sacraments.

The proper observance of precepts and divine works—which exceed all human intellect—and the wonderful power of **symbols** and **sacraments** <note>original: *sacramenta*; here referring to the ritual tools and mysteries of the theurgic tradition</note>, known only to the gods themselves, provides us with deifying union. When we engage in these sacred acts, we do not complete the sacrament through our own intellect; if we did, their action would be merely intellectual and would originate from us. On the contrary, even when we do not understand them, these rites perform their own work by their own power. The power of the gods, to which these rites are directed, recognizes its own ineffable images within the rituals—images arising from the gods themselves, not stirred up by our own thoughts. For universal causes [are not moved] by particular effects...

For this reason, divine beings are not principally moved to action by our **intellects** <term>intelligentia: the higher faculty of the soul capable of grasping spiritual truths</term>; rather, it is necessary that our intellects, a most excellent disposition, and purity precede as certain co-causes. However, the things that principally stir the divine will are the divine **sacraments** <note>original: *sacramenta*; in this context, the word refers to theurgy—ritual acts and symbols that connect the human to the divine</note> themselves. Therefore, do not think that the entire authority of efficacious reason in the sacraments resides within us, nor that their work is completed through the truth of our own understanding, or that these mysteries are somehow falsified by our own deceptions. For even if we were to know the specific properties that belong to every class of being, we would not suddenly achieve the actual truth of those things in practice. 

Without knowledge, an effective unity with the divine never occurs; however, that unity is not entirely the same thing as knowledge. For this reason, divine purity is not produced by correct knowledge in the same way that the purity of the body is produced by health. Instead, this purity is united **above knowledge** <note>Iamblichus emphasizes that the final union with God is "supra-rational," meaning it goes beyond what the logical mind can grasp</note> and is a "purified purity"—that is, achieved through a power superior to cognition. Consequently, no other human quality within us contributes anything to the final goal of these divine actions.

### *What prophecy is, and from where it comes.*

Prophecy itself is produced neither by human art, nor by nature, nor by any natural or animal reasoning or movement. It does not occur by chance in any way; rather, it is sent to us eternally from the divine realm. Its entire power of foretelling is attributed to the gods; all authority for it resides in them, is handed down from them, and is brought to completion through divine works or signs. It truly possesses divine spectacles and contemplations endowed with authentic knowledge. All other things, however, are made subservient as mere instruments to this divinely sent gift of foreknowledge—whether they pertain to the soul, the body, or the nature of the universe or individual natures. Even physical locations and similar things are only required for prophecy as the "matter" <note>original: *vice materiæ*; Iamblichus argues that while a prophet might need a specific place or body, these are just the "raw materials" and not the cause of the vision itself</note>. It is improper to derive prophecy without a true cause—namely, from things that possess no foreknowledge in themselves. Instead, it must be traced to the gods, who contain within themselves the boundaries of all knowledge of things. It is right to contemplate prophecy...

### ON THE MYSTERIES.

There are various types of those divinely inspired, both due to the variety of the gods—who inspire in different ways—and because of the difference in the modes of the inspirations. According to these diversities, the signs, effects, and works of the inspired are different. ->*The inspired person is free from their own action, and possesses a god in place of a soul.*<-

The greatest sign of divine inspiration <term>afflatio: literally a 'breathing upon,' referring to the divine breath or influence filling a human</term> is that the practitioner who brings down and introduces the divinity <term>numen: the divine presence or power of a god</term> actually sees the spirit descending—witnessing its magnitude and its character—and is mystically instructed and governed by it. Furthermore, the one who receives the divinity beholds a certain appearance of fire before the reception. At times, this vision is even visible to those standing by, appearing either as the god arrives or as he departs. 

By this sign, those who are skilled in these sacred matters can most truly discern the specific power of the divinity, its rank, the truths it speaks, and the works it accomplishes. However, those who introduce spirits secretly without such manifestations are like people lurking in the darkness; they are merely shaken, and they do not understand what they are doing, except for a few minor signs visible in the body of the inspired person itself. 

Therefore, when the excellence of the divine fire and an ineffable form of light settles upon the one who is possessed from without, filling them entirely, dominating them deeply, and embracing them on all sides so that they cannot perform any action of their own, what personal sense, perception, or awareness could possibly remain in a soul that has received the divine fire? Iamblichus says that in a soul divinely inspired, neither the human mind nor human thought is carried along, if the person is truly held by a god. Nor is this inspiration from demons, but rather from the gods; nor, again, should it be defined as a "departure" or an "alienation." For these terms signify a fall into a worse state, whereas it should instead be called a "leading back" and a "restoration" into a better state. 

Inspiration, therefore, is nothing other than the soul being entirely occupied and held by the god. From this state, ecstasy <term>ecstasis: a state of being "outside oneself" or beyond normal consciousness</term> follows—that is, a certain departure or alienation—but only as a secondary consequence or accident that follows the act of inspiration. 

Plato in his dialogue *Phaedrus* says that the ancients called the act of prophecy <term>vaticinium: the foretelling of the future</term> *mania* <note>original: "maniam," from the Greek word for madness</note>, that is, madness, because only those seized by divine madness truly prophesy. ### IAMBLICHVS

...to be called a conjectural opinion, and to be of no importance if it is compared with divine inspiration and prophecy. Iamblichus <note>A Syrian Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who focused on theurgy, the ritual practice of invoking the gods</note> says that divine inspiration <term>afflatus: literally a "breathing-upon," describing the influx of divine power into a human</term> and prophecy <term>vaticinium: the act of foretelling the future through divine revelation</term> are not located in the mind or the soul—neither as a quality residing in a subject nor as an action performed by an agent—but are instead entirely the act of God himself, depending purely upon God.

I call it an act performed by God within the mind or soul, which serve simply as instruments that are empty of all their own motion; and in this way, true omens are given. But if any motion from the body or the soul, or any such quality, should be introduced during the process or should precede it, the visions are confused. In such cases, there will be no true prophecy, nor can there be a legitimate divine inspiration where anything human is mixed in. 

Generally, there were three opinions concerning divine inspiration and prophecy: the first referred its cause to the soul, the second to the body, and the third to the composite <note>the "composite" refers to the human being viewed as a unified whole of both body and soul together</note>. The first opinion places it in that state where the soul is entirely returned to its own divine nature, or to the mind, or when its activity has become more intense or more expansive, or when thought has become sharp and most rapid in its movement, or when the mind has grown "inflamed." The second opinion places the cause of inspiration in the body, specifically when it possesses a certain temperament <term>complexio: the physical makeup or balance of "humors" in a person’s body</term>, such as a melancholic or a balanced one, or some other quality...

### IAMBLICHUS

...and to change the conditions of the body, to stir up a frenzy <term>furore: a state of divine madness or intense religious excitement, often called "theia mania" in Greek</term>, or to restrain that frenzy. Iamblichus grants these points, but he denies that these are the actual causes of divine inspiration. He argues they are merely human—partly natural and partly artificial—and possess nothing divine within themselves. This is what Porphyry <note>Porphyry (c. 234–305 AD) was Iamblichus’s teacher and a fellow Neoplatonist who often voiced skeptical questions about how rituals and music could actually affect the gods</note> seems to suspect when he says that some people are inspired when they hear flutes, cymbals, or drums, while others are moved by different melodies.

In the world, various types of motions correspond to the various ranks of the gods; specific motions belong to specific gods. From these divine motions, various melodies flow forth. These melodies agree with the specific gods—who are the very principles of motion—through their own rhythmic movements. Since the gods are everywhere and impart what is theirs to those things that belong to them, they are especially present in the melodies that most closely align with them. By insinuating themselves into our spirits <term>spiritibus: refers to the "pneuma" or "spirit-body," a subtle substance that Neoplatonists believed acted as a bridge between the physical body and the immaterial soul</term> through these melodies, the gods occupy the human being and soon fill them completely with their own essence and power. 

Thus, the cause of this inspiration is not so much the human emotion stirred up by music, but rather the musical harmony’s own congruence <note>original: "congruentia"; the idea that "like attracts like," where a physical sound can resonate with a divine frequency</note> with the god—a harmony to which the god is naturally present. Things perceived by sight are overly focused on images and refer more to things of the intellect. Things perceived by senses "below" hearing <note>referring to touch, taste, and smell</note> are too material. However, things perceived by hearing are in the middle and agree with the soul. Having insinuated themselves into the spirit with movement, emotion, and meaning...

[The divine power] is present everywhere to those who are capable of suddenly participating in it, illuminating them from the outside and filling all things, while running through all the elements. It does not leave behind any living creature or any part of nature upon which it does not impress something of itself, according to that thing's capacity, thus contributing to foreknowledge <term>præsagium: a divine inkling or premonition of future events</term>. This power is able to fill all things equally precisely because it is equally independent from all of them.

Porphyry <note>Porphyry (c. 234–305 AD) was a philosopher who wrote a famous "Letter to Anebo" questioning the mechanics of Egyptian and Chaldean magic</note>, in addition to those prophecies that are publicly celebrated, mentions a certain private kind: specifically, the practices of those who claim they can attract spirits for the purpose of prophecy by using certain characters <term>characteres: ritual symbols, sigils, or secret names believed to hold divine power</term>. He argues that because such people neglect all religion and holiness <term>sanctimoniam: a state of ritual purity and moral devotion</term>, trusting in symbols alone, they are unable to reach the presence of any actual god or good deity <term>numinis: a divine power or presiding spirit</term>, through which true prophecies are typically granted.

Instead, they are deceived in this: although they use symbols appropriate to the gods and maintain a focus of the mind, they only bring back a kind of imaginary, small, and obscure apparition from the higher beings. Furthermore, because they neglect holiness in the process, they fall under the power of evil demons <term>dæmonum: in this context, lower-ranking spirits that can be deceptive or malicious</term> who lie and deceive. These spirits pervert and confuse whatever small amount of true signs or appearances might have been granted by the gods. When those things suitable for prophecy <term>vaticinio: the act of foretelling or divine inspiration</term> are applied, the attention and thought of the soul take notice of what is happening. This occurs even when the divine light does not properly reach these—namely, the rational powers—but meanwhile the imagination rages in a state of alienation, because it is incited from above beyond the normal human manner.

Sometimes they keep the person who is to divine in darkness, for nothing in the dark stands against the coming light. ### ON THE MYSTERIES.

...they confess <note>referring to those who practice or study divination</note> that they obtain prophecy through gods or **daimones**, because they cannot see the future unless it is through those who are the causes and masters of the future, and through whom others may also see. **Porphyry** <note>a third-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote a critical letter questioning various mystical practices</note> wonders how it is that the gods so serve humans that some prophets even provide prophecies through flour <note>original: *per farinam vaticinentur*; this refers to aleuromancy, an ancient form of divination using grain or meal</note>. 

**Iamblichus** <note>the philosopher defending the mysteries; he argues that divine action is effortless and does not diminish the gods</note> responds that the gods do not provide this out of a sense of obedience to us, but out of an excess of their own power and goodness. As the cause that contains all things within itself, while they remain in themselves without any <term>conversio: a "turning" or redirection of attention; humans must turn away from one thing to focus on another, but gods do not</term> toward subordinate things, they bestow gifts and signs upon them according to the level of their preparation—just as the sun provides light to transparent objects and to eyes, and heat to this world. 

Because we see that humans care for subordinate matters by a certain "turning" toward their works, and by being distracted by diverse things, and are pulled away from themselves and labor, we therefore suspect that the gods provide for us in a similar way. On the contrary, however, insofar as the gods are turned toward themselves and toward their own single form (which is the cause of all lower things), they act, move, and rule all things. They are not distracted by diverse matters, but from a single principle and with a simple **nod** <note>original: *nutus*; a classical term for the effortless expression of divine will</note>, they set all things in motion, which hang from that principle in a certain succession. 

Nor do they themselves bend toward subordinate things, but by their firm standing and most full power, they make all things similar to themselves. **God** supplies different modes of prophecy, and is not indeed distracted himself, but suggests them all with an indivisible nod and a simple form; and he suggests them at different times...

And just as God often speaks wisdom through foolish men, demonstrating that it is not the human speaking but God Himself, so too does He portend the future through the most lowly things. He remains utterly superior to these means, instructing our <term>intellect: the higher capacity of the human mind to grasp divine truths</term> through all of them. God reveals things of a higher knowledge through the lowest things that lack knowledge themselves; in this, He testifies that He far surpasses nature.

While He offers these diverse signs, He is not constrained by them, nor is He distracted by them. ->*No work of any efficacy occurs in sacred rites except through the power, and indeed the presence, of some divinity.*<-

In religion, no work of any wondrous efficacy can be performed unless some one of the higher beings is present there as a witness and fulfiller of the work. Indeed, the gods lead the most perfect works, the <term>angels: celestial messengers or intermediaries</term> lead the middle works, and <term>daemons: spirits that act as intermediaries between gods and humans, not necessarily evil in this context</term> lead the third and lowest rank. Human nature can neither grasp reason nor speech concerning the gods without the gods themselves, much less is it capable of performing divine works without them. For human nature is so weak and dull that it has no remedy for its own nothingness except for a certain portion of divine light descending from above; without this light, nothing we do is divine. Just as those are mistaken who believe they can create a soul from inanimate objects or a mind from the mindless, so too are those who try to create divine things from non-divine things, or to perform the gods' own works—such as <term>prophecies: the foretelling of future events</term>, miracles, and similar things like apparitions and <term>purifications: ritual cleansings to restore spiritual purity</term>—without the help of the gods.

Even less does any passion affect the divinities, who do not enter into human souls unless those souls are entirely free from such disturbances. 

One should not say that the prophetic mind is merely a middle instrument of divine matters, nor that the priest who performs the invocation is the effective cause of divine works. The human soul is both constrained within a single species and greatly overshadowed by the <term>perishable body: the physical, mortal frame that decays over time</term> <note>original: *caduco corpore*</note>. For this reason, it possesses no effective power of its own for <term>divine work: supernatural acts or theurgy</term> <note>original: *diuinum opus*</note>. If ever we seem to be capable of such a thing in some manner, we perform it only through a divine illumination flowing down from above; it is through this light that we appear to be participants in divine action. 

If divine works were performed by the soul itself—by the soul's own nature and its own inherent power—then any soul possessing <term>virtue: moral excellence or spiritual power</term> <note>original: *virtutis*</note> and <term>prudence: practical wisdom and discernment</term> <note>original: *prudentiæ*</note>, or perhaps even every soul, would perform such feats. Yet, in reality, not every soul does so; even a soul that appears "perfect" by human standards remains imperfect in relation to divine things. Therefore, it is not the soul, but divinity itself that is the cause of divine works. 

Otherwise, <term>religion: the practice of ritual worship and sacred obligation</term> <note>original: *religio*</note> would not be necessary for us. Instead, we would be masters of divine works without any worship of the gods if these things were achieved by the power of the soul alone. Furthermore, if the soul performed divine things by its own authority, either every soul would do them, or at least those souls that possessed the virtue and perfection proper to the soul—specifically <term>knowledge: systematic understanding or science</term> <note>original: *scientiam*</note>, art, prudence, and the moral character acquired through wisdom. 

However, in practice, it is not these types of rational people who perform these works. Rather, it is those who are <term>inspired: those moved by a divine frenzy or excitement</term> <note>original: *concitati*</note> and <term>withdrawn: those whose minds are detached from the physical world</term> <note>original: *abstracti*</note>. 

<term>Porphyry: a philosopher who questioned the mechanics of divine intervention</term> <note>original: *Porphyrius*</note> had proposed three points concerning divine works. ...sometimes being the primary cause. Third, that the soul could be an equal co-cause in such a way that from it and the <term>divine spirit: the higher, godly breath or influence</term> <note>original: *spirituque divino*</note>, a third type of <term>substance: the essential nature of a thing</term> or <term>subsistence: an independent, self-existing reality</term> <note>original: *substantiae, vel subsistentiae*</note> is created.

Iamblichus says that when one thing is formed from many, those many parts must be related to each other and capable of change; they move from what they were to be mixed into something else. This is how the four <term>elements: earth, air, fire, and water</term> combine into a single "fifth" thing <note>original: *in unum quintum* - referring to the quintessence or ether</note>. However, divinity is exempt from all things and does not merge into a single mixture.

...to receive something from a god; which is absurd, especially because it would mean admitting that the gods, like physical <term>elements: the basic components of the universe, like earth or fire</term> <note>original: *elementorum*</note>, would merge in their effects into a single form created within time. Thus, despite being <term>eternal: existing forever without beginning or end</term> <note>original: *sempiternis*</note>, they would be contained within a <term>temporal: existing only within time and subject to decay</term> <note>original: *temporali*</note> thing. 

When it is said that from the soul and a god—or from gods joining with one another—a single temporal thing is produced, we must ask whether a new result arises beyond the individual parts or not. If nothing new results, then there is no true union, nor is the result truly "one"; just as in a craft, where the result depends on the art alone. But if a new thing does result, then these eternal beings will fall from their unchanging state so that something temporal may be made; for unless the parts are changed, a third thing cannot result. 

Indeed, it is altogether absurd to claim that this very thing, which is produced through a kind of temporal birth, is eternal. Yet, it is also improper to call it temporal, lest eternal things be made to serve what is temporary. Nor is it right to claim that this result can be dissolved or broken apart, even though it was made from eternal parts on both sides. And yet, because it was born through a new creation, it would appear to be dissolvable. Therefore, that opinion is absurd.

...[appear to] perish. <note>The text continues a sentence from the previous page regarding the impossibility of an eternal thing being subject to dissolution.</note> Iamblichus denies that <term>daemons: intermediate spirits that act as messengers between the gods and humanity</term> <note>original: *dæmones*</note> are born or pass away. For he denies that daemons—who are superior to both bodies and the soul—can be generated by the soul out of physical forces. He denies that the actions of a particular soul, which is enclosed within a body, can result in <term>essences: the fundamental nature or "being" of a thing</term> <note>original: *essentias*</note> that exist independently outside of the soul. He denies that the powers of bodies, which are entirely tied to matter, can be released from them to generate daemons.

Furthermore, he asks: what exactly is this power that releases material forces from matter and then "forges" them back together into one to generate a daemon? It would seem that such a power must itself be "daemonic." If that were the case, a daemon would have to exist even before it was supposedly generated. 

A soul—especially one that is <term>prophetic: having the power to reveal the future or divine will</term> <note>original: *fatidica*</note>—cannot be generated from things that lack both a soul and the gift of <term>prophecy</term> <note>original: *vaticinio*</note>. Something more excellent cannot be procreated from something inferior. Nor can any essence or <term>substance: a distinct, self-existing reality</term> <note>original: *substantia*</note> be established from the movements of the soul or from bodily forces, which are neither substances nor essences themselves. 

Likewise, nothing that is "seeded" through the process of generation possesses any quality greater than what was given to it by its primary generating cause. Therefore, since neither the body nor the soul possesses prophecy in and of itself, the soul cannot procreate a prophetic daemon out of its own movements and physical components. Perhaps someone might say that daemons are not generated by us, but that they are [assigned] to living beings in a set order...

### *On Divine and Human Dreams*

Porphyry <note>Porphyry of Tyre (c. 234–305 AD), a scholar whose "Letter to Anebo" contained the questions that Iamblichus is answering in this text.</note> says that the <term>forewarnings</term> <note>original: *praesagia*</note> of dreams come partly from within ourselves and partly from an external source. Iamblichus argues that they come only from an external source: for we often study and perform specific acts to capture such a forewarning, yet it is not granted; conversely, it is often given to those who are not seeking it. If the effect of dreaming arose from our own nature and human will, it would happen whenever we planned for it. However, it is sent by the gods according to their own judgment—specifically when and how they wish to show the future through their benevolence. An Orphic hymn <note>Ancient Greek religious poems attributed to the mythical Orpheus, often used as authoritative texts in Neoplatonist philosophy.</note> declares the same. Porphyry claims that the cause of prophecy is a certain <term>passion: an impression or state of mind acting upon the soul</term> <note>original: *passionem*</note> of the soul. True <term>prophecy</term> <note>original: *vaticinium*; here meaning the divine gift of foretelling the future or "divination."</note>, however, ought to be entirely stable and ordered, and therefore cannot be involved in a state of <term>passion</term> <note>original: *passio*; in this philosophical context, "passion" refers not to strong emotion, but to the state of being "passive"—acted upon or disturbed by external, physical, or irrational forces.</note>. Likewise, when the soul is prudent and constant, and acts according to its more excellent powers—namely, the intellectual and rational ones—it does not foresee the future. How, then, could it achieve these things when it "suffers" or undergoes disordered and disturbed movements? Furthermore, passion has no innate quality for the contemplation of beings and truth, but rather brings an impediment.

Moreover, if things in the world were themselves constituted by passions, then passion might reach them through a certain similarity. But since they are constituted and governed by <term>reasons and forms</term> <note>original: *rationibus, speciebusque*; the underlying logic and ideal structures that Neoplatonists believed governed the universe.</note>, certainly <term>foreknowledge</term> <note>original: *praenotio*</note> is something entirely different and alien to all passions. Again, passion only feels present things. Since, therefore, prophecy also reaches the future, it is not situated in passion.

**Porphyry** <note>Porphyry of Tyre, whose skeptical questions regarding the mechanics of religion Iamblichus is answering.</note> says that prophecy is a certain passion arising in the <term>imagination</term> <note>original: *phantasia*</note>, originating either from our own thoughts, or by the instinct of the bodily nature within us, or occurring in a similar way to how prophecy happens to the <term>frenzied</term> <note>original: *phreneticis*; referring to those in a state of delirium or clinical madness.</note>. To support this, he points to signs: that in the state of prophecy, the imagination indeed acts vehemently, while the senses are meanwhile occupied and restrained. Likewise, that [incense] smokes... <note>original catchword: *migat*, completing *suffumigat* (smokes/fumigates), referring to the ritual use of incense to induce states of trance.</note>

The **universe** <term>universum</term> does indeed contain traces of divination everywhere, though they are not everywhere clear. Just as the image of the **Good** itself presents God in all things, so too is there some trace of divination in everything.

...by human strength and art combined. For that which is made by man is inferior to man; and that which is made in this way, such as an <term>image</term> <note>original: *idolum*; in this context, it refers to a man-made ritual object or a mere likeness, which Iamblichus considers a "shadow" compared to a true divine presence.</note>, is a kind of shadowing, appearing rather than truly existing, and even as it is being made, it immediately vanishes. Truly, God the <term>Craftsman</term> <note>original: *opifex*; the divine architect or Demiurge who shapes the universe.</note> of the world does not fabricate all things through celestial motions, nor through particular matter, nor through powers divided in such a way. Instead, he brings worlds into being through intelligences, through divine pleasures, through immaterial forms, and through the eternal, super-mundane <note>Existing above or beyond the physical world.</note> soul as well as the soul of the world itself. 

While a maker of such images is indeed said to work through the stars, he does not work through them in the way it might appear. For although there are innumerable powers within the celestial gods, the lowest of all is their natural power. Within that very natural power of the celestial gods are <term>seminal reasons</term> <note>original: *rationes seminales*; these are the formative "seed-principles" or blueprints that govern how life and physical forms develop in the material world.</note>—that is, the generative principles of forms—as well as certain other immobile principles that precede the seminal ones in that same place, which are the coordinating principles of forms. Therefore, the authority of both types of principles precedes the whole of generation. Following these, there are qualities, powers, and motions within the celestial bodies, and from these come the "outpourings" <note>original: *defluxus*; the downward flow of astral influence from the heavens to the earth.</note> which, governed by those higher principles, dominate the entire arrangement of worldly things:

<summary>Iamblichus distinguishes between human artifice, which only creates fleeting imitations, and divine creation, which shapes the world through eternal intellectual principles and "seminal reasons."</summary>

### ON THE MYSTERIES.

...generation. Indeed, the lowest power of the celestial beings, as I have said, guides the generation of earthly things. Many arts—such as medicine, gymnastics, and agriculture—namely, whatever works in cooperation with the operations of nature, utilize the qualities and powers transmitted to these lower realms through **celestial emanations** <note>original: *defluxus cœleſtes*; refers to the Neoplatonic idea of divine power "flowing down" from the stars to the earth like light or water.</note>. And yet, even the **maker of images** <note>original: *idolo-ficus*; someone who constructs ritual statues or idols.</note> himself draws some generative portion from these celestial emanations, however small and weak it may be. 

For he does not utilize the actual motions of the heavens, nor the very powers inherent within them, nor the powers naturally established around those celestial motions. He cannot even reach them; instead, he concerns himself with certain powers that have flowed down from their nature to the very last degree, having fallen to the lowest place in the world. 

He certainly employs a kind of art, but it is not a pious or **deific** <term>deific</term> <note>original: *deifica*; an art that makes one like a god or connects one directly to the divine.</note> art. These lowest celestial powers, working in concert upon some particular **matter** <note>original: *materia*; the physical substance used to make the idol.</note>, are able to transmute, transfigure, and transform it in various ways. Furthermore, they facilitate a transposition from one thing to another among those powers that reside in particular objects. 

When someone fabricates images of this kind from many materials and under celestial influences, then the variety of celestial actions on the one hand, and the material powers gathered on the other, does indeed produce...

Man, being superior and born from superior origins, ought not to devote himself to the fabrication of idols, which are not truly **ensouled** <note>original: *animata*; possessing a soul or life-force.</note> but are merely inflated with a certain outward show of life. They are held together not by an internal or true **harmony** <note>original: *harmonia*; here referring to the mathematical and spiritual order that binds a living being together</note>, but by one that is external and feigned, destined to last only a short time. Nor do they possess anything genuine or legitimate, being fashioned solely by human art. Indeed, only that which is simple and uniform in their action or composition carries any weight within them. 

Thus, they are greatly deficient, for they are heaped together from qualities that are vastly diverse and contrary. They lack any perfected power because this multitude of emanations is captured from many different sources and blended into something external that is utterly meager and weak. Nor do these idols possess any stability; indeed, they vanish more quickly than the reflections seen in mirrors.
