<meta>This page continues Iamblichus's rebuttal to Porphyry's skepticism regarding theurgy. On the previous page, Iamblichus argued that human-made idols, even those constructed according to astrological timings, lack true divine power because they are made of base matter.</meta>

-># IAMBLICHUS<-

...possess nothing of divine power. There are no powers within matter that serve as the fundamental elements of **daemons** <note>original: *daemonum*; in the Neoplatonic tradition, these are intermediary spirits between gods and humans, acting as messengers or guardians.</note>; nor can these beings be generated from individual physical bodies. On the contrary, it is by the daemons that these bodies are generated and preserved. Nor is man able, through his own mechanical devices, to procreate the very forms of daemons; rather, it is we who have been formed by the daemons in accordance with our physical bodies. It must not be thought that from the union of the physical elements there flows together any sort of multitude or composition that possesses a power inherent to daemons. For the daemon himself—existing simply, uniformly, and independently—gathers diverse elements into a single whole and generates composite things from them; and whatever degree of persistence or stability exists within those things, he himself bestows it. It is not fitting to call **idols** <note>original: *idola*; here referring to man-made ritual statues or "simulacra."</note> daemons. For the creator of idols is one thing, but a great daemon—a leader of other daemons—is quite another. Furthermore, the very substance of daemons is distinct from the **phantasms** <note>original: *phantasmatis*; illusory images or mental shadows that lack true substance.</note> of idols, concerning which you yourself, **Porphyry** <note>Porphyry of Tyre (c. 234–305 AD), a philosopher whose letter of doubts regarding Egyptian and Chaldean religion prompted this defense by Iamblichus.</note>, admit that neither a god nor any daemon can be dragged down from above. Therefore, this craft of making idols, being devoid of both god and daemon, brings about neither **prophecy** <note>original: *vaticinium*; the foretelling of the future through divine oracles.</note> nor any sacred work.

### ON THE MYSTERIES.

**Porphyry** <note>Porphyry of Tyre (c. 234–305 AD), the philosopher who wrote a critical letter to the Egyptian priest Anebo, questioning the foundations of theurgy.</note> mentions the opinion of those who say that all **prophecies** <note>original: *vaticinia*; refers to divinely inspired predictions or oracles.</note> are infused into us by **evil daemons** <note>original: *daemonibus malis*; in this context, these are lower, deceptive spirits rather than the higher, protective intermediary beings.</note>, whose nature is deceitful, multiform, and ever-changing. These spirits pretend to be gods, or sublime daemons, or the souls of the dead; by meeting us through this deception, they provide us with false portents. Porphyry mentions this opinion even though he does not approve of it, nonetheless consulting **the Egyptian** <note>Referring to Anebo, an Egyptian priest to whom Porphyry addressed his inquiries.</note> about this matter as well. 

**Iamblichus** <note>Iamblichus (c. 245–325 AD), the author of "On the Mysteries," who wrote this defense of ritual magic and religious tradition under the pseudonym "Abammon."</note> also condemns the practice of mentioning profane things in the midst of sacred ones, and then recounts the **mysteries** <note>original: *mysteria*; the secret rites and hidden knowledge of the divine.</note> which the Egyptian heard from the **prophets of the Chaldeans** <note>original: *prophetis Chaldaeorum*; the "Chaldeans" were ancient Mesopotamian sages whose "Chaldean Oracles" were a primary source of wisdom for later Neoplatonist philosophers.</note>, which are as follows: 

The Gods give true blessings to those good men who have been purified through **sacrifices** <note>original: *sacrificia*; the ritual acts intended to align the human soul with the divine order.</note>. The Gods associate with such men and, through this holy interaction, they drive far away from them all wickedness and **passion** <note>original: *passionem*; here meaning irrational emotional disturbances or suffering that distorts the soul’s clarity.</note>, warding off dark spirits with their own splendor. For just as darkness slips away before the sun, evil spirits flee when the light of the gods enters. They can no longer disturb the pious practitioner of sacrifice, who is now free from all wickedness, perversity, and passion. 

However, those who are destructive, and who meanwhile insolently intrude upon sacred rites against the proper custom and order of the ceremonies—these men are unable to reach the gods, surely because of the weakness of their actions and their lack of power. Instead, because of certain impurities, they are both kept away from the gods and [rendered subject] to evil daemons

To answer the question: commands and forceful orders are directed toward those **spirits** <term>spiritus: in this Neoplatonic context, these are lower-level entities or natural forces that lack independent rational will</term> who neither use their own **reason** <note>original: *ratio*</note> nor possess the principle of judgment and **discernment** <note>original: *discretio*</note>. The practitioner invokes them, therefore, as superiors, because he seeks to draw forces that contribute to the whole from the entire world that surrounds us, and apply them toward specific, individual matters. Yet he commands them, again, as if they were inferiors, because our **intellectual** <note>original: *intellectualis*; referring to the higher, spiritual part of the human soul</note> nature is more excellent than that which lacks intellect—even if those spirits have a wider field of action in the physical world.

The **priest** <note>original: *sacerdos*; referring to the theurgist or practitioner of divine works</note>, therefore, does not summon a multitude of spirits as if he were absent from them, nor does he mandate that something be performed by a separate or segregated being—as humans are accustomed to do among themselves. Rather, there is a certain single and identical action of **divine fire** <note>In Neoplatonic theurgy, 'divine fire' is the purifying, animating power of the gods that effects the ritual's goal</note>, which is ready of its own accord, present, and acting out of itself; it shines forth and operates. It works in the same way through all things simultaneously—both through those things that are passed down from the source to others, and through those things that are able to receive something from that source. 

Therefore, those divine works fulfilled in the sacred rites are not accomplished through the opposition of one thing to another (as is the case with things subject to birth and decay), nor are they summoned through the mere difference of the one calling or moving them, nor are they conducted by mechanical motion as human affairs are. Instead, the whole is fulfilled by identity, union, and consensus; and with all **difference**

# ON THE MYSTERIES

...passive things, that very thing which acts, and by whose power the action is performed, is everywhere a certain common and simple thing. *Porphyry* <note>original: *Porphyrius*; a 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher whose "Letter to Anebo" contained the questions Iamblichus is answering here</note> asks why the higher beings often command their worshippers to be just, yet sometimes, when entreated, they seem to inflict injury. *Iamblichus* <note>original: *Iamblichus*; the author and defender of theurgical practice</note> responds that they do not inflict injuries, but rather just punishments. And if perhaps these acts appear unjust, they are not from the gods, but from wicked **daemons** <term>daemon: intermediary spirits between gods and humans; in this context, lower spirits that might be susceptible to human manipulation or malevolence</term>. 

The gods perceive not just a certain part of this life, but the whole; and not this life alone, but the entire life of the **soul** <note>original: *animae*</note> from age to age. Thus, according to the merits contracted in a previous life, they often punish in a subsequent one, whether they are asked to punish or not. Meanwhile, we, who see nothing beyond the present, believe that adversities sometimes happen to us without merit; yet we often suffer in this life what we have already inflicted in another, and what we do now, we will eventually suffer. 

Furthermore, many sins of men are hidden from us, which are not at all hidden from the gods. Similarly, we define **justice** <note>original: *iustitia*</note> as each person doing their own duty according to the current laws of their country. But the gods define it far more broadly, looking toward the whole order of the universe, and looking especially to that principle by which souls are led to the gods; from that basis, they carry out their judgment. ### ON THE MYSTERIES ###

...they share in a certain material **poverty** <note>original: *indigentiam*; the lack of fullness or perfection inherent in matter</note> of nature: finally, in individual things, there is a **formlessness** <note>original: *informitatem*; a state of lacking divine shape or order</note>; and those things that are united in the "wholes" are divided in the "particulars." Moreover, certain small parts are corrupted so that the "wholes," which are constituted according to nature, might be preserved; and some parts are crushed and pressed, while the "wholes" arising from them remain meanwhile free from **suffering** <note>original: *passio*; in this philosophical context, it refers to the state of being acted upon or undergoing change, rather than emotional pain</note>. 

Whenever some **sorcerer** <note>original: *veneficus*; literally a "poison-maker," but used here for one who uses illicit magic</note> brings down a calamity upon someone through his imprecations—clearly using certain natural and bodily powers for this purpose—the **transmission** <note>original: *traditio*; the downward flow of influence or energy from the heavens to the earth</note> of such an action indeed comes from above without choice or any inherent wickedness. Even though the **evildoer** <note>original: *maleficus*</note> using this very thing deflects the transmission toward things that are entirely contrary and evil, the transmission itself and the action descending from above is moved by a certain "sympathy" because of the likeness [of parts], though it is stirred by the "passions" of opposites. 

The evildoer, however, through his own choice, drags that which has been transmitted toward evil, contrary to what is just. Now indeed, the transmission itself operates according to the single **harmony of the world** <note>original: *harmonia mundi*; the Neoplatonic idea that the universe is a single, vibrating, interconnected organism</note>, so that even those things that are very distant nonetheless cooperate. If someone, meanwhile perceiving this, strives to lead parts or "lots" of the whole unfairly into other parts, thereby causing harm, the universe is not the cause of such damage. Rather, it is the human abuse that transgresses the order of the universe, the law—

Finally, that which descends from heaven for a good purpose is here often transferred to evil. The world is **one living being** <note>original: *vnum animal*; a central Neoplatonic and Stoic concept that the universe is a single, interconnected organism</note> in which the parts, although distant in location, are nevertheless drawn toward one another because of their single nature. By its very nature, this kind of attraction and **appetite** <note>original: *appetitus*; a natural impulse, desire, or instinctual drive toward an object</note> can be increased beyond the ordinary order by a certain art. Indeed, the reconciling force implanted in all things is good, and is everywhere the cause of **entanglement** <note>original: *implexionis*; the complex interweaving of various elements in the cosmos</note>, communion, harmony, mutual love, and the worldly **union** <note>original: *vnionis*; the Neoplatonic concept of distinct things being brought into a single unity</note>—all of which exist and occur by the command of the Sustainer.

And thus, an appetite for necessary union—which is naturally moderated—is rendered unrestrained by these mechanical means, as Art both provides the matter especially conducive to **procreation** <note>original: *genituræ*; the act of generation, birth, or creating new life</note> and mixes together diverse natural forces into one. By this mixing, Art rules at its own discretion and brings about encounters for the purpose of generation. 

Furthermore, since there are in herbs and stones both dissipative and congregative forces—and these are far greater in higher things and natures—the drive toward union can certainly be intensified by employing such things. Even without the work of Art, love can be kindled and attraction can be triggered by these very things. We have discovered that **demons** <note>original: *dæmones*; in this context, these are not "demons" in the modern sense but intermediary spirits who manage the laws of nature and the material world</note>...

### *On Sacrifices: From where they derive their power, and what they contribute.* ###

The question is asked: by what logic are sacrifices appropriate for the higher beings <note>original: *superis*; the celestial gods</note>, how do they benefit mankind, and what effect do they have in the world? The World Soul <note>original: *Anima mundi*; the spiritual essence that permeates and animates the entire universe</note> and the celestial beings, by virtue of their presence in their own bodies, neither receive passions from them nor are they distracted from the higher Intellects <note>original: *intelligentiis*; the pure, immaterial spiritual forms that exist above the physical realm</note>. For the condition of universal things is not the same as that of particular things, nor is the state of primary causes <note>original: *principiorum*</note> equal to that of their effects. 

To feed upon bodies that were once joined to a soul undoubtedly brings a burden and defilement upon us; it creates a leaning in the soul through which it may melt into and succumb to pleasures, and it produces many other diseases in the soul. But the vapor exhaling from animals, and the sacred incense <note>original: *suffumigatio*; the ritual burning of substances to create smoke</note> when correctly performed, does no harm to the gods or to worldly and universal causes. For the ritual vapor does not contain or organize the higher beings toward itself; rather, the vapor is contained by them, and it is coordinated with the universe as well as with the gods. Therefore, by the command of those higher beings, the ritual can be fitted to them and agree harmoniously with them. 

The religious <note>original: *religiosi*; those dedicated to sacred rites and the priestly life</note> therefore abstain from eating animals, yet not because the gods could be defiled by the vapors of those animals. ### *The reason for sacrifices and their utility.*

Porphyry thinks that sacrifices are offered to the gods for this reason: so that we may honor them with such gifts, just as we often do for our superiors <note>original: *maiores*; literally "greater ones," referring to those higher in social or familial rank.</note>. He also believes we offer them to return thanks for the blessings received from the divine, giving back good things in exchange for good things. Iamblichus argues that this reasoning is drawn from common human social customs and is not appropriate for the nature of the gods, which transcends human ways <note>original: *mores*; customs, habits, or character.</note> beyond all measure. However, such explanations do not fully demonstrate the true, great power <note>original: *efficaciam*; efficacy or the ability to produce a desired effect.</note> of sacrifices—a power, I say, without which we are not delivered from plague, famine, or scarcity, nor do we obtain timely rains. Indeed, it is through this power that we achieve the purification and perfection of our souls, and gain freedom from this realm of generation <note>original: *generationis prouincia*; the physical world of birth, decay, and constant change, from which the soul seeks to escape.</note>. Therefore, one will not much approve of these methods based on your reasoning, as if you had assigned a worthy cause for their effects. And even if one were to approve them, he would surely accept them only as secondary...

<meta>catchword: place [loco]</meta>

<summary>Iamblichus critiques Porphyry’s view that sacrifices are merely social gifts or tokens of gratitude, arguing instead that they possess a divine power necessary for both physical survival and the soul's spiritual liberation.</summary>
<keywords>Porphyry, Iamblichus, sacrifice, divine nature, purification, realm of generation, efficacy of ritual</keywords>

--- Page 120 ---
<meta>This page continues the transition from the previous page's critique of Porphyry's view on sacrifice. Iamblichus is arguing that sacrifices are not merely social gifts or mechanical reactions within nature, but are linked to higher divine causes.</meta>

<page-num>114</page-num>
->IAMBLICHUS<-

...placed as if they were consequences, and joined in a secondary manner to the primary and most ancient causes of such works. Therefore, we seek the reason why sacrifices have efficacy <note>original: *efficaciam*; the ability to produce a desired effect or magical result.</note> in bringing things about, and from where they are joined to the principal gods, the causes, and the principles of those things which occur. 

Someone might say that because the world is a single living being <note>original: *animal unum*; Iamblichus refers to the "World Soul" or *Anima Mundi*, a concept where the universe is viewed as a single, interconnected organism.</note> and possesses one and the same life everywhere, there is a community of similar forces, or even a distance between dissimilar ones, or certainly a certain fitness of the agent toward the patient <note>original: *agentis ad patiens*; the relationship between something that acts and something that is acted upon.</note> to move similar things, adapted in the same way; while indeed it flows according to a single sympathy <note>original: *compassionem*; here used in the philosophical sense of "cosmic sympathy," where parts of the universe resonate with each other without physical contact.</note> even from the most distant thing to the most distant, as if these too were close together. 

For even among these things, the very community of life is an equal distribution of this sort; indeed, whoever says this speaks the truth, and it is something that necessarily follows regarding sacrifices, yet the true mode of sacrifices is not demonstrated in this way. For the very essence of the gods is placed neither in nature nor in natural necessities, by which obligation they might be stirred up by natural passions <note>original: *passionibus*; not "emotions" in the modern sense, but "undergoings" or being affected by external physical forces.</note>, or moved by powers extended through all of nature. Rather, the divine essence is determined according to itself, standing outside of these things, having nothing in common with them, whether in essence, power, or in action and passion simultaneously.

### ON THE MYSTERIES.

To the previous explanation, some add a certain congruence <note>original: *congruentiam*; a harmonious correspondence or fittingness between different levels of reality.</note> in lower things toward those that are higher. And therefore, they attribute the efficacy <note>original: *efficaciam*; the power to produce a desired result.</note> of sacrifices to this correspondence; for example, they say that in the Crocodile, the number six <note>original: *hexagonarius numerus*; refers to the number six, which ancient observers associated with solar cycles and the crocodile's behavior.</note> corresponds with the sun. Again, in the Dog and the Dog-headed Baboon <note>original: *Cynocephalo*; the baboon was sacred to the Egyptian god Thoth and was believed to react physically to the moon's phases.</note>, there are certain physical reasons and powers shared with the Moon. 

Likewise, in other material species—as in sacred animals—colors, figures, and forms may match some of the higher beings; even certain limbs of an animal, such as the heart of a rooster <note>original: *cor galli*; the rooster was a solar symbol, and its heart was often used in ancient ritual practices.</note>, and other similar natural things used in sacrifices, are the causes of wonderful works. From the previous assignment of causes, however, the divine cause is not being assigned—for the divine is entirely supernatural—nor is it moved by natural motions. Instead, what is being assigned is a certain natural power contained within matter and bodies; therefore, it is excited by corporeal motions and material things, and again calmed—naturally, I mean—along with those things which pertain to nature. 

If indeed anything of this sort follows from the sacrifices, it is joined to the preceding causes as a co-cause <note>original: *concausa*; a secondary or contributing factor that assists the primary cause but is not the sole reason for the effect.</note>, without which the work would not occur. It is better, therefore, to say that the wonderful effects of sacrifices proceed, as if from a primary cause, from a certain friendship <note>original: *amicitia*; in a Neoplatonic context, this refers to "sympathy" or the attraction between like things in the cosmos.</note>, an accommodation, and a conciliating disposition...

...as creators to their creations, and parents to their offspring. When, therefore, under the guidance and leadership of this common principle, we take some animal or other living creature born from the earth which sincerely and exactly preserves the will and purpose of its creator <note>original: *opificis*; referring to the Demiurge or the divine craftsman who shaped the world.</note>, then through such an object we properly stir the creative cause that is set over this mixed nature. 

However, since there are many such causes—some of which preside directly and intimately, like daimons <note>original: *daemonia*; in Neoplatonism, these are not "demons" but intermediate spirits that act as messengers between gods and humans.</note>, while others are ranked higher than these, such as the divine causes in their proper order—and since one most ancient cause <note>The "One" or the supreme source of all existence.</note> presides over all of these, it follows that in a **perfect sacrifice**, all these causes are moved in their proper sequence. 

According to the order which each has been allotted, they are intimately accommodated and (so to speak) appropriated to the sacrifice through a certain kindred condition. But if the sacrifice happens to be **imperfect**, it rises only to a certain level but does not transcend any further. This is why many people believe that sacrifices are made only to "good daimons," and many others believe they reach only the "lowest powers of the gods." Others still think they are directed toward the worldly or earthly powers of daimons or gods. 

While these people are indeed explaining a *part* of what happens in sacrifices, they remain ignorant of the total power of these rites and all the benefits they provide, which extend deep into the heart of the entire divine realm. But we, on the other hand...

...we admit, and at the same time understand, that natural things—and those things which, as if within a single living organism <note>The Neoplatonic concept of the *Anima Mundi* or World Soul, where the entire universe is viewed as one living being.</note>, are moved in relation to one another according to natural fitness, or sympathy <note>original: *compassionem*</note>, or reaction <note>original: *repassionem*</note>—are accepted merely as subordinates. Since in a **perfect sacrifice** the subsequent causes are moved in their proper order along with the highest and creative causes, a common benefit then flows from all of them into the whole of **generation** <note>original: *generationem*; the realm of physical birth, change, and material existence.</note>. Sometimes this benefit reaches entire cities, peoples, and nations of every kind—whether in larger or smaller territories—and sometimes these good things reach individual households or each particular person. ...since their divine works are prepared so abundantly, why would he <note>Referring to the Creator or the natural order</note> want additional nourishment to be provided by humans for the **daimons** <note>intermediary spirits between the divine and the human</note> alone? Therefore, if we nourished the daimons, we would also be their creators, and we would be superior to them. But the reality is quite the opposite: for they themselves nourish us, and everywhere the superior nourishes the inferior, just as the celestial things nourish the terrestrial.

The soul indeed is perfected and nourished by the **Intellect** <note>original: *intellectu*; referring to the Neoplatonic *Nous*, the divine realm of pure thought</note>, and it in turn perfects nature. Furthermore, the offering of sacrifices through fire consumes the matter, and assimilates it entirely to itself; it does not make itself similar to the matter, but leads it back to the divine, celestial, and immaterial fire, and in no way does it sink down toward matter and the realm of generation.

For if it were necessary for there to be an exhalation of vapors from the sacrifices, it would be necessary for there to be material nourishment and for the matter to remain intact. In that way, a more abundant influx would come to those intended to receive it. But as it is, all the matter is burned and consumed, and is thoroughly transformed into the very purity and subtlety of fire; this indicates the exact opposite of what you yourself were saying. For the higher beings are free from **suffering** <note>original: *passionis*; in the philosophical sense of being "acted upon" or experiencing change/emotion</note>, since it pleases them that matter be dispersed by fire...

Therefore, it is impossible for nourishment for these spirits to be produced from elemental essence, as that is entirely foreign to them.

In the same way, it releases us from the bonds of generation <note>original: "generationis," referring to the cycle of birth, decay, and the physical world</note>, makes us like the gods, and renders us fit for the friendship of the gods, raising our material nature toward the immaterial...

<center>h 5</center>

...lifts up our material nature. This common theory of sacrifices is, I believe, sufficient for those who are gifted and able to investigate the specific details of each sacrifice based on a general rule. However, to accommodate those of a slower intellect, we shall add certain specific points, bringing clearer arguments into the light. Indeed, the best starting point for these matters is the one that clarifies the sequence of sacrifices as being connected to the order of the gods.

We categorize some gods as material and others as immaterial. Material gods are those who encompass matter within themselves and organize it; immaterial gods are those who are entirely and utterly separated from matter. Therefore, according to the priestly art <term>priestly art: often called 'theurgy,' this refers to ritual practices intended to invoke the presence of the gods or achieve union with them</term>, it is proper to begin sacrifices with the material gods, for otherwise there is no path open for an ascent to the immaterial gods. These material gods have a certain communion with matter, insofar as they preside over it and dwell upon it <note>original: "incubāt," implying a protective or animating presence, like a bird brooding over an egg</note>. They also rule over the processes that occur within matter, such as division, the impact of forces, change, birth, decay <note>original: "corruptioni," referring to the natural breaking down of physical things</note>, and all material bodies. 

If anyone wishes to worship these gods correctly, they must offer worship in accordance with the gods' nature and their rank; I mean that one must offer material worship to material beings. For in this way, we—as whole beings—shall be led through all things toward them as whole beings, into a proper intimacy and kin-

...and we shall offer to them the worship that is fitting for their nature. For even if they are fundamentally separate from matter, they are nonetheless present with it at the same time; and though they hold matter within an immaterial power, they nevertheless exist together with it.

Indeed, those things that are governed are not foreign to their governors, just as those things that are adorned are not foreign to their adorners. Moreover, things that serve as instruments are easily adapted through specific proportions to those who use them. Therefore, it is foreign to employ matter in sacrifices to the immaterial gods, but it is entirely fitting for all the material gods.

It is worthwhile, in addition to these things, to consider the dual condition of our own life. At certain times, we become entirely soul, situated outside the body and elevated in mind; together with the whole company of immaterial gods, we raise ourselves through the sublime heights. At other times, however, we are bound to the earthly body and are corporeal, clearly encompassed by matter. Similarly, there will be a twofold method of divine worship. One will be simple, incorporeal, and pure from all generation <term>generation: in this philosophical context, "generation" refers to the realm of birth, death, and physical change, as opposed to the eternal and unchanging divine realm</term>...

->### IAMBLICHUS ###<-

...set apart <note>original: *segregati*. This completes the word from the bottom of the previous page.</note>, can they confer anything to us for the purpose of driving away poverty and sterility, or for bringing abundance, or for leading us to other necessities of life? Not at all. For those who are liberated from all things do not handle gifts of this kind. 

If someone were to say that those immaterial gods encompass in themselves other immaterial gods, and that they contain their gifts according to one primary cause, he would certainly be speaking of a certain abundance of divine bounty descending from that high place to lower levels. But no one should be permitted to say that those gods, in handling these matters, perform actions or manage things in close proximity to human life. 

For the administration of things here <note>referring to the material world</note> is divided and particular, and it is carried out with a certain "turning" toward these physical matters; it is neither entirely separated from bodies, nor can it admit a pure and unmixed governance and supervision. Therefore, the mode of sacrificing for such things is appropriate only when it has commerce with bodies and **generation** <term>generation: the natural cycle of birth, change, and decay in the material world</term>, and not the mode of sacrifice which is entirely separated from matter and the body. 

For that which is pure entirely transcends such things and has no proportion <note>or "mathematical relationship"</note> to them. But the power that uses bodies and their forces is most closely related to all such material things; it is able to supply certain prosperous things of life, and to avoid the adversities hanging over us, and...

They fulfill the dispensation of **fate**, and they receive the order of those works dictated by fate, exercising their practical reason only regarding natural things. 

A very few, relying on the supernatural power of the mind, depart from nature and turn themselves toward the separate and unmixed **intellect** <term>intellect: in Neoplatonism, this refers to *Nous*, the higher divine consciousness that exists above the physical world</term>, whereby they become superior to natural powers.

Those, therefore, who are governed by universal nature and lead a life enslaved to their own nature, enjoying the powers of nature, will practice a worship suitable to nature and consistent with bodies moved by nature. ...sacred <note>original: *sacrorum*. This word begins on the previous page. The text describes the "law of sacred rites."</note> rites. Therefore, the law of sacred rites duly distributes like to like, and proceeds from the highest things to the lowest through all the intermediate stages; it applies physical things to physical entities and incorporeal things to incorporeal ones, rendering to each its own proper due. 

However, if a religious seeker attains a supramundane <term>supramundane: *supermundanum*, referring to divine realities that exist beyond the physical universe and the laws of nature</term> deity—though this happens very rarely—this person, being placed alone and apart from bodies and matter, pursues such a mode of worship through a supramundane power, being united with the supramundane gods. 

But because such an attainment is barely achieved by one person at the very end of their sacred service <term>sacred service: *sacerdotij*, the path of the priest or theurgist</term>, it is not fitting to establish it as a common law for everyone at the beginning or middle of their religious life. For these practitioners perform worship that is, in some manner, corporeal <note>original: *corporeum*. Iamblichus argues that because humans have bodies, our initial religious acts must involve physical elements like incense or sacrifices.</note>. 

Therefore, anyone skilled in the sacred arts will admit that worship of the higher beings must be offered neither partially nor imperfectly, but in a manner that is appropriate and complete. Since, before the gods are present and descend to earth, all the powers underlying them are set in motion and precede them like forerunners and a ceremonial procession, anyone who does not distribute to all what is fitting for each, nor accords to each their own particular honor, will fail to attain the presence of the gods themselves.

While this one thing is missing, the sacred work lacks its proper structure and integrity.

What then? The present discussion, however, does not establish laws for such a man—for he is superior to the law—but rather for those who stand in need of law, it enacts these rules of sacred rites for the present: the multitude of divine powers is like a world, having many ranks **working together** <note>original: *conspirantes*, literally "breathing together," implying a cosmic harmony</note> into a single order. Similarly, **sacrifices** <note>original: *sacrificia*</note> ought to possess an order of numbers likewise harmonizing into a single arrangement, so that each element corresponds rightly to the deities. In the same way, the things around us and within us are manifold; they should not correspond to the divine causes of our circumstances from only one part, but should respond congruously from all parts, and thus [lead] to the supreme **ascents**...

Around him, many gods and angels revolve, and under him, throughout whatever nations exist on earth, some divinity has obtained a **prefecture** <term>prefecture: *praefectura*; an administrative jurisdiction or oversight exercised by a higher power</term> and a common province. Likewise, from that same source, a specific divinity is assigned to each individual temple.

In the same way, for the sacred rites which we perform for the gods, some god is the observer and governor; for those performed for the angels, an angel; for those to the **demons** <note>original: *daemones*; in this Neoplatonic context, these are not "evil spirits" but intermediary beings between humans and gods</note>, a demon. And in other cases, following the same pattern according to their own kind, a perfect being has obtained a kindred prefecture. Since, therefore, we handle sacrifices under the watchful eyes of the divinities who are the authors of the sacred rites, we ought to revere the laws of divine holiness and the legitimate sacrifices; and for that reason, we should place our hope in them, because under the leadership of the divinities and the gods...

Since adoration is of such a nature and maintains such a connection with sacrifices, it is evident that the ultimate goal of sacrifices shares in a contact with the **Demiurge** <term>Demiurge: *opificis*; the divine craftsman or creator-god who fashions the material world</term>. It shows how prayer is effective, how it brings about union, and how it maintains a common bond granted by the gods. It further demonstrates how adoration and sacrifice mutually strengthen each other, bestowing a power upon one another that results in the wondrous effects of religion. 

From this, it appears again that the priestly discipline and its ritual operations possess a **harmony** <note>original: *conspirationem*; literally a "breathing together," implying an organic, unified functioning</note> among their various parts no less than an animal possesses among its limbs. Just as an animal cannot complete its natural function through any single part without the cooperation of all the others, so too must these sacred acts work in unison.

# ON THE MYSTERIES

<page-num>139</page-num>

Iamblichus resolves the matter in this way. The **prophets** <note>original: *vates*; refers to the inspired priests or seers of the ancient mysteries</note> command the **initiate** <note>original: *spectatorem*; literally "the viewer," referring to one who observes or participates in the divine mysteries</note> of divine matters not to touch a lifeless body that has not been consecrated; however, they permit the touching of that which is being consecrated. Furthermore, they forbid even the looking upon human bodies which the soul has already abandoned. For a certain trace, or image, or manifestation of divine life is extinguished in the human body by death; however, no religious law forbids the touching of the dead bodies of other animals, since they did not share in a more divine life while they lived. 

Furthermore, insofar as we rise up toward the **immaterial gods** <note>original: *immateriales deos*; higher divine beings who exist entirely apart from physical matter</note>, it is beneficial not to have touched such a body; but insofar as we strive to approach the **material gods** <note>original: *materiales*; gods who preside over the physical world and its elements</note>, it will frequently be beneficial to touch them. For it is through animals that we are accustomed to summon gods of this kind: those, clearly, who preside over such animals, and especially those who govern them closely and, as it were, through a certain kindred condition. 

Likewise, for men who are enclosed in matter, bodies deprived of life inflict a certain **stain** <note>original: *maculam*; ritual defilement or impurity</note>—namely, that which is not living upon that which is living, the filthy upon the pure, and that which is deprived of its state upon that which possesses it. The dead body affects the one who has the potential for dying because of a certain common **affinity** <note>original: *habitudinem*; a natural relationship or shared quality</note> between them. But to a **demon** <note>original: *dæmoni*; in this context, a benevolent intermediary spirit, not a modern "demon"</note> who is entirely incorporeal and **impassible** <term>impassible: *impassibili*; a philosophical term for a being that cannot be affected, changed, or harmed by external material things</term>, such bodies do no harm at all.

### *On divination through animals.*

When **divination** <note>original: *vaticinium*; the practice of foretelling the future through supernatural means</note> is conducted through the bodies of sacred animals, such as **hawks** <note>original: *asturum*; likely referring to the goshawk or hawk, which was sacred to Horus in Egyptian tradition</note>, one must not think that the gods themselves approach these things—that is to say, the universal providers do not stoop to a divided, particular, material, and proportional care for individual animals. 

Rather, it is **daemons** <note>original: *daemones*; in this context, intermediate spirits that act as messengers or administrators between the high gods and the physical world, not "demons" in the modern evil sense</note>, and specifically those who are highly "divided" <note>meaning spirits assigned to specific, localized tasks rather than universal ones</note>, being distributed among each individual species of animal, who have been allotted the immediate care and **governance** <note>original: *praefecturam*</note> of animals. For these spirits have obtained a leadership that is not entirely self-sufficient or free from matter. Therefore, they are accustomed to making use of such instruments in a fitting manner. 

Thus, in order that we might obtain this kind of divination from these daemons through animals, it is necessary to prepare for them a **seat** <note>original: *sedem*; a ritual "dwelling" or medium through which a spirit can act</note> of such a kind through which they may be observed among men and make use of us. This seat must be incorporeal, so that the incorporeal daemons may be present to us through it. This seat will therefore be the **soul** of such animals, now released from the body. 

For insofar as this soul is also in some way separated from the body, it is compatible with the nature of daemons; and yet it is also compatible with us because of a certain kinship of life. Therefore, acting as a middle-ground, the soul serves the daemon who presides over it to suggest a **prophetic sign** <note>original: *praesagium*</note> to man...

[to be revealed] to us, and to declare the commands of the **daemon** <note>original: *daemonis*; an intermediary spirit between gods and humans</note>, and it reconciles us with that daemon. But the soul, when it makes use of this kind of **prophecy** <note>original: *vaticinium*; specifically the act of foretelling through signs</note>, does not only hear or receive the prophecy, but it also contributes a significant amount from its own nature toward the execution of the tasks required by these works. For the soul is moved and cooperates, and it simultaneously foresees the future through a certain **sympathetic necessity** <note>original: *compatientem necessitatem*; the idea that because all things in the universe are connected, one part can "feel" or react to changes in another</note>. 

But this kind of prophecy is very far removed from the divine and the true kind; it concerns only small and fleeting matters. These are things situated within "divided" nature <note>referring to the physical world where things are separate and distinct, unlike the unified divine realm</note>, and whatever things are currently swept up together in the realm of **generation** <note>original: *generationem*; the physical world of birth, death, and constant change</note>. These things offer certain impressions of themselves to those who are capable of receiving them, and they inflict various **passions** <note>original: *passiones*; in this philosophical context, "passions" are not just emotions, but states of being "acted upon" or "affected" by external material forces</note> upon those things which are naturally inclined toward sympathy. 

Therefore, a **foretelling** <note>original: *praesagium*</note> of this kind arises through this shared sympathy. However, a perfect foreknowledge cannot happen through being affected by such passions. For it is that which is immutable and pure in the world which is especially accustomed to grasping the future; whereas that which has commerce with the material, the subject-to-change, and the dark, is instead overwhelmed by ignorance. 

Therefore, we judge this artificial mechanism of foretelling to be neither worthy of the name of legitimate prophecy, nor should it be treated with serious concern, nor should the person using it be believed as if they were a teller of truth.

### *How those who offer prayers used to threaten the daemons.*

**Porphyry** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher and student of Plotinus who often questioned the logic of religious rituals</note> relates that priests were accustomed to using certain violent threats against the higher powers. For instance: “Unless you do as I say,” or conversely, “If you do this thing, I will shatter the heavens,” or “I will expose the hidden things of **Isis** <note>The preeminent Egyptian goddess associated with magic and secrets</note>,” or “I will divulge the secret hidden in the abyss,” or “I will halt the **baris** <note>original: *barim*; a sacred Egyptian boat used in religious processions and the transit of the gods</note>,” or “I will scatter the limbs of **Osiris** to **Typhon** <note>original: *Osiridis Typhoni*; referring to the myth where the chaotic god Typhon/Set tore Osiris into pieces; the priest threatens to repeat this cosmic trauma</note>,” and other similar things.

**Iamblichus** <note>A Syrian Neoplatonist who defended the use of ritual magic (theurgy) as a way to reach the divine</note> adds that these practitioners did not usually direct such threats toward the Sun and Moon, or other celestial beings, as Porphyry believes. Instead, there is a certain class of powers in the world that is greatly “divided” <note>separated from divine unity and entangled with the material world</note>, undiscerning, and reckless. This class receives reason or speech from another and listens to it, but possesses no intelligence of its own; it can distinguish neither truth from falsehood, nor the possible from the impossible.

Therefore, when this class of spirits is provoked by threats, it is immediately stirred up and stunned—precisely because it is naturally agitated by more vehement words. It is then led and drawn along through a certain mindless and unstable **imagination** <note>original: *phantasiam*; here meaning a spirit's capacity to be impressed upon by images or commands without rational thought</note>. Furthermore, the priest often commands and threatens these worldly spirits not through human strength, but through the divine power of the **ineffable sacraments** <note>original: *sacramentorum ineffabilium*; sacred rites or mysteries that are too holy or powerful to be spoken aloud</note>. He himself then...

They have received such an immutable order for themselves because the unchanging order of the gods remains within them. ### An Explanation of the Symbols of Egyptian Theology.

Imitating the very nature of the universe and the craftsmanship <note>original: *fabricam*; the way the gods "build" or "construct" reality</note> of the gods, the Egyptians also display certain images of mystical and hidden notions in the construction of their symbols. Just as nature expresses hidden principles <note>original: *rationes*; referring to the *logoi* or the underlying blueprints of the natural world</note> in visible forms as if through symbols, and the gods explain the truth of the Ideas through manifest images, [so too do the priests]. Since they perceive that all superior beings take delight in the resemblance of inferior things, and moreover desire to be filled with goodness from the higher powers so that they might imitate them as much as possible, they deservedly offer a way of acting that is appropriate to the higher beings to the best of their ability. This occurs when they embed hidden mysteries within manifest symbols, in the interpretation of which one must **dismiss the sounds and receive the sense.**

Therefore, when they name **mud** <note>original: *lutum*; often referring to the primordial slime or the "First Matter" from which the world was formed</note> in their sacred rites, or introduce it into their ceremonies, understand this to mean the body and matter of the world, and the **generative power** <term>generative power: the divine life-force or "virtue" (*virtutem*) that animates physical matter</term> inserted into it, which is, as it were, stirred up alongside it.

Therefore, the god himself remains within himself even above this action, surpassing such sovereignty as one who is holy, venerable, and [established] within himself...

### DE MYSTERIIS.

For names translated into another language do not preserve exactly the same meaning. Instead, there are certain properties peculiar to individual nations which cannot be expressed to other nations through speech. Furthermore, even if we were able to translate the properties of the meanings into another language, they nevertheless do not preserve the same **power** <note>original: *potentiam*; in theurgical terms, this refers to the "efficacy" or ritual "charge" of the spoken sound itself</note> once they have been changed.

...nonetheless, it is permitted for Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a major Neoplatonic philosopher who sought to synthesize all ancient Greek and Egyptian theology into a single logical system.</note> to arrange the levels in this way. In this way, the Egyptian treatise on principles, proceeding from the highest things to the very last, descends from the **One** into the **multitude**.

->## ON THE MYSTERIES<-

...namely, from a derivative essence, which the craftsman <term>craftsman: or Demiurge, the divine intelligence that shapes the physical universe</term>, assuming a vital quality, used to create simple and impassive <term>impassive: unchanging or unable to be affected by external suffering/change</term> spheres. Yet he received the final portion of this essence for the creation of things that are generated and subject to decay <note>original: "generabilia, & corruptibilia corpora"—referring to physical bodies on Earth that are born and eventually die, unlike the eternal stars</note>. With these distinctions made, the doubts you say you have conceived regarding the Egyptian books you have read are easily resolved. 

For those works circulated under the name of Mercury <note>Mercury: the Roman name for the Greek Hermes, specifically referring here to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Egyptian sage to whom many occult and philosophical works were attributed</note> contain Mercurial teachings. Even if they often speak in the style of Greek philosophers, they were translated from the Egyptian language into Greek by men skilled in philosophy. 

I would wish, however, that whoever touches upon the primary causes of worldly things would also declare the ultimate principles. Likewise, I would wish that whoever treats of the planets, the zodiac, the decans <term>decans: 36 groups of stars (small constellations) used in ancient Egyptian astronomy to divide the zodiac</term>, horoscopes, stars, and powerful leaders <note>original: "potentes duces"—referring to the divine beings or "archons" that govern the celestial bodies</note> would hand down the specific distributions of principles. 

Therefore, the doctrines found in the *Salaminiaca* <note>original: "Salaminiacis"—likely a reference to a specific set of Hermetic or astrological texts known in the ancient world</note> contain only a very small part of the Mercurial arrangements. Similarly, those matters discussed concerning the appearances or disappearances of stars, or the waxing or waning of the Moon, hold the lowest place in the Egyptians' assignment of causes. 

Indeed, the Egyptians do not think that all things are merely natural; rather, they distinguish intellectual life and the life of the soul from nature itself. This is true not only in the world at large, but also in human beings,

### *Concerning the judgments of astrologers, and the guardian spirit.*

Porphyry says that if anyone were to know the configuration of their birth <note>original: "figuram natiuitatis"—the natal horoscope or birth chart</note> and the lord of that configuration, they would find their own personal guardian spirit and, through it, be released from the fate dictated by birth. But he adds that it is impossible to know that chart and impossible to find this spirit; he claims that the rules of astronomy and astrology are incomprehensible and uncertain, citing Chaeremon <note>A 1st-century Stoic philosopher and Egyptian priest</note> as a witness. 

Iamblichus, however, asserts that the guardian spirit is neither recognized nor assigned by that birth chart or its planetary power. Otherwise, it would not be able to release us from the fate of birth. Instead, the spirit is granted by a more ancient and higher principle—namely, from the superior gods—at the very moment the soul first inclines toward the realm of the senses <note>the physical world</note> even before conception. Furthermore, we are released from fate not so much through the spirit itself as through the worship of a higher divinity <note>original: "numinis"—a divine power or godhead</note>. 

In truth, those statements by Porphyry are not only inconsistent with themselves, but they also stray from the truth. For the guardian spirit is not assigned to each person solely from the specific configuration of their birth; there is an even more ancient origin. Furthermore, if the spirit were recognized only by these means, the person who identified their natal guardian spirit <note>original: "genesicum... dæmonem"—the spirit associated specifically with the moment of birth or "genesis"</note> would not necessarily become blessed because of it.

Nor can we find our own <term>guardian spirit<note>original: "dæmon"—in Neoplatonic philosophy, a *daimon* is not a "demon" in the modern sense, but a mediating spirit or "genius" that guides an individual's life and connects them to the divine.</note></term> through human arts, but only through divine ones. Each person’s own guardian spirit is not assigned from some particular arrangement of the heavens or the elements, but from the entire arrangement of the world. This happens when the soul descends while the universe is in its specific state, which assigns a specific guardian spirit to the soul as the <term>executor of life<note>original: "executorem vitæ"—the agent responsible for carrying out the destiny or life-path the soul has chosen.</note></term> that the soul has chosen. This spirit joins the soul to the body, cares for the life shared with the body, directs the soul’s own particular life, and constantly provides the foundations for our thoughts. We act according to what this spirit brings to our minds, and it governs us until, having been perfected by sacred rites, we exchange the guardian spirit for a <term>Lord<note>original: "dominum"—referring to a higher deity or a more direct connection to the divine mind that supersedes the intermediary spirit.</note></term>. Then the spirit, yielding to God, either rests from its labor or assists in the same divine work. A personal lot is assigned to the soul as it descends from the whole body of the world, and life is shaped by how it relates to the soul at that moment; that lot is guided and fulfilled by a specific guardian spirit. Therefore, it is impossible to predict certain outcomes, since we cannot grasp the meeting of all causes unless we achieve this through divine inspiration.

There is, therefore, one personal spirit who acts as a private governor for each of us. ### *The Way to Happiness.*

Next, you asked what the way to <term>happiness<note>original: "felicitatem"—representing the Greek "eudaimonia," which implies a state of blessedness or flourishing rather than just a fleeting emotion.</note></term> is, and in what thing happiness itself consists. Just as the essence of evils is the forgetfulness of goods and the deception concerning evil; for that knowledge [of the Good] goes together with the divine. But the latter [forgetfulness], falling away from principles and being repelled, throws itself down to measure the corporeal form.

->*The Conclusion regarding Religion and Happiness among the Egyptians.*<-

The former preserves true life by recalling the soul to the Father; the latter leads man, the ruler of <term>generation<note>original: "genituræ"—the realm of physical birth and becoming, as opposed to the eternal realm of Being.</note></term>, down to that which never remains stable, but is instead tossed about in a perpetual flux. Let this, then, be your first path toward happiness: one that possesses the intellectual fullness of divine union within the power of souls.

The sacred and deifying tradition of happiness is indeed called the "gate" to the <term>Maker-God<note>original: "opificem deum"—the Demiurge or divine craftsman who shaped the universe.</note></term> of all things, or the "place," or the "court" of the Good. It possesses a power that is, first of all, a chaste and sober holiness of the soul—which is far more useful than any sober chastity of the body. Secondly, it offers the adaptation of thought to the actual participation in and vision of the Good, and simultaneously the expulsion of all opposing influences. Thirdly, it provides union with the gods, who are the givers of all good things. 

Once it has joined the soul, individually and properly, both to the parts of the world and to the divine powers diffused through those parts, it then joins the soul to the Maker in His entirety. This grants the soul total harmony with Him and places it outside of all matter, for it is then joined with the alone-eternal <term>Reason<note>original: "ratione"—likely referring to the Logos or the underlying rational structure of the universe.</note></term> of the universe, and is un-

### *Conclusion regarding Religion and Happiness among the Egyptians.*

And this, among the Egyptians, is the goal of the religious and sacred ascent. They believe that the "Good" itself is twofold: one is divine, namely the <term>pre-intellectual God<note>original: "præintellectum deum"—referring to a primordial state of the divine that exists before or above the level of pure thought and being.</note></term>; the other is human, which is the union with the Lord himself, as the prophet <term>Bytis<note>Bytis is a legendary Egyptian priest or prophet frequently cited in Hermetic literature as a source of secret divine wisdom.</note></term> explained from the <term>Books of Hermes<note>original: "libris Mercurialibus"—referring to the Hermetic corpus, the collection of mystical and philosophical texts attributed to Hermes Trismegistus (the Roman Mercury).</note></term>. Therefore, this part of the path has not been neglected by the Egyptians, as you suspect, but has been correctly passed down to us in a way that pertains to holiness. ## THE GREEK WORKS OF PROCLUS
### *On the first commentary on Plato’s Alcibiades.*

They <note>Referring to the Platonic philosophers.</note> consider the knowledge of our own nature to be the beginning of the Platonic dialogues, and the principal and most firm foundation of all philosophy. For when this is correctly known, we will be able to know more perfectly both the good that is suited to us and the evil that is at odds with us. Nature is certainly arranged in such a way that, just as the <term>essences<note>original: "essentiæ"—the fundamental "being" or core nature of a thing that makes it what it is.</note></term> of things differ among themselves, so too do the specific perfections of those things. 

Therefore, so that we may find what the perfection of our nature is and how it is obtained (for we must first of all recognize our own essence, which is indeed the objective proposed in the *Alcibiades* <note>The *First Alcibiades* is a Platonic dialogue where Socrates teaches a young, ambitious Alcibiades that he cannot lead others until he knows himself.</note> and is the ultimate goal of all Plato’s teaching), when we consider the essences of things, we must investigate whether the essence of a thing is from among those that are <term>indivisible<note>original: "indiuiduæ"—referring to entities like the Soul or Intellect that cannot be physically broken into parts.</note></term>, or from that kind which are divided around bodies, or from those that are placed in the middle. Likewise, we must ask whether the essence is eternal, or exists through all time...

...[time] existing throughout all **time**, or whether it comes into being in some specific part of time. Again, we must ask whether it is **simple** and existing before any composition, or whether it is indeed **composed**, but held together by indissoluble bonds; or whether it can, in turn, be resolved back into the parts from which it was composed. And indeed, if we consider each thing in this way, we will thereafter be able to more easily judge what sort of **good** belongs to it. 

For it is established that for an <term>essence<note>original: "essentiæ"—the fundamental "being" or core nature of a thing.</note></term> that is entirely indivisible, its good is **eternal**. For a divisible essence, however, its good is involved in **time** and **motion**. Finally, for an essence of a middle nature, its perfection is weighed according to the specific measures of that substance itself. For a perfection of this kind requires time, but a "first time" <note>This refers to a Neoplatonic concept of time as a pure measure of the soul's activity, distinct from the physical time of the material world.</note>, which can indeed be aptly measured in relation to the revolutions of the body. 

We are indeed ignorant of ourselves, because we are occupied by the **forgetfulness of birth** <note>original: "oblivione genetica"—the Neoplatonic idea that the soul forgets its divine origin and true nature when it enters a physical body.</note>, and we are struck by the disturbance inherent in the life of rational forms. Meanwhile, however, we think we know many things that we actually do not know, because we possess the <term>rational principles<note>original: "rationes"—the inner blueprints or logical structures of reality that Neoplatonists believed were innate to the human soul.</note></term> of things within our own essence.

1.  Turns toward something **worse** than itself, while it slips away from its own perfection; 
2.  Rises toward something **better**, due to the vigor of its own life and natural action; 
3.  Or it is reflected back **upon itself**, because of a knowledge that is suited to it, and a middle...

Rather, as Socrates taught in the *Republic*, the soul knows all intellectual things in a unified way through simple, uniform, and <term>intellectual knowledge<note>original: "intellectuali"—referring to *noēsis*, or direct, intuitive understanding of eternal truths.</note></term>. ...having acquired an amatory nature, and settling upon the mere images of beauty, they admire and love bodily forms because of their ignorance of true beauty, remaining unaware of the nature of their own passion. For just as in the writings of <note>original: "apud Plotinum"</note> **Plotinus** the "down-flow" of the mind produces mere cunning, and a fallen portion of wisdom creates <term>sophistry<note>original: "sophisticam"—the use of clever but fallacious reasoning, often for personal gain rather than truth.</note></term>, so too the gift of love, when it falls into a perverted vessel, produces a life that is intemperate and tyrannical.

*A superior cause acts upon a work earlier and later than an inferior cause; it acts together with it, and is more present to the work.*

Those things which are more perfect in every respect, and which possess the character of an <term>exemplar<note>original: "rationem exemplaris"—the divine model or "Idea" upon which material things are patterned.</note></term>, completely encompass the actions of their own images. Indeed, inferior things are never present in any instance where more perfect things have not, much earlier, bestowed something of themselves. Furthermore, through all the orders of reality, the **One** itself <note>The "One" is the ultimate, absolute principle in Neoplatonism from which all existence flows.</note> encompasses all other things; it acts before them, after them, and in union with them.

*Evil daemons also appear in sacred rites, and they deceive under the pretext of being good.*

We have discovered in <term>expiations<note>original: "expiationibus"—rituals of purification or atonement intended to cleanse the soul or a space of spiritual impurity.</note></term> and sacred rites that, everywhere, something from the lower orders puts on an appearance of perfection. Through this mask, it entices souls that are not yet perfected toward itself, turning them away from the higher powers.

Similarly, in all the most holy **expiations** and sacred rites, before the god himself is present, the attacks of certain earthly <term>daemons<note>original: "dæmonum"—in this Neoplatonic context, these are not necessarily "demons" in the modern sense, but intermediary spirits. Just as, therefore, in the sacred rites, the divine first appears only when we have driven out all this demonic influence that drags souls into matter; so too the divine lover meets the beloved only after the rejection of common, worldly lovers.

<header>PROCLUS</header>

Just as, therefore, in physical <term>contemplation<note>original: "contemplatione"—the philosophical study of the natural world and its laws.</note></term>, the <term>sophistic<note>original: "sophistica"—referring to a life of superficial cleverness and rhetoric rather than a search for genuine truth.</note></term> life is an impediment, and a tendency drawing the weaker person toward it away from the contemplation of true beings toward an imagination familiar with perishable things; so too, in the elevation of love, the crowd of common lovers is an impediment, pretending to be a true lover and twisting the soul of the younger person from celestial goods toward earthly and dark things.

Similarly, in all the most holy purifications and sacred rites, before the god himself is present, the attacks of certain earthly <term>daemons<note>original: "dæmonum"—in this context, intermediary spirits that inhabit the lower realms and can distract or deceive the practitioner.</note></term> openly occur. These new appearances disturb those who are being purified and perfected, deflecting them from pure goods toward <term>matter<note>original: "materiam"—the lowest level of reality in Neoplatonism, often associated with darkness, chaos, and the physical body.</note></term>. 

For this reason, the gods command that you do not look upon them before you have shielded your eyes by the power of the sacred rites. For thus the divine <term>oracles<note>original: "eloquia"—likely a reference to the Chaldean Oracles, a sacred text for Neoplatonists.</note></term> say: <note>original: "Non expedit tibi illos aspicere prius quàm corpus expiaueris, atq; sacraueris. quoniam illi mulcentes animas à sacrificiis vbique deflectunt."</note> *It is not profitable for you to look upon them before you have purified and consecrated your body; for they, by enticing souls, turn them away from the sacrifices on every side.* 

Just as, therefore, in the sacred rites, the divine first appears only when we have driven out all this demonic influence that draws souls into matter, so too the divine lover meets the beloved after the rejection of common lovers. 

Likewise, just as the good daemon of each person guards everyone from childhood, and [guards] all his actions...

[The daemon] investigates even our words, and provides for us even before our parents; he remains present after our parents as a constant governor of our entire life, and after our death, he is our guide to the judges. In this same way, Socrates relates to Alcibiades. Finally, just as a <term>good daemon<note>original: "bonus dæmon"—in the Platonic tradition, a 'daemon' is not an evil spirit, but a benevolent intermediary or guardian spirit that links the human and the divine.</note></term> is present to us, largely hidden, providing for us secretly, counseling us in silence, and correcting us in an ineffable manner, so Socrates behaves toward Alcibiades.

### *The intellect within us is always active through illumination, yet we do not always notice it.*

The <term>intellect<note>original: "intellectus"—referring to the higher, intuitive part of the mind that perceives eternal truths directly, rather than through step-by-step reasoning.</note></term> itself is indeed always active around us, and it always offers the light of understanding, even before we fall into an irrational state. Both when we live our lives amidst passions, and sometimes even when those passions have been calmed, we do not always take notice. But when we are cleansed from the great tumult of <term>generation<note>original: "generationis"—in Neoplatonism, this refers to the cycle of birth, change, and physical existence in the material world.</note></term> and live tranquilly—for it is then that the intellect shines out to us—it is then that it speaks with us, as it were, and communicates its voice to us, though it was present in silence before.

In general, that which is <term>unparticipated<note>original: "imparticipabile"—referring to a higher principle that remains pure and transcendent, rather than being "shared" or divided among lower things.</note></term> differs from that which is <term>participated<note>original: "participabile"—referring to a higher principle as it is received or "shared" by a lower being.</note></term>. Finally, that which is transcendent differs from that which has obtained a coordination with another thing.

Since, therefore, Alcibiades is understood in two ways—both as a soul in its simple essence and as a soul using a body—insofar as he is simply a certain soul, Socrates acts as his <term>Mind<note>original: "mens"—the higher, intuitive faculty that perceives truth.</note></term>. Indeed, when we consider the nature of the daemon as an intermediary, we place it between gods and men. ### *How the god Love is neither first nor last: and how Goodness, Wisdom, and Beauty are among divine things; likewise Faith, Truth, and Love.*

We ought to place the Lord Love <note>original: "Amorem domini"—Love (Eros) viewed as a governing or divine power.</note> neither among the first of beings, nor among the last. Not among the first, because the <term>lovable<note>original: "amabile"—the object of desire or the source of beauty itself.</note></term> itself is higher than Love. Not among the last, because the lover is a participant in love. It is necessary, therefore, to establish Love between the lovable and the lover, and to assert that it is later than Beauty itself, but prior to all other things that love. Where, then, did it exist from the beginning? In what way does it proceed through the whole universe, and with what "unities" <note>original: "vnitatibus"—in Neoplatonism, these are the 'Henads', the highest, most unified principles of reality.</note> does it come forth?

**Faith** <note>original: "Fides"—in this philosophical context, Faith is not a belief in dogmas, but a mystical "grounding" or "steadfastness" that anchors a being in the Good.</note> establishes all things in the Good. **Truth** <note>original: "Veritas"—the clarity and reality of beings as they are known by the mind.</note> unfolds every kind of knowledge within beings. Truly, a trinity of this kind proceeds from this point through all the ranks of the gods, and it radiates a sense of union toward the intelligible itself for all things.

Yet, it manifests differently through different orders, everywhere weaving its own powers together with the specific traits of those gods. In some places, it exists ineffably, unknowingly, and uniquely; in others, through the logic of containment and connection; in others, as a perfecting and shaping force. Here again, it acts intellectually and paternally; there, it acts as a motive, life-giving, and effective force; elsewhere, as a commanding and assimilating power. In one place, it is entirely absolute and pure; in another, it is already manifold and divided.

Therefore, **Love** descends from the heights of the intelligible realm down to the mundane world, calling all things toward divine beauty. It also proceeds through all [things of] truth...

For this reason, <term>Plato<note>The Greek philosopher (c. 427–347 BCE) whose Theory of Forms is central to this discussion.</note></term> proves that the archetypes of all virtues and even bodily goods—such as health, strength, justice, and temperance—exist beforehand within God. Gods, therefore, love gods: the older gods indeed love the lesser ones by the gift of <term>providence<note>original: "prouidentię"—the divine care or foresight that orders the universe.</note></term>, while the lesser ones in turn love the greater ones through a certain duty of <term>reversion<note>original: "conuerfionis"—referring to the Neoplatonic concept of *epistrophe*, where a created being "turns back" toward its divine source in contemplation or love.</note></term>. For it is for this very reason that they descend: for the sake of providence over things that are born and for the care of mortals. 

Yet, to provide for governed things in such a way as to be neither mixed with them, nor affected as if bound to them, nor to receive anything from them, is the unique property of the gods and the good <term>daimons<note>original: "dæmonum"—intermediary spirits that bridge the gap between humanity and the divine.</note></term>. And whenever this occurs in human souls, it happens through divine or daimonic generosity. <sig>n 3</sig>

Those who have obtained their substance from the **first life-giving idea** <note>The Neoplatonic source of all life, often identified with the "World Soul" or a high-level Intellect.</note>, and flowing from there as if from a spring, have attained an essence of the soul. This essence is indeed more **intellectual** <note>In this context, "intellectual" refers to direct, intuitive divine knowledge, rather than mere logic.</note> for those who possess a greater and more perfect substance; but it is less intellectual and rather more **rational** <note>Relating to the "ratio" or the step-by-step reasoning used by human souls.</note> for those who hold the middle rank. 

However, those of the third and **daimonic order** <note>Daimons in Neoplatonism are not "demons" but intermediary spirits that bridge the gap between gods and humans.</note>, who occupy the lowest positions, possess a varied and more rational nature, which is also material. Being constituted of such a substance, they are divided in accordance with the division of the gods, inasmuch as they serve as ministers to the gods. 

For they respond and serve in one way to the gods who are entirely **absolute** <note>original: "absolutis" — referring to transcendent gods who exist entirely separate from and prior to the physical material world.</note>, who originate and lead all things before the world exists; and they serve in another way to the **mundane gods** <note>Gods who govern specific parts of the physical cosmos.</note>, who are directly in charge of the parts of the world, and who are distributed according to the **twelve super-celestial gods**. 

These [daimons] are distributed according to all the properties of the mundane gods. For every mundane god commands a certain order of daimons, to whom he imparts his own power because they are close to him. For the **Creator-God** <term>Opifex: the Demiurge or "craftsman" who shapes the universe.</term> bestows a creative power. The **unchangeable god** provides an incorruptible faculty, and the **perfecter** god likewise provides a perfecting power. Indeed, around every single god there is an innumerable multitude of daimons, possessing the same [characteristics] as the

Consequently, mortal beings obtain divine **influences** <note>original: "influxus" — the flow of divine power or energy from the higher realms into the material world.</note> through these daimons. *He refutes two opinions: the first, which claims there are no other spirits except our own souls released from the denser body; the second, that of Amelius, who believes spirits are certain wandering gods.*

We will not, therefore, admit the views of those who say that daimons are merely our own souls, having already finished this life and been transferred into another state. For it is not fitting to equate a "spirit" considered as a temporary state <note>original: "per habitudinem" — a condition or habit that a soul might take on, rather than its permanent nature.</note> with that which is a spirit by its very essence. Nor should we establish the eternal middle-ground of all worldly things from a type of life that undergoes many-sided changes within itself. For the daimonic guardianship itself stands forever in the same way, maintaining the continuity of the universe. 

The soul, however, does not keep its rank in this manner, as **Socrates** says in the ***Republic***: for at different times it chooses different lives. Nor will we, on the other hand, approve of those who judge that some of the gods are daimons—essentially "wandering gods"—as **Amelius** <note>Amelius Gentilianus (3rd century AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher and student of Plotinus.</note> thinks. Instead, we shall follow **Plato** himself, who calls the gods the lords of the universe, yet subjects the "herds" of daimons to those gods. Everywhere we will uphold the reasoning of **Diotima** <note>A figure in Plato's *Symposium* who explains that spirits (daimons) act as intermediaries between the divine and the mortal.</note>, who assigns to daimons a middle rank between gods and mortals.
