Since, therefore, daimons <term>daimones: In the Platonic tradition, these are not "demons" in the modern sense, but intermediary spirits that act as a bridge between the high gods and the material world.</term> are positioned in the middle, as we have said, the first and highest among them are the **divine daimons**. Because of their excellent likeness to the gods, they frequently appear as gods themselves. For indeed, in every rank, the first member takes on the form of the rank above it. Just as the Intellect <note>original: "intellectus" — often referring to the "Divine Mind" or the realm of pure forms.</note> appears by its own nature as a god, and the most ancient of souls is intellectual in nature, so too the highest genus of daimons, being closest to the gods, is uniform and divine.

The **second** group after these are the daimons already endowed with an intellectual character. They preside over the ascents and descents <note>This refers to the journey of human souls as they rise toward the divine or descend into physical bodies.</note> of souls, and they reveal and hand down the works of the gods to all. 

The **third** are those daimons who distribute the operations of divine souls to the beings that follow them; they complete the bond of those who receive the spiritual flow descending toward them. 

The **fourth** group transmit the effective powers of universal natures into the realm of generation <note>original: "generabilia" — the world of things that are born, change, and die.</note>. They inspire life, order, and rational principles <note>original: "rationes" — the *logoi* or underlying patterns that give structure to nature.</note> into particular natures, as well as the entire production of mortal things. 

The **fifth** are in some sense corporeal <note>original: "corporei" — relating to physical bodies or matter.</note> and they bind together the outer limits of bodies. For in what way would eternal bodies harmonize with those that are perishable? How would the active causes harmonize with their effects, unless they were bound <note>The text ends with the fragment "collig," the catchword for the Latin *colligantur* or *colligentur*, meaning "linked" or "fastened together."</note> by such a middle ground...

### OF THE SOUL AND THE DAEMON.

But we should not approve of those who, setting aside the rational soul, claim that the **daemon** <term>daemon</term> <note>original: "dæmonē"; in this Platonic context, a daemon is a mediating spirit between gods and mortals, acting as a guardian, not an evil "demon."</note> is simply that which operates within the soul. For example, they might say that for those living according to reason, the daemon is **reason**; but for those living by anger, it is the **irascible** <note>original: "irascibile"; the spirited part of the soul that deals with anger and courage.</note> part; and for those living by desire, it is the **concupiscible** <note>original: "concupiscibile"; the part of the soul associated with physical appetites and desires.</note> part.

Nor, again, should we listen to those who say the daemon is that which, in our very life, most closely presides over whatever part is active—as if reason were the daemon for the angry man, or the power of anger were the daemon for the lustful.

In the first place, to say that daemons are parts of the human soul belongs to those who admire human life too much. Such people do not accept that **Socrates**, in the *Republic* <note>Plato’s dialogue concerning justice and the order of the soul and the state.</note>, arranges the heroic and human races only after the **gods** and **daemons**. He rebukes the poets for introducing heroes who are no better than men, but are instead enslaved to similar passions. Socrates, therefore, in rebuking such things, would be very far from the opinion that he would place daemons—who are superior even to heroes—among the parts and powers of the soul. For it would follow from this that things which are better by their very essence would be brought inside to "complete" or fill out things that are inferior.

Furthermore, if this were true, various changes in our lives would force a change of daemons. For a greedy man is often changed to an ambitious life; the ambitious man to a state of living by **right opinion**; and this man, in turn, to a state endowed with **knowledge**. Therefore, the daemon at one time...

It references Socrates' hierarchy of beings (Gods, Daemons, Heroes, Humans) to prove that a daemon cannot be a mere "power" within the soul.</summary>

it will similarly be another. For the very part that acts within the soul exists as one thing at one time, and another at another. Yet no one considering the matter rightly will find any other single providence so close to us, pertaining to all our affairs, besides this daemonic providence and care. For the intellect is participated in by the **rational soul** <term>rational soul</term> <note>original: "anima rationalis"; the human faculty of reason.</note> (as we have said), but by the body not at all. Nature is participated in by the body, but not at all by the intelligence. The rational soul indeed rules over anger and desire, but it has no command over fortuitous events. The daemon alone moves all things, governs all, and refines and arranges all our affairs; for indeed, he brings reason to perfection and [tempers] our disturbances...

<header>PROCLUS</header>

<note>The text begins with a fragment of the word "animae" (of the soul) carried over from the previous page.</note> [The soul's] **essence** <term>essence</term> <note>original: "essentiam"; the fundamental nature or "whatness" of a thing.</note> is not easy for everyone to grasp. Therefore, **Timaeus** <note>The narrator of Plato’s dialogue *Timaeus*, which describes the creation of the soul and the universe.</note> alone declared its entire essence. For what its nature is entirely, being divine, requires a long exposition to be declared, as **Socrates** says in the ***Phaedrus*** <note>A dialogue by Plato where Socrates discusses the soul as a self-moving entity.</note>. However, it is easy to explain the **powers** <term>powers</term> <note>original: "potentias"; the capacities or potential of a being to produce an effect.</note> of the divinities; for we perceive those very powers from their **actions** <term>actions</term> <note>original: "actionibus"; the external operations or results.</note>, of which the forces themselves are the immediate mothers. For **Power** is the medium between action and essence, being produced indeed from the essence, but in turn producing the action.

Moreover, power itself has the greatest familiarity with **daemons** <term>daemons</term> <note>Benevolent intermediary spirits in Neoplatonism that bridge the gap between gods and mortals.</note>. For everywhere, power holds the middle place, just like a daemon: and in the realm of **intelligible things** <note>original: "intelligibilibus"; the highest realm of pure being and thought, accessible only to the intellect.</note>, it joins the Father and the Intellect. For power exists simultaneously with the Father, but the intellect exists from the Father. In the realm of intellectual things, however, power couples actions with essences: for action is the offspring of power, but essence gives birth to powers from itself.

Therefore, the divinities that are intermediate between us and the gods are properly designated by the name of **Power**, as they possess the middle place in all things. For true **essence** and true being exist in the hands of the gods. But **power**, properly ministering to the gods, has its place in the daemons. Finally, **action** and effect, having progressed outward through the power of those daemons, reside within us.

<page-num>214</page-num>
# PROCLUS

[The soul] holds the judgment of our reason, even if something irrational—whether within us or outside of us—should move our intellect.

Why would it not be absurd for a merely conjectural <note>Based on guesswork rather than certain knowledge.</note> foreknowledge of the future to be found in some places, yet for a stable, determined, and indubitable knowledge to be found nowhere? For the very nature of things cannot take its starting point from the imperfect, the impure, or from things mixed with their opposite. If, however, our human "guessing" at the future is a partner to ignorance and remains uncertain, where then exists that knowledge of the future which is certain in itself? Where is that pure knowledge from which everything that comes after—and which desires that knowledge—has received its very substance, if not among the higher beings?

->*The higher beings counsel us well, even if they*<-
->*foresee that we will not obey them.*<-

**Pythian Apollo** <note>original: "Apollo Pythius"; the title of Apollo as the deity of the Oracle at Delphi.</note> answered **Laius** <note>In Greek mythology, the King of Thebes and father of Oedipus.</note> by advising him not to father a son; otherwise, he would be subjected to the violence of **daemons** <term>daemons</term> <note>original: "dæmonum"; here referring to the tragic spirits or vengeful forces of fate that would haunt his lineage.</note>. Meanwhile, the god foresaw that Laius would not obey the oracle. Nevertheless, **Phoebus** <note>original: "Phœbus"; a common epithet for Apollo meaning "bright" or "pure."</note>, acting as a good being, set before him the choice of a better life. And Laius certainly did not believe him, but because of his own ignorance, he was overtaken by future dangers. Indeed, all the actions of upright men tend toward their own innermost depths. Therefore, if a man has acted beneficially and divinely, he already possesses his goal within the action itself.

<summary>Proclus argues that certain divine foreknowledge must exist as the source of our own imperfect intuition, using the tragedy of Laius to show that gods offer virtuous choices even when they foresee human failure.</summary>

and mixed with a stable nature, it undoubtedly results in our knowledge of this very matter being indefinite and ambiguous. For knowledge of unstable things is not secure from refutation <note>original: "redargutione"; the process of proving an argument wrong or showing its inconsistency.</note>, but such things are scarcely grasped even through a kind of assimilation <note>The idea that the mind must "become like" the object it is trying to understand.</note>. **Self-sufficiency** <term>sufficiency</term> <note>original: "sufficientia"; in Greek philosophy, this is *autarkeia*, the state of needing nothing external to be happy or complete.</note> itself resides first with the gods. For the gods are good, and are themselves certain super-essential goodnesses and the fullnesses of all beings. It is through them that sufficiency is granted to all others: to intellects, divine souls, **daemons**, and to us. While these others are sufficient by a certain participation, the gods are so by their very substance. For this reason, a common and immutable opinion defines happiness as sufficiency; for those who are fit to fare well, it is fitting to possess sufficiency.

For there are two types of **causes**: some are **immobile**, being present to all things everywhere; others are **mobile**, being sometimes present to the things they must perfect, and sometimes distant from them. Certainly, **intelligible realities** <note>Spiritual or intellectual truths that exist beyond the physical world and can only be grasped by the mind.</note> are present everywhere in the same way, always bestowing their gifts upon all in the same manner. In contrast, **sensible things** <note>Physical objects or forces perceived through the five senses.</note> can be present to those participating in them, yet they can also be absent—just as the sun is present now, filling the world with light, and then departs. 

Since this is the case, I say that whenever a subject possesses the **aptitude** to participate in one of the **immobile causes**, that cause is immediately present, and the work of the **efficient cause** <note>The active force or agent that brings an effect into being.</note> is completed. In such instances, it is usually only the unfitness of the subjects that prevents the gifts from being received; for the powers that are destined to give are always giving, and they exist everywhere and always in the same way. Therefore, once a subject has emerged and become fit, it suddenly becomes a participant in that cause. 

However, when something is made ready for a **mobile cause**, it often happens that even if the subject is prepared, the source of the gift is absent. For it is necessary that this mobile cause also be present at that moment, since it requires a specific place and time to bestow its influence. In general, as we have said, it is necessary that through all the ranks of **good things**...

A **good daemon** acted as the cause of this opportune meeting, determining the right time for Socrates to encounter him.

One type of opportunity is determined by the **gods**; another is **daemonic**; another belongs to **fate**; and yet another is **fortuitous** <note>Arising by chance or luck.</note>. For "Fortune and Opportunity," as it is said, "govern all human affairs."

->PROCLUS<-

These things are clearly described in the *Republic* <note>Referring to the "Myth of Er" in Book 10 of Plato's *Republic*, which describes the afterlife and reincarnation.</note>, where the prophet proposes various lives to the souls from the lap of **Lachesis** <note>One of the three Fates; she is the "allotter" who determines the span and destiny of a life.</note>. Now truly, the prophet there, anticipating all the choices of the souls within himself, only then throws the lots. Certainly, the matter of choice—which seems unstable and indefinite to us—is always previously comprehended by **higher and more perfect beings** <note>The divine intellects or gods who oversee the cosmic order.</note> according to a single certain limit, and is understood by them in a stable and orderly fashion.

### *Three Maxims of Plato.*

From the words of **Plato** here, we gather three things: 

First, that to be in a state of evil is to be judged altogether worse than not being at all. 

Second, that the **separation of the soul from the body** <note>A philosophical way of describing death, which for the Neoplatonist is a liberation of the spirit from material weight.</note> frees us from the evils that dwell in this decaying region, and from the obstacles that here prevent the attainment of our fitting end. 

Third, that the very desires of souls are the most powerful factors in determining their forms of life; we are not the kind of beings who are formed and moved by external things alone. For from within ourselves, we bring forth the choices through which we lead our lives.

<page-num>227</page-num>

->ON THE SOUL AND THE DAEMON<- <note>original: "DE ANIMA ET DAEM." A daemon (or daimon) in this context is not a "demon" in the modern sense, but a guardian spirit or intermediary being between the divine and the human.</note>

->*The higher beings hold with certain judgment those things which,*<-
->*in the world of matter, are uncertain.*<-

Receive from here a wonderful teaching: namely, that more excellent things, in a uniform way, everywhere anticipate those that are inferior; yet, the inferior things never equal the power of the superior. Likewise, the <term>cognitions</term> <note>The ways of knowing or intellectual grasp.</note> of higher beings firmly encompass the actions of inferior beings within themselves. However, the cognitions of lower beings can never fully comprehend the entire action of the superior. That which is higher receives nothing from the inferior into itself, just as the heavens receive no suffering or "passion" from the changes occurring in the lower atmosphere; nor does the <term>immobile cause</term> <note>A reference to the "Unmoved Mover" or the primary divine source that causes change without being changed itself.</note> admit anything of the world into itself because of the motion of worldly things. Nor, in general, do those things which are eternal admit anything temporal into themselves from the things acting upon them. Finally, that which is necessary, while it knows all things, does not undergo any change even in the act of knowing that which is <term>contingent</term> <note>Things that are not guaranteed to happen; the "uncertain" events of human life.</note>.

->*Argumentation is twofold, through negation*<-
->*and affirmation. The former resolves; the latter*<-

### PROCLUS

[...matters] about which he now consults, certainly he never sought those things out at any time, nor did he ever learn them from teachers. But if he neither sought them nor received them from others, then surely he neither learned nor discovered them. If he neither learned nor discovered them, he deservedly does not know them. If he does not know, he is not a good judge in matters where he cannot identify a time when he realized he was ignorant. 

You see clearly how, if a discussion is conducted in this manner, we proceed sometimes by **composition** and sometimes by **resolution**—using affirmative statements for composition and negative ones for resolution. 

Indeed, this very process of composition and resolution corresponds perfectly to the nature of the soul. The soul glides from more perfect things down to lesser ones through the "composition" of rational arguments and the adding on of various "foreign garments" <note>In Neoplatonism, "garments" refer to the layers of materiality or lower psychic functions the soul acquires as it descends from the stars into a human body.</note>, until it is imprisoned within this thick and solid bond <note>A reference to the physical body as a "prison" or "tomb" of the soul, a concept shared with Orphism and Platonism.</note>. 

Conversely, the soul rises again to the heights through <term>resolution</term> <note>original: "resolutionem." In this context, it refers to analysis or "unweaving"—stripping away complex, material layers to return to a simple, unified state.</note> and the expulsion of those things which are at odds with its own nature. It continues until, emerging "naked"—as the <term>sacred oracles</term> <note>original: "sacra eloquia." Likely a reference to the Chaldean Oracles, a set of mystical texts that Proclus and other late Platonists treated as divine revelation.</note> describe—it is joined to the <term>Forms</term> <note>original: "speciebus." The eternal, immaterial archetypes of all things that exist outside of space and time.</note> that are entirely separated from matter. 

For this reason, argumentation that proceeds through affirmative statements descends from the more perfect to the more imperfect; however, when it proceeds through negatives, it moves in the opposite direction <note>This refers to "apophatic" or negative theology, where one describes the divine by what it is *not*, thereby ascending away from material limitations.</note>.

<summary>Proclus explains that logical synthesis (composition) and analysis (resolution) mirror the soul's own journey: descending into the "garments" of the body and ascending back to the immaterial Forms by stripping away material influences.</summary>

*The Good itself: although it transcends intellectual essence, it alone extends itself down to the very lowest point.* <note>In Neoplatonism, "The Good" is the ultimate principle, synonymous with "The One," from which all reality flows.</note>

The Good itself, as if existing in itself above intellectual nature—if it is right to say so—descends to the last of things, illuminating all things, and preserving them, and adorning them, and meanwhile turning them back toward itself. First, indeed, it is present to those things that truly exist <note>original: "verè existentibus." These are the eternal, unchanging Platonic Forms or Archetypes, which possess the highest degree of reality.</note>; second, to divine souls; third, to the deities <note>original: "numinibus." These are intermediary spirits or *daimones* that bridge the gap between gods and humans.</note> presiding over the human race; fourth, to our own souls, and thereafter to animals, plants, and all bodies. Finally, even to formless matter itself—the lowest dregs of things—the Good indeed secretly and ineffably, before any order was established, offers its own gift to all. 

These things, moreover, participate in it everywhere, each in a different way according to its own order. And to the extent that each is naturally suited, they carry away goodness from it. Some [receive it] more weakly, others more effectively; some more uniformly, others in a more divisible condition; some, moreover, eternally, others changeably. For just as more divine things have an indivisible essence, so they also possess an undivided and unified good. But those things that have departed further from the starting principles, being now situated at a certain distance and division, obtain their own goodness [accordingly].

For each of these principles stands firm within itself. **Material forms**, however, because they cannot exist apart from matter, rightly struggle among themselves for a "shared lodging," since matter is unable to receive two contrary forms into itself at the same time without confusion.

->*How the soul is variously clothed as it descends, and is again purified, and returns in its turn.*<-

The descent of the soul into the body has indeed separated it from the divine souls, by whom it was once filled with intelligence, power, and purity. Instead, this descent has joined the soul to **becoming** <note>original: "generationi," the realm of birth, death, and constant change</note>, to the laws of nature, and to material things, by which it has been tainted with forgetfulness, error, and ignorance.

<page-num>239</page-num>

# ON THE SOUL AND DAEMONS.

For as the soul descends, many forms of life and various "garments" <note>original: "vestes"; in Neoplatonic thought, these are the "vehicles" or subtle bodies the soul acquires as it passes through the planetary spheres</note> grow upon it from the world. These garments indeed drag the soul into a perishable composition and stand in the way of its contemplation of separate, divine things. It is necessary, therefore, to lead the soul from this state back to its ever-watchful and upright nature. To do this, one must prune away the secondary and tertiary powers that grew upon it during its descent—much like seaweed, rocks, and shells cling to the sea-god Glaucus <note>A reference to Plato's *Republic* (Book X), where the soul is compared to Glaucus, a fisherman who became a sea-god but was so encrusted with marine growth that his original form was unrecognizable</note>. One must also restrain the impulses that carry the soul toward external things. It must remember once again those separate realities and that divine essence from which its descent began, and toward which it is proper for all life to strive.

->*The soul is movable by itself, while the body is moved by another; yet, because of their mutual interaction, each takes on the condition of the other.*<-

By its very essence, the soul is self-moving <note>original: "mobilis ex seipsa"; a central Platonic concept where the soul is defined as the source of its own motion, unlike matter</note>, but when it is joined to a body, it somehow also becomes "movable from another source." Just as the soul, by its presence, gives to the body a final trace of self-motion, so too does the soul, because of its shared lodging with the body, take on the mark of being moved by external things. Therefore, because of its power of self-motion, the soul is fertile and more inclined toward discovery, giving birth to rational principles and sciences. # PROCLUS

...[more per]fect souls are more ready for discovery, while more imperfect ones stand more in need of external aids. For the former are more self-moving and share less in a lower nature; the latter, however, move themselves less, suffering more of a bodily fate. Yet these souls too, when they make progress—rising up, evidently, from the body and gathering themselves out of matter—become more fertile. They immediately emerge as discoverers regarding those things about which they were previously sterile and uncertain, due to the unfit sluggishness of life caused by matter and the foul torpor contracted from the process of generation <note>original: "generatione"; in Neoplatonism, "generation" refers to the realm of physical birth, change, and decay, as opposed to the eternal realm of "Being"</note>.

But whoever, in assigning reasons for these things, fails to keep to this middle ground—instead either rising too high toward the better or sinking too low toward the worse—wanders far from the truth of the soul. 

For we do not approve of those who teach that the soul, having fallen into a "moist" body <note>A reference to the ancient idea, often associated with Heraclitus, that "a dry soul is wisest" and that the "moisture" of physical incarnation clouds the intellect</note> and being hindered by its obstacle, is mindless from the start, and that only as the moisture gradually evaporates due to innate heat and becomes more tempered does the soul’s power of wisdom regain its strength. Furthermore, you will see the perfection of souls—not eternal, not existing entirely as a whole at once, but unfolded through time and turning within discursive movements <note>original: "discursionibus"; the step-by-step reasoning process characteristic of the human mind, as opposed to the instant intuition of a higher divine mind.</note>. For such is the nature of the soul.

For it is not fitting to think that those things which do not truly exist are the primary causes of the knowledge existing in the soul; and things which disagree among themselves, and require the soul's reasons and arguments, and are ambiguous, cannot be thought to entirely precede a knowledge that remains consistently the same. Nor is it right to think that reasons which are variously changed can produce those which consist in unity, nor that indeterminate things can be the causes of a determinate intelligence. 

Therefore, it is not right to receive the truth of eternal things from the many; nor should we seek a judgment and distinction of universals <term>universals: general concepts or "Forms" that apply to all members of a group, such as "Beauty" itself rather than a single beautiful object.</term> from sensible things <note>sensible things: things perceived through the five senses (sight, touch, etc.) rather than through the mind.</note>, nor a judgment and opinion of good things from things that lack reason. Instead, the soul, entering into itself, ought to search there for the true, the good, and the true reasons of all things. For the essence of the soul itself is full of these, though they lie hidden because of a "forgetfulness of birth" <note>original: "oblivione genesica"; the Neoplatonic idea that the soul forgets its divine knowledge when it enters the physical world of "becoming" or *genesis*.</note>. 

The soul, therefore, seeks the truth while looking at external things, even though it possesses that truth within its own essence; it explores the good outside itself, having deserted itself. From here, therefore, everyone ought to begin the knowledge of themselves. For if we distract our gaze toward the multitude of men, we shall never discern the one species <note>species: here meaning the "Form" or the essential "Idea" of humanity.</note> belonging to them, as it is obscured by the multitude, division, discord, and the manifold changes of those who participate in that species. # ON THE SOUL AND THE DAEMON

...consistent. Therefore, when they are involved in **generation** <term>generation: the realm of physical birth, change, and decay, as opposed to the eternal realm of Being.</term>, they are like people inhabiting a plague-ridden region; but when they live outside generation, as **Plato** says, they are like those dwelling in meadows <note>meadows: a reference to the "Meadow of Truth" in Plato's *Phaedrus*, symbolizing the celestial realm where souls find nourishment.</note>. Therefore, just as it is not surprising that among those who inhabit pestilential places, the vast majority languish while very few preserve their natural health, so you should not wonder that many souls placed in generation are indeed liable to passions and are depraved. 

On the contrary, it would be astonishing if souls, wrapped in such bodies and bound by these knots, surrounded by such great change, were ever found to be sober, pure, and undisturbed. Is it not amazing for the soul to live immaterially within material things, and to keep itself uncontaminated anywhere among decaying things? ### OF THE SOUL AND THE DAEMON

*Why the evil and ignorant person disagrees with himself and others; why the good person agrees, and those with knowledge are in harmony with one another.*

It is only right that frequent discord with themselves happens to most people: for they admit some things through the senses, some again from the imagination, some often from opinion, several from anger, and many from desire. For such passions are not only stirred in men by their opinions—as the **Stoics** <note>original: *Stoici*. A school of Hellenistic philosophy that taught that destructive emotions resulted from errors in judgment.</note> teach—but also, conversely, because of certain passions and impulses, they often change their opinions; sometimes they report the worst opinions in place of the best. These people, therefore, receiving multifaceted movements within themselves from many principles and powers—and indeed from these baser ones—naturally possess a soul that is at odds and in discord.

But those endowed with knowledge receive their entire cognition from a single, higher principle; for the **intellect** <term>intellect: *intellectus*. In this Neoplatonic context, this refers to *Nous*, the highest faculty of the soul that perceives divine and eternal truths directly, rather than through step-by-step reasoning.</term> provides the principles to them. Now indeed, all true judgments are the daughters of the intellect. Since, therefore, they all proceed from such a principle of simplicity, they are all rightly in harmony with one another.

*Those who think that man is composed of soul and body consequently separate the useful from the just; but those who believe man is the soul itself join them together.*

# PROCLUS

Whether the **just** <term>just: *iustum*. In a Platonic sense, this refers to moral rectitude and the natural order of the soul.</term> and the **useful** <term>useful: *utile*. Also translated as "advantageous" or "expedient"; that which serves one's own well-being.</term> are the same thing is a point upon which others indeed disagree. The **Platonists** <note>Followers of Plato who believed that the soul is the true self and that moral virtue is the highest good.</note> however, judge them to be the same. 

For the **Epicureans** <note>original: *Epicurei*. A school of philosophy that held pleasure and the absence of pain to be the highest good.</note> certainly, and some of the **Stoics**—who place our ultimate goal in living according to nature—as well as the **Peripatetics** <note>original: *Peripatetici*. Followers of Aristotle, so named for his habit of walking while teaching.</note>, who fulfill our "good" from necessary physical requirements, cannot easily confirm that the just and the useful are the same. This is likewise true for whoever says that man is an animated body, or a composite of body and soul. For such a person will flee from wounds and slaughter, even by acting unjustly, so that the "animal" [the physical living creature] may be preserved. Since the good of any animal is to exist according to its nature and to be preserved in that state, in this case, the "useful" (preserving the body) disagrees with the "just" (facing death for a moral cause).

But those who place the goal of life within the soul itself—not needing bodily things—and who believe that man himself *is* the soul using the body as a tool, these certainly judge the just and the useful to be easily the same. For they place both qualities in the soul, and they understand that the sufferings of the "instruments" [the body] are separate from the ones who use them [the souls]. 

The argument proving that the just is useful proceeds in this way: 
1. Everything just is **beautiful** <note>original: *pulchrum*. In Greek and Latin philosophy, this term (*kalon*) implies moral nobility and excellence, not just visual beauty.</note>.
2. Everything beautiful is good. 
3. Therefore, everything just is good. 
4. And since the good and the useful are the same, everything just is therefore useful.

*The soul draws into itself the likeness of the thing to which it adheres; likewise concerning the vehicles of divine souls, and of our own.*

# PROCLUS

The celebration of knowledge <term>knowledge: *scientia*. How great and of what kind each branch of knowledge is becomes apparent from this: that by the imitation of the **Intellect** <note>original: *intellectus*. These facts certainly prove that our essence is separate from the body and remains within itself. For if knowledge, which is our perfection, possesses such a power, it follows that our soul must be immaterial. When physical powers give of themselves, they are diminished. Knowledge, however, remains one and the same; it stays undiminished even as it offers itself sufficiently to one person and to many people equally. Therefore, the soul is similarly present to the whole body and to all its members, even though different members participate in it in different ways.

In ancient philosophy, "Form" or "Species" is the internal structure or "blueprint" that makes a thing what it is.</term>. 

That which is "sensible" <note>Anything that can be perceived by the five senses.</note> possesses traces of **Beauty**, but it possesses no share of **Justice**. For this reason, *Socrates* says in the *Phaedrus* <note>One of Plato’s most famous dialogues, discussing love, beauty, and the soul.</note> that among these fleeting, earthly images, there is no visible splendor of **Justice** or **Temperance** <note>original: *temperantiae*. Self-control or moderation.</note>. Only **Beauty** has the unique privilege of being most clearly visible everywhere and being the most intensely desired of all things.

Therefore, wherever there is the **Just**, there is also the **Beautiful**. Wherever there is the **Beautiful**, there is also the **Good**—whether you choose to look at the primary principles themselves, or at the reflections of those principles as they extend down to the furthest limits of creation. 

All things participate in the **Good** itself, for it is the beginning and source of everything. However, only those things that possess some kind of Form participate in the **Beautiful**. Finally, only souls participate in **Justice**. 

Now, in the very center of all things—which is the station of the **Soul**—all these qualities are woven together. The soul's "Good" consists of its **Beauty** and **Justice**. ...let this indeed be the first, that the middle, and that the last <note>Proclus refers to the three parts of the soul defined by Plato: Reason (the first), Spirit (the middle), and Appetite (the last).</note>. But if it were the case that the worse prevail over the better, those things would no longer be "worse" by nature. For that which is fit to rule is better and more honorable by nature. *A human being is a soul using a body as an instrument.* <note>This is a foundational concept in Platonic philosophy: the "True Self" is the rational soul, while the physical body is merely a tool it employs to navigate the material world.</note> *Therefore, the evils of the body do not pertain to the soul, nor to the human being, just as the defects of tools do not pertain to the craftsman or to his craft.*

Most people falsely think that wounds and death are evils. But what is truly evil for us in these things? They do not pass into the soul, which is what we ourselves actually are. For the sufferings of the tools do not change the skills <term>virtutes; here meaning the functional excellence or "virtues" of the user</term> of those who use them. A blacksmith, for instance, does not lose the art of sawing just because his saw <note>original: *seca*. Even if our happiness consisted entirely in the blacksmith’s craft, we would not consider the blacksmith unhappy simply because he lacked a saw. 

Now, just as the soul has an instrument <note>the body</note>, the body also has certain instruments <note>external tools or limbs</note> through which it moves external things. A defect in these external tools does not harm the healthy state of the body; in the same way, the sufferings of the body do not pass over into the soul. For this reason, death—though it is an evil for the physical body—is nonetheless not an evil for the soul. If, therefore, beauty...

<header>P R O C L V S</header>

...the action belongs to the soul, but if evil should meanwhile exist in something else, it has not yet been shown that the same thing is sometimes beautiful and simultaneously evil. It is also possible to distinguish through dialectical reasoning <term>dialectica ratione; the use of logic or philosophical argument to find truth</term> that one thing may be something in itself <term>secundum seipsum; essentially or by its own nature</term>, while another thing is so only by accident <term>secundum accidens; a philosophical term for a property that is not essential to a thing's nature, like a person being a "brave runner"—the bravery is essential to the act, but the running is incidental to the bravery</term>. 

For a brave action is beautiful in itself; but it is evil, if it ever becomes evil, only by accident—since it happens that one acting bravely might die. For let us grant, if you wish, that death is numbered among evils. Therefore, a brave duty is not evil because of the very fact that it is brave (and thus beautiful), but is evil perhaps by accident. Thus, the beautiful is one thing, and the evil is another. Nor has it been shown that a thing is sometimes evil for the same reason that it is beautiful; rather, it is considered evil only by accident because of death. 

Accordingly, he who separates the "good" from the "beautiful" is ignorant of the human essence <note>original: *essentiam*</note>. Such a person places one in one thing and the other in another, putting the "good" in the body and the "beautiful" in the actions of the soul. But in truth, the human being himself is the mind <note>original: *animus*. In Neoplatonic thought, the "true self" is the rational intellect or soul, distinct from the biological shell.</note>, the very essence separated from the body, in which whatever exists is both beautiful and good, even if a physical disadvantage to the body follows from it. For the body is not a part of the human being, but an instrument; and the evil of the instrument does not concern the user.

<vocab>Proclus, soul, beautiful, evil, dialectic, in itself, by accident, essence, body, mind</vocab>

He uses the logical distinction between "essence" and "accident" to prove that a brave act remains beautiful even if it results in the death of the body.</summary>

### *How these two differ: namely, "in itself" and*
### *"insofar as it is itself."*

Phrases of this kind—namely, "in itself" <term>secundum seipsum; essentially or by its own nature</term> and "insofar as it is itself" <term>qua ipsum; specifically in its capacity as that thing</term>—are distinguished even in the works of Aristotle. For that which belongs to something "in itself" might not belong to it primarily. However, that which fits "insofar as it is itself," beyond merely fitting the thing in itself, also belongs to it primarily and is perfectly equal to it.

Therefore, the Beautiful—if it is the cause of the soul's proportion <term>commensurationis; the balanced harmony of the parts of the soul</term>, and for this very reason is called "beautiful," and if it causes the better part of the soul to rule over the worse, and perfects us, and cleanses the soul's deformity—is for this very reason "the Good." It is not good merely by accident, but by the very reason that it is beautiful. For if, insofar as it is beautiful, it is proportionate, it is also good. Since the Good is a measure, then certainly insofar as a thing is beautiful, it also exists as a good.

Similarly, the base <note>original: *turpe*; can mean physically ugly or morally foul</note>, insofar as it is base, is evil. For insofar as it is base, it is formless, indeterminate, and disorganized; and for this very reason, it is evil. Therefore, insofar as it is base, it is certainly evil. Thus, the same thing is always both beautiful and good; and conversely, a thing is equally base and evil. You must keep this rule in mind here, as Aristotle also used it later: if any two terms are interchangeable, their opposites are likewise <meta>catchword: opposite</meta>

### *On the nature of corporeal and incorporeal things.*

<image-desc>A decorative square woodcut initial 'O' featuring a central rosette pattern surrounded by symmetrical floral and scrollwork motifs.</image-desc>

Every body exists within a place. However, none of those things which are <term>incorporeal<note>Original: *incorporea*. These are things that lack physical form, such as the mind, the soul, or mathematical truths.</note></term> in their own nature, or anything of that kind, exists in a place. Those things which are incorporeal in themselves are everywhere, precisely because they are more excellent than every body and every place; yet they are present everywhere not in a spread-out or distant way, but in a certain indivisible condition <note>The author is explaining that a soul or a thought doesn't have "parts" that are spread out like water in a bowl; instead, the whole of it is present everywhere at once.</note>. Those things which are incorporeal in themselves are not present to bodies in a "local" way <note>That is, they do not occupy a specific set of coordinates like a physical object.</note>; they are present to them whenever they wish, by turning and inclining toward them, insofar as they naturally turn and lean in that direction. But indeed, since they are not present to bodies by any condition of location, they are present to them through a certain <term>disposition<note>Original: *habitudine*. This refers to a relationship or "state of being" rather than a physical connection.</note></term>. Those things which are incorporeal in themselves are certainly not present to bodies through their substance or their essence.

->*On the nature, the binding, and the release of the soul.*<-

The soul is indeed a sort of middle ground between <term>indivisible essence<note>Original: *essentiam individuam*. This refers to pure spirit or mind, which cannot be cut into pieces or spread out in space.</note></term> and the essence which is divisible among physical bodies. <term>Intellect<note>Original: *Intellectus*. In this philosophical system, the Intellect is the level of reality above the soul, consisting of pure, unchanging truth.</note></term>, however, is an essence that is solely indivisible. But qualities and material forms are divisible according to the bodies they inhabit. Not everything that acts upon another does so through physical proximity and touch; indeed, even those things that do act by approaching and touching do so by <term>accident<note>Original: *secundum accidens*. A philosophical term meaning a non-essential or secondary characteristic. Here, it suggests that the physical contact is less important than the underlying power being exerted.</note></term>, and they do not essentially rely on being close. The soul is bound to the body by a certain <term>turning<note>Original: *conversione*. This describes a shift in the soul's focus or attention away from higher truths and toward physical sensations.</note></term> toward the <term>passions<note>Original: *passiones*. In this context, these are not just emotions, but any physical sensations or "stirs" the body experiences, such as pain, hunger, or sensory input.</note></term> arising from the body. And conversely, it is released insofar as it is no longer affected by the body. What nature has bound, nature itself also releases. Again, what the soul has brought together, the soul itself pulls apart. Nature indeed binds the body within the soul, but the soul binds itself within the body. Therefore, nature separates the body from the soul, but the soul separates itself from the body <note>Porphyry is making a distinction between "natural" death (the body failing and releasing the soul) and "philosophical" death (the soul choosing to detach its desires and attention from the physical world).</note>.

->*All things are in all things in a certain way, according to the condition of those things in which they reside.*<-

We do not understand "all things in all things" in a uniform manner; rather, the essence of each thing has its own specific relationship to the whole. In the <term>intellect<note>Original: *intellectus*. In this philosophical system, the Intellect is the realm of pure, eternal truths above the human soul.</note></term>, things exist intellectually; in the soul, they exist rationally; in plants, <term>seminarily<note>Original: *seminariè*. This refers to things existing as "seeds" or formative principles—potentialities that guide growth and development.</note></term>; and in physical bodies, <term>imaginarily<note>Original: *imaginariè*. This suggests that in the physical world, things are merely "images" or shadows of their true, spiritual forms.</note></term>. Moreover, in that which is above all these (the One), they exist in a manner that is <term>super-intellectual<note>Original: *superintellectuali*. A state of being that transcends even the highest form of thought.</note></term> and <term>super-essential<note>Original: *supereſſentiali*. Existing beyond the very category of "being" or "essence."</note></term>.

->*In the highest things there is unity with power; in the lowest, multiplicity with weakness.*<-

When <term>incorporeal substances<note>Spiritual entities that do not have physical bodies, such as souls or minds.</note></term> descend, they are partitioned and multiplied into individual parts through a deficiency of power. However, when they ascend, they are unified and return together into the One through the abundance of their power.

### On the kinds of life.

This <term>equivocal<note>Original: *æquivoca*. Meaning that the word "life" is used for many different things that are not identical in nature.</note></term> condition exists not only in bodies, but life itself is spoken of in many different ways. For the life of a plant is one thing, and that of an animal is another. One kind belongs to intellectual essence, another to a superior nature, another to the soul, and another to the intellect. For these higher beings also live, even if none of the things that arise from them are granted a life similar to their own.

## *Of those things which generate, some turn toward their offspring, while others do not at all.*

Everything that generates by its own <term>essence<note>Original: *essentia*. Here, it refers to the fundamental nature of a being that allows it to produce something else.</note></term> produces something inferior to itself. Furthermore, everything that is generated naturally turns back toward its generator. However, regarding those things which generate, some in no way turn toward what they have produced; others are partially inclined toward them and partially not; finally, others are only turned downward toward their offspring, and in the meantime, they do not reflect back upon themselves.

## *Sensation, imagination, memory, intelligence.*

Memory is not a certain preservation of mental images, <note>original Greek: "ἀλλὰ τῶν μελετηθέντων προβαλέσθαι ἐννοίας προβλήματα"</note> but rather the bringing forward of the concepts of things that have been practiced or studied. That is, it is to draw out the very propositions—or the active productions—of those things which the soul has recently contemplated. Indeed, the soul possesses the <term>rational principles<note>Original: *rationes*. These are the blueprints or logical structures of all things that exist within the soul's nature.</note></term> of all things. It acts according to these principles, either because it is provoked by something else to perform such an action, or because it turns itself inward toward these principles. When it is provoked by an external source, it employs the senses to introduce outside information; but when it enters into itself, it reaches the <term>intelligences<note>Original: *intelligentias*. Higher, purely mental insights that transcend physical sensation.</note></term>. Therefore, neither are the senses entirely outside of the imagination, nor—as someone might say—are the intelligences, insofar as they belong to a living being.

### *The properties assigned to prime matter by Plotinus in a similar way.*

The properties of <term>prime matter<note>Original: *materia prima*. What is called <term>non-being<note>original: *non ens*. In Neoplatonic thought, "non-being" isn't just "nothing." It refers to things outside the realm of defined "Being" (the Intellect). For just as that which is devoid of mass is incomprehensible to a physical body and has no relation to it, so to the incorporeal, that which is stretched out by mass is not an obstacle; it is treated as if it were non-being.

->*The soul sleeps in this body.*<-

### *On the Descent and Ascent of the Soul*

It is necessary for us, if we are indeed to return to those things which are truly our own, to entirely lay aside these things which we have taken upon ourselves from our mortal nature, together with the <term>inclination<note>original: *affectione*. In this context, it refers to the soul's emotional or psychological "leaning" or "gravity" toward material things.</note></term> toward them through which our descent occurred. Furthermore, we must remember that blessed and eternal substance; and while we strive to ascend to the <term>incorporeal<note>original: *incorporeum*. That which has no physical body, referring to the spiritual or intellectual realm.</note></term>, we must meditate on two things especially: first, by what means we may lay aside this material and fleeting existence, and second, by what path we may chiefly return—namely, returning by a path contrary to the path through which we descended to these present conditions of ours.

For we were, and still are, <term>intellectual essences<note>original: *intellectuales essentiae*. This refers to the Neoplatonic belief that the true human self is a rational, spiritual entity existing before and beyond the physical body.</note></term>, pure from all sense-perception and living apart from irrational nature; yet we have been coupled to a sensible nature, both through the weakening of our eternal union with the <term>intelligible<note>original: *intelligibile*. The realm of pure thought and divine reality, which can only be grasped by the intellect rather than the physical senses.</note></term>, and through a power that turns toward lower things. For all those powers that act in tandem with the senses and the body only then first sprout into effect when the soul fails to persist in the intelligible itself...

<summary>Porphyry describes the soul's need to shed mortal attachments and "ascend" back to its original state as a pure intellectual essence. He argues that the soul's descent into the material world was caused by a turning away from the divine realm and a weakening of its eternal union with the Intellect.</summary>

### *On the release of the soul.*

The ancient wise men diligently avoided everything that could fasten the soul to the body. Thus the **Pythagoreans** and similar sages partly withdrew themselves into solitude, and partly lived in the temples and sacred groves of cities, from which the entire crowd was far removed. **Plato**, moreover, chose to live in the **Academy**, a field that was not only solitary and removed from the city, but also (as it is said) unhealthy <note>Ancient sources suggest Plato chose an "unhealthy" location for his school specifically to suppress the excessive vigor of the body, believing it would help the mind focus on higher things.</note>. A philosopher, indeed, will not thrust the soul from the body by violence; for if he employs force, in no way...

The first to perform sacrifices did not offer animals, but first herbs and flowers, then trees, and they burned incense as offerings. The first people who began to feed upon animals did so because of a scarcity of crops; for before that time, they fed upon the fruits of the earth. 

There are three reasons why one must sacrifice to the gods: to show **veneration** <note>original: *veneremur*. This refers to showing honor or deep respect to a higher power.</note>, to return **thanks**, and to ask for **necessities** from them and ward off evils. To obtain these things, however, a vow of the mind is sufficient, to which small gifts from the fruits of the earth may be added. But to slaughter animals is a **sin** <note>original: *nefas*. In a Roman religious context, *nefas* refers to an action that is divinely forbidden or contrary to cosmic law.</note>. 

We also shall certainly dedicate sacred things to the gods, but we will offer different sacrifices, as is appropriate, just as we will also sacrifice to different powers. To God himself indeed,

To him who reigns in all things—as a certain wise man <note>likely referring to Apollonius of Tyana, whom Porphyry often cites regarding pure worship.</note> once said—we shall offer nothing perceptible to the senses, neither burning incense nor calling him by names. For there is no material thing that is not immediately impure to the one who is entirely immaterial. For this reason, neither spoken words nor even the internal speech of the mind can be suitable for him when it is stained by any passion of the soul; instead, we shall worship him rightly through pure silence and with pure thoughts about him.

It is necessary, therefore, that those who have already become joined and made similar to God should dedicate this <term>elevation</term> <note>original: *elevationem*. In Neoplatonic thought, this is the 'anagoge' or the upward journey of the soul back to its source.</note> of ourselves to God as if it were a **sacred victim**, which is itself both divine praise and our salvation. In the very contemplation of this God, which is free from all passion, this sacrifice is fulfilled. 

To his sons, however—who are also <term>intelligible gods</term> <note>original: *intelligibiles dij*. These are divine beings that can be grasped by the intellect, existing between the Supreme One and the physical world.</note>—we must now offer praise through speech. For a just offering of <term>first-fruits</term> <note>original: *primitiarum*. Historically, the first part of a harvest given to the gods; here, it is used metaphorically for intellectual offerings.</note> is made to each of the deities from those things which they bestow, through which they nourish us and keep us in existence so that we may have the capacity to sacrifice. There remains the multitude of invisible beings, whom **Plato** called "daemons without distinction" <note>original: *dæmones indistinctos*. ### *On sacrifices to evil daemons, and on abstinence, and caution regarding evil daemons.*

Therefore, the theologians <note>In this context, Porphyry refers to ancient priests and philosophers who studied the nature of the divine and religious ritual.</note>, if they ever allow the slaughter of animals for wicked daemons <term>daemons<gloss>In Neoplatonic thought, these are intermediate spirits. For these kinds of lewdness are what usually summon wicked daemons.

<page-num>327</page-num>
<header>ON THE SOUL.</header>

...which makes all things <note>Likely referring to Nature or the Creator, continuing the thought from the previous page.</note>, and made the sentient animal, not merely so that it might simply feel and experience sensations, but so that it might perceive which things were advantageous to it and which were disadvantageous—following the former and fleeing the latter. Therefore, the senses provide the knowledge of both to each individual animal. However, those actions which follow the senses—namely, the pursuit and grasping of useful things, and the avoidance of harmful ones—must be thought not to exist except in those beings possessing a certain reasoning, judgment, and memory.

Even though Strato the Physicist <note>Strato of Lampsacus (c. 335–269 BCE), a Greek Peripatetic philosopher who emphasized the physical and psychological aspects of the soul.</note> says that the senses do nothing without the aid of intelligence—since we do not perceive things present to our senses while we are intently thinking about something else—nonetheless, even if we grant that the senses do not need the mind for their basic function, yet when the senses apply themselves to what is familiar and what is foreign, and establish a difference between the two, fleeing the one and following the other, and shrewdly find the means of following or escaping, then reason must be present. We can conclude that these qualities are proper to reason, and they are present in all animals—that is, in all those capable of movement.

->*He who lives content with few things, and is innocent, is like a god.*<-

Since the goal for souls is to become similar to God, and since God is in need of nothing, no... <note>original: "ceátue." This is a catchword referring to the first word of the next page, likely part of a word like "noceatue" or "nobis."</note>

...harmful to none <note>The text begins mid-sentence, likely completing the thought from the previous page: "innocent" or "harmful to none."</note>, he is certainly the most happy and most similar to God who so prepares himself that he needs as little as possible from others and harms as little as possible. The cause of this want <term>inopia: a state of lack or poverty, as opposed to divine fullness</term> is generation <note>The Neoplatonic concept of "generation" refers to the process of being born into the physical, material world.</note>, because we have been placed in this very state of want through birth, being now more remote from abundance <term>copia: abundance, referring to the spiritual plenitude of the divine</term>. 

Want, indeed, seeks its safety from external things. He who needs more external things is more closely joined to want and is separated further from God. For he who is like God possesses true abundance by that very likeness. But the rich man, truly enjoying riches, inflicts injury on no one. Indeed, as long as he inflicts injury—even if he should possess all the money in the world and occupy the entire earth—he must be considered poor, since he is an intimate of want. 

For this reason, the unjust man is profane and polluted by every depravity. This vice was brought upon us by a certain ruin of the soul as it descends into matter, departing from the Good <note>original: "bono." The soul is in need of everything as long as it does not [look up to] <note>The original Latin ends with the catchword "ſuſpic," likely for "suspicit," meaning "looks up to" or "aspires to."</note> that very fullness...

...was judged. He adds that they killed no animal. Truly, they found nothing better for health than to minimize the accumulation of excess. Therefore, they did not wish to consume nourishment more powerful than their own nature, but rather that by which their nature might be made stronger. Therefore, they did not honor animals without reason, and they restrained themselves from [consuming] them as much as was possible.

He notes that they held all things in common and cultivated mutual charity, abstinence, and patience above all else, being ever intent upon divine worship.

The **Gymnosophists** <term>Gymnosophists</term><note>Literally "naked wise men," a term used by the Greeks to describe Indian philosophers who practiced extreme asceticism and renounced clothing and worldly comforts.</note>, in addition to their other moderation and holiness, abstained from eating animals. Because of this, iron—which is naturally very heavy—becomes light and is lifted up by the "spirit" of the magnet as it joins itself to it. If someone, therefore, has escaped toward God—having become suspended there as something incorporeal and intellectual—he rightly should not nourish...

<header>ON ANCIENT ABSTINENCE</header>

...[one should not] seek nourishment by which the body grows fat, for this blocks the path to the mind. Instead, one should reduce the body to the minimum and strictly necessary food. Then he himself will be nourished by divinity, joined to God more naturally than iron is to a magnet. Indeed, if we did not even require the smallest amount of food, we would be as much happier as we would be more immortal. But as it is, living in this mortal state, we secretly make ourselves even more mortal (so to speak) while we enlarge the body and (as **Theophrastus** <term>Theophrastus</term><note>A Greek philosopher and successor to Aristotle; Porphyry frequently cites him to support the idea that animal sacrifice and meat-eating are harmful to the soul.</note> says):

> while the soul, through its familiarity with inhabiting the body, 
> contracts a heavy rent <note>original Greek: ἐνοίκιον (enoikion). This refers to the "habitation tax" or rent the soul pays to stay in the body, representing the burden of physical needs.</note>—that is, a great deal of 
> dependency—and moreover devotes its entire self to it.

But would that we had been able to lead a life entirely without food and drink, so that by restraining the body’s constant flowing away <note>A Platonic concept suggesting that the material body is in a state of constant decay and flux, requiring constant "refilling" through food.</note>, we might be joined immediately to the highest things, in which God exists as God. Truly, why do we cry out these things in vain to men and lament over them? They are so blinded that they continually cherish their own evil, while hating first themselves and their true Father <note>Referring to the divine source or Creator from which the soul originates.</note>, and finally hating even those who warn and encourage them to eventually wake up from their drunkenness <note>A common philosophical metaphor for being lost in material desires and the "sleep" of the soul.</note>. **Democrates** <term>Democrates</term><note>A Pythagorean philosopher known for his moral maxims; his name is often associated with Democritus in ancient collections of sayings.</note> says:

> to live without wisdom, without restraint, and without piety, 
> is not so much to live poorly as it is to die for a long time.

# FROM MICHAEL
## P S E L L U S ON DEMONS,

->*Translated by Marsilio Ficino.*<-

<image-desc>An ornate woodcut decorative initial 'N' featuring scrolling foliate and floral patterns in a square frame.</image-desc>

The nature of demons is not entirely without a body; rather, it possesses a body and occupies itself with physical things. This is the judgment of our venerable fathers <note>This refers to the "Church Fathers," early influential Christian theologians like Basil the Great.</note>, and there are even those who assert that demons have appeared to them through their own physical presence. Indeed, the divine **Basil** <term>Basil</term><note>St. Basil the Great (c. 330–379 AD), a leading Greek bishop and theologian who helped define early Christian doctrine on the Trinity and the spiritual world.</note>, that inspector of mysteries hidden from us, attributed bodies not only to demons but even to pure angels, describing them as certain thin, airy, and pure spirits. To support this, he cites **David** <note>Reference to Psalm 104:4.</note> who says: *He makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a flame of fire.* This is indeed necessary. For as the divine **Paul** <note>Reference to Hebrews 1:14.</note> asserts, those ministering spirits who are sent forth must have a body by which they are moved, take their stand, and appear openly. For they know that these services cannot be fulfilled in any other way than through some kind of body. If you should read anywhere in the Scriptures that they are called "incorporeal," I respond that both our writers and others are accustomed to calling only the thicker, heavier bodies "corporeal,"

...[designate them as such,] yet they frequently call those bodies "incorporeal" which are thin and escape both sight and touch. Whether the demonic body was ever like this, I cannot say. ...if anyone else had truly advanced in the worship of demons and witnessed their apparitions, it was he [Marcus]. Previously, he had despised and detested such things as empty and false. <meta>This page continues the dialogue between Michael Psellus and Marcus. Having previously discussed the physical sensations and biology of demons, Marcus now begins to categorize them. He uses a mixture of Pythagorean number theory and Euclidean geometry to explain why there are six types and how their natures correspond to different geometric shapes.</meta>

<page-num>338</page-num>
<header>P S E L L V S</header>

I asked him these things: "Tell me, Marcus, are there many kinds of demons?" 

"Many," he replied, "and of various types, both in their shapes and their bodies. In fact, the air above us and the air around us is full of demons; the earth is full of them, as is the sea, and the secret, deep places." 

"Unless it is a burden," I said, "list them." 

"Generally," he said, "there are six kinds of demons. I am not certain, however, whether it is better to categorize demons by the places they inhabit, or rather by the fact that the entire demonic race is drawn by a certain love toward the physical body. I do know that the number six <term>senarium numerum</term> <note>original: "senarium numerum"; the number six was considered "perfect" and "worldly" in ancient mathematics because it is the sum of its factors (1+2+3=6).</note> is associated with the body and the world. For physical circumstances are contained within it, and the world is structured through this number—perhaps because this is the first number that can form a scalene triangle <term>triangulum scalenum</term> <note>original: "triangulum scalenum"; a triangle with three unequal sides. In ancient geometry, the first right-angled scalene triangle with whole-number sides (3, 4, and 5) has an area of 6.</note>."

"The nature of the equilateral triangle <term>æquilateri</term> is divine and heavenly, as it is perfectly equal to itself and is only with great difficulty moved toward evil. The nature of the isosceles triangle <term>æquicrurij</term> <note>original: "æquicrurij"; literally "equal-legged," referring to a triangle with two equal sides and one unequal side.</note> represents the human race, which may wander from its intended path in one respect, but through repentance becomes better. The nature of the scalene triangle, however, is the property of the demonic, as it is entirely unequal and never comes close to the good. 

Whether the matter stands this way or another, he listed six kinds of demons in total; and the first one he named in a foreign, barbaric tongue..."

# PSELLUS

For this reason, after these events, I began to wonder how it was that a demon troubling a woman appeared as a woman. And I was not wrong to wonder whether some demons are male and others are female, in the manner of **mortal creatures** <term>animalium caducorum; literally "falling" or "perishing" animals, referring to beings subject to death and decay</term>. Then, I wondered how the demon restrained itself at the threats of that magician <note>original: "magi"; here referring to the Armenian exorcist mentioned on the previous page</note> and why he feared the drawn sword; for what harm could an indivisible and immortal demon suffer from a blade? 

Then Marcus, noticing my uncertainty, said: "No demon is by its own nature male or female. For such characteristics belong only to **composite beings** <note>original: "compositorum"; referring to beings made of physical matter and parts, unlike the "simple" spiritual substance of a demon</note>. But the bodies of demons are simple and easy to mold and bend, naturally suited to take on any configuration. Just as we look up at the clouds and see them taking the shapes of men, or bears, or dragons, or other things, so it is with the bodies of demons. 

But there is this difference: clouds are driven by external winds to form various shapes, whereas demons, by their own will and as they please, vary the forms of their bodies. At one moment, they contract into a smaller mass; at another, they stretch themselves out into a longer one."

Just as it seems to happen with **worms** <note>original: "lumbricis"; here referring generally to soft, pliable creatures like earthworms or larvae</note> on account of their better substance, which is very easy to stretch and mold: in them, a diversity occurs not only in size, but they also vary in many-shaped figures and colors. But while the air is colored by external factors, the body of a demon receives the appearance of colors from the innermost action of its **imagination** <term>phantasię; in the Neoplatonic sense used here, this refers to the demon's internal power to project mental images onto its own ethereal "envelope"</term>. Just as our cheeks turn pale when we are terrified, or grow red when we are affected by shame—since the soul, when it is affected one way or another, transmits such passions into the body—we must think of demons in the same way. For they also transfer various colors from within themselves into their own bodies. Therefore, each demon can transform its own body into whatever shape it chooses, bringing a specific color all the way to the surface of its body. In this way, it might appear as a man, and then a moment later show itself as a woman; it might roar like a lion, leap like a **leopard** <note>original: "pardalis"</note>, bark like a dog, or even take the form of various other things. For a spirit of this kind is wandering everywhere, since it has obtained a solar rank <note>original: "solarem ordinem." But can the bodies of demons be struck? Indeed they can, and they feel pain when struck by a solid body. But in what way, since they are spirits, and have neither a solid nor a composite nature <note>The "composite nature" refers to the Aristotelian idea of a being made of both matter and soul. Psellus is exploring how a being made of pure "spirit" or "vapor" can feel physical impact.</note>—and sensation belongs to composite things? But surely in those things that perceive, it is not the nerve <note>In ancient and medieval medicine, "nerves" (nervus) were thought to be conduits for the "pneuma" or vital spirit that allowed for sensation and movement.</note> itself that feels, but the spirit that is within them. Therefore, if a nerve is worn down, or if it becomes cold, or if it suffers anything else, since spirit is sent into spirit, pain occurs. 

Certainly, a composite thing would never feel pain by itself, but only when it participates in the spirit, deprived of which it is also deprived of sensation. Thus the demonic body is naturally sentient throughout its whole self; according to its individual parts, it sees, hears, and touches without a medium <note>Unlike humans, who need eyes to see and ears to hear, Psellus argues that a demon's entire "body" is a single sensing organ.</note>. It suffers by touching, and feels pain when divided, just as solid bodies do. But there is this difference, that...

They called him **Trismegistus**, or "Thrice-Greatest," because he stood out as the greatest philosopher, the greatest priest, and the greatest king. For it was the custom of the Egyptians (as **Plato** writes) to choose priests from the ranks of philosophers, and to elect the king from the assembly of priests. He, therefore, just as he had surpassed all philosophers in sharp intelligence and learning, so having been appointed a priest therefrom, he excelled all priests in the holiness of his life and the worship of divine things; and finally, having obtained the royal dignity, he [surpassed] the glory <note>The catchword 'riam' at the bottom of the page indicates the next page begins with 'gloriam' (glory).</note> of previous kings in the administration of laws and in his deeds...

...[glo]ry <note>original: "gloriam" — completing the word from the previous page's catchword.</note> obscured the fame of others, so that he was deservedly named **Thrice-Greatest**. He was the first among philosophers to turn his mind from physics and mathematics to the contemplation of divine things. He was the first to dispute most wisely concerning the majesty of God, the order of demons <note>In this context, *demons* (daemons) refers to intermediary spirits or guardian beings, not necessarily evil entities.</note>, and the transmigration of souls <note>original: "animarum mutationibus"</note>. He was therefore called the first author of theology. 

**Orpheus** followed him, holding the second rank in this <term>Ancient Theology</term> <note>original: "prisca theologia" — the Renaissance idea that a single, true theology existed in antiquity and was passed down through a chain of pagan prophets.</note>. **Aglaophemus** was initiated into the sacred rites of Orpheus; **Pythagoras** succeeded Aglaophemus in theology; and he was followed by **Philolaus**, the teacher of our divine **Plato**. 

Thus, a single sect of ancient theology, everywhere consistent with itself, was forged from these six theologians in a wondrous order, beginning with **Mercury** <note>Hermes Trismegistus</note> and reaching its complete perfection with the divine **Plato**. 

Moreover, Mercury wrote a great many books pertaining to the knowledge of divine things, in which—O immortal God!—what secret mysteries, what stupendous oracles are revealed! He speaks not only as a philosopher, but frequently as a prophet, and sings of the future. He foresaw the ruin of the ancient religion, the birth of the new faith, the coming of **Christ**, the future judgment, the resurrection of the age, the glory of the blessed, and the punishments of sinners. Because of this, **Aurelius Augustine** <note>St. Augustine of Hippo, the influential 4th-century Christian theologian who discussed Hermes in his work *The City of God*.</note> doubted whether it was through his skill in the stars, or...

### ARGUMENT <note>original: "ARGVMENTVM" — This serves as the introductory summary or "argument" for the work.</note>

through the revelation of spirits <note>original: "dæmonum" — in the Neoplatonic sense, these are intermediary beings between gods and humans, not necessarily evil spirits.</note>, he brought forth many things; **Lactantius** <note>A 4th-century Christian author who often cited Hermes to prove Christian truths to pagans.</note>, moreover, does not hesitate to count him among the **Sibyls** and **Prophetesses**. Finally, out of the many books of **Mercury**, two are especially divine: one concerning the *Divine Will*, the other concerning the *Power and Wisdom of God*. The former is titled **Asclepius**, the latter **Pimander**. **Apuleius the Platonist** translated the former into Latin; the latter remained among the Greeks until these times; but recently, it was brought from Macedonia into Italy through the diligence of **Leonardo of Pistoia**, a learned and upright monk, and has reached us.

I, however, having been moved by your exhortations and having decided to translate it from the Greek language into Latin, thought it only right, **O blessed Cosimo**, that I should dedicate this little work to your name. For it is fitting that I offer the first-fruits of my Greek studies to the one by whose resources I was aided and with whose books I was abundantly supplied while I devoted myself to those studies. Nor would it be right to dedicate the work of so wise a philosopher, so pious a priest, and so powerful a king to anyone unless he to whom it is dedicated surpassed all others in piety, wisdom, power, and all other things.

Moreover (to descend to the writings of **Mercury**), the title of this book is **Pimander**, because out of the four persons who debate in the dialogue, the primary parts are assigned to **Pimander**. Indeed, he published the book in Egy- <note>original: catchword "ptiis" completing "Aegyptiis" (Egyptians).</note>

...[with his] own letters; the same man (being highly skilled in the Greek language) then shared the mysteries of the Egyptians by translating them from that source into Greek. The purpose of this work is to discuss the power and wisdom of God. And since the operations of these attributes are twofold—the first remains within the very nature of God, while the second extends to external things—and since the former conceives the first and eternal world <note>This refers to the "Intelligible World" or the realm of pure ideas and divine thought.</note>, while the latter brings forth the second and temporal world <note>The physical, material universe that exists within time.</note>, Hermes conducts a most serious discussion concerning both operations and both worlds: what the power of God is, what His wisdom is, by what order they conceive inwardly, and by what progression they bring forth outwardly.

Furthermore, he discusses how those things that have been produced relate to one another, in what ways they agree or disagree, and finally, by what means they look back toward their author. The structure of the book, however, is such that we distinguish it into fourteen dialogues: the first parts of the dialogue are given to **Pimander** <note>original: "Pimandro" — Also known as Poimandres, representing the "Divine Mind" or "Shepherd of Men" who reveals truths to Hermes.</note>; **Trismegistus** <note>Hermes himself.</note> holds the second parts; **Aesculapius** <note>The legendary physician, here depicted as a disciple of Hermes.</note> holds the third; and **Tatius** <note>The son and disciple of Hermes in these Hermetic texts.</note> occupies the fourth place. **Mercury** <note>The Roman name for Hermes.</note> therefore intends to instruct Aesculapius and Tatius in divine matters. Yet, he who has not learned cannot teach divine things, and we cannot discover those things which are above nature through human intellect alone. Therefore, there is a need for divine light, just as we look upon the sun itself by the light of the sun. Indeed, the [divine] light...
