The light of the divine mind <note>original: "divinae mentis"</note> is never poured into the soul unless the soul itself, like the moon toward the sun, is turned completely toward the mind of God. The soul is not turned toward the mind unless it too has become mind <note>In Ficino’s philosophy, the "mind" (mens) is the highest part of the soul, capable of direct spiritual intuition.</note>. But it does not become mind until it has cast off the deceptions of the senses and the mists of the imagination <note>original: "phantasiae nebulas"</note>. For this reason, Mercury <note>Hermes Trismegistus.</note> has just now stripped away the darkness of the senses and imagination, calling himself back to the threshold of the mind; soon **Pimander** <note>The "Divine Mind" or "Shepherd of Men."</note>—that is, the divine mind—flows into him, from which he contemplates the order of all things existing in God and flowing out from God. Finally, he explains to other men those things revealed by the divine power. Such, then, is the title of the book, its purpose, and its order.

<meta>This page continues the philosophical dialogue between Hermes Trismegistus and his disciple Aesculapius. While the previous page focused on the creation of Man and the comparison to Mosaic law, this page shifts to the metaphysical nature of God and the mechanics of the cosmos.</meta>

<header>THE WORKS OF MERCURY TRISMEGISTUS. The Universal Discourse of Mercury to Aesculapius.</header>

God and divinity itself—I speak now not of that which is born, for he is unbegotten <note>original: *ingenitum*; in Hermetic thought, the supreme God is the "unbegotten" source of all, having no beginning or creator.</note>. If, therefore, it is a divine thing, it is an essence; but if it is God, it is even beyond essence. This may be understood in the following way: the first intelligible God exists not for himself, but for us. For that which is "intelligible" <note>original: *intelligibile*; something that can be grasped by the intellect rather than the physical senses.</note> falls under the perception of the one who understands through the senses. God, therefore, is not at all "intelligible" to himself; for he is not some other thing existing apart from that which he understands, such that he could be understood by himself as an object. He is, however, something different from us, and for that reason, he is understood by us. 

If the Word <term>Word: original *logos*, referring to the divine reason or second person of the Hermetic trinity</term> is "intelligible," then it is not God. But if it is as God, it is certainly not as the Word; for the Word is spoken of as something distinct. Now, everything that is moved is moved not in something that is itself moving, but in something stable. That which moves also remains constant; for it is impossible for the mover to be agitated along with the thing it moves.

**AESCULAPIUS:** In what way then, Trismegistus, are those things that are in the world changed together with the things that move? For you used to say that the erratic spheres <term>erratic spheres: the "wandering stars" or planets (Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, the Sun, and Moon) which appear to move independently</term> are moved by the fixed sphere <term>fixed sphere: original *aplane*, the outermost vault of the stars that remains constant</term>.

**TRISMEGISTUS:** That is not motion, O Aesculapius, but resistance. For they do not travel in the same direction, but in contrary ways. This opposition contains a stable reverberation of motion. For the recoil of the stationary...

<meta>This page continues the dialogue on cosmic motion. This section explores the Hermetic paradox of how the universe can be in constant motion yet remain stable.</meta>

<page-num>383</page-num>
<header>PIMANDER.</header>
<meta>catchword: ab</meta>

...of motion, there is an agitation. And therefore, the wandering spheres <note>original: *erraticae sphaerae*; the planets, so called because they appear to "wander" across the sky unlike the fixed stars.</note>, by moving in a contrary direction and alternating with the fixed sphere <term>fixed sphere: original *aplane*, the outermost celestial shell containing the stars that do not "wander"</term> in a contrary meeting around such an opposition, are moved by that which stands firm; indeed, it cannot be otherwise. For the Bears themselves <note>original: *arctos*; the constellations Ursa Major and Ursa Minor. From a northern perspective, these "circumpolar" stars never drop below the horizon (sink) or rise, but circle the pole eternally.</note>, which our people say neither ever rise nor set, but perpetually circle around the same point—do you think they move, or rather stay still? 

**A E S C.** They move, O Trismegistus. 

**T R I S.** By what motion, Aesculapius? 

**A E S C.** By a motion that runs eternally around the same point. 

**T R I S.** But indeed, that circulation is both the same and around the same: it is a motion contained by stability. For the fact that it is "around the same" prevents that which is above it <note>This refers to the celestial mechanics where one sphere's motion is constrained or balanced by another.</note> [from straying]. Moreover, that which is above, being hindered, remains around the same point. And thus, the contrary agitation is firm, perpetually stabilized by the opposition itself. 

I will place an example before your eyes from the living things on earth: just as when a man swims (in flowing water, of course), the counter-action of his hands and feet together causes the man to stay in place, lest he be carried away by the water or sink into it. 

**A E S C.** You have brought forth a very clear example, O Trismegistus. 

**T R I S M.** Therefore, whatever is moved in a state of stability is moved by stability. The motion of every living being <note>original: *animalis*; in Hermetic thought, the planets and the world itself were considered living, "animated" beings.</note> that consists of matter is by no means caused by things that are outside the world. But...

<summary>Trismegistus explains the paradox of celestial motion, using the "Bears" and a swimming man as metaphors to show how opposing forces create a stable, eternal movement. He concludes that the motion of material beings is governed by internal stability rather than external forces.</summary>

...from internal things to external, whether from the soul, from the spirit, or from some incorporeal <term>incorporeal: having no physical body or material substance</term> mind. **AESC.** For what reason do you assert this, O Trismegistus? 

**TRIS.** Do wood, stones, and all other things which have a soul <note>original: *quæcunque animam habent*. In Hermetic philosophy, even "inanimate" objects like stones were often thought to possess a low-level "soul" or vital spark that allowed them to be part of the living cosmos.</note> not move by bodies, O Aesculapius? For what is it within the body that moves the inanimate thing itself? It is certainly not the body itself by which both are moved—the body of that which carries and that which is carried? Is not that which we spoke of animated for the primary reason that it *moves*? Do you not see then that the soul is most burdened when it alone sustains two bodies? Furthermore, it is manifest that whatever is moved, is moved within something else, and is moved by something that is standing still. 

**AESC.** In that case, O Trismegistus, those things which are changed must be changed within something [that contains them]. 

**TRIS.** You speak rightly, O Aesculapius. Nothing in the order of things is empty <term>empty: original *vacuum*; the philosophical concept of a "void" or space containing absolutely nothing</term>; rather, only that which does not exist, which is deprived of existence, should be called a "vacuum." For nothing can be found which, while it exists, is empty. 

**AESC.** Are there not certain empty things found, Trismegistus? Like an empty jar, an empty well, and many other similar things? 

**TRIS.** Alas, how far you wander from the truth!

Nor should you ever call God anything other than the Good alone, for you would fall into the same impiety. # PIMANDER.

## B 2

...by everyone. But on account of ignorance, people call both the gods and even certain humans "good." Yet they can never be truly good, nor can they even become so <note>original: *boni possunt, nec etiam fieri*; Hermes argues that "Goodness" is an essential quality of the Creator alone, not an attribute a creature can acquire</note>. Therefore, all the other immortal gods are simply honored with the name of "God." But God is the Good, not by some honorific title, but by His very nature. For the nature of God is one: specifically, the Good itself. This is one and the same in both names, and from this single source all kinds of things flow. For the Good bestows all things and receives nothing. God offers all things and takes in nothing. Therefore, God is the Good, and the Good is God.

Another title for God is "Father," for this reason: because He begets all things. For the duty of a father is to generate. For which reason, the procreation of children is considered a most excellent pursuit in life, and is held in the highest esteem among the wise. Truly, the ultimate calamity and impiety happens to him who departs from life without children. For this cause, he pays the penalty to the spirits <term>spirits: original *dæmones*; in this context, these are intermediary divine agents or "daemons" who act as administrators of justice in the afterlife</term> after his death. 

The punishment is finally of this sort: that the sterile soul, through judgment, migrates into a certain body which possesses neither the nature of male nor female <note>this refers to a "neuter" or unproductive existence, mirroring the soul's failure to generate life on earth</note>, a body which is indeed lifted up by the sun and bound to it. Therefore, O Aesculapius, have no fellowship with a man who has begotten no children. Yet have pity on his unhappiness, since you know what evils await him after his passing—

## COMMENTARIES

The commentator argues that God is intelligible in a rational way to man alone. He "hunts" for God himself by looking at the center, the pole, the location, and the forms of things—around whom, in whom, and by whom all things are moved. He describes God as stable, immobile, and always remaining exactly the same as Himself. He asserts that nothing in the world can be a vacuum <term>vacuum: the philosophical concept of "empty space." The author argues that even "empty" space is filled with divine presence</term>; indeed, those things which seem to be empty are actually filled with a more fertile abundance, emulating the highest Plenitude <note>original: *plenitudinem*; often referred to in Greek philosophy as the *Pleroma*, or the totality of divine powers</note>. 

Next, he suggests to Aesculapius through his answers that it is easier to state what God is *not*, rather than what He *is* <note>this is a classic example of "apophatic" or negative theology, where God is defined by His transcendence beyond human categories</note>. Nevertheless, he maintains that God is the absolute Good and the Father, whose duty is to beget all things. When this is understood as an "internal generation"—one that remains within the very nature of God—it inspires the piety of divine religion. 

His contention that the name of "the Good" belongs to God alone harmonizes with the truth of the Gospel: *Why do you call me good? No one is good but God alone* <note>original: "Quid me vocas bonum? nemo bonus nisi solus Deus"; a reference to the words of Jesus in Matthew 19:17, Mark 10:18, or Luke 18:19</note>. 

Furthermore, what he adds regarding the "ultimate calamity" for those who die without children is a veiled discourse <note>original: *velatus sermo*; an allegorical or symbolic teaching</note>. For one should not conceive of this as a physical birth, but as a birth of the soul. Consider its "infants" and "sons" to be the fruits of the virtues, and consider "masculine wisdom" to be the capacity for contemplating God and His most divine powers. He openly hints at this when...

<meta>catchword: he says,</meta>

He says, "Finally, the punishment is of this sort: that a sterile soul <note>original: *sterilis anima*; referring to a soul that has produced no spiritual fruit or knowledge during its life</note> migrates by judgment into a certain body in which there is the nature of neither male nor female." It is as if he were saying openly that through such a body, the soul might never perform good works, nor would it ever be capable of receiving anything of the Good. Therefore, you must flee the sterility of the soul with all your might, and instead beget offspring <note>In Hermetic thought, "offspring" usually refers to virtues, wisdom, or the pursuit of divine truth</note> which shall one day make you blessed. In this way, imitate the fecundity of the Father—who is always begetting—with the fecundity of your own mind, as much as you are able. This is the summary of Aesculapius.

### The Sacred Discourse of Mercury. III.

The glory of all things is God: the divine, and divine nature, is the principle of the universe. God is mind, nature, action, necessity, the end, and renewal. For there was an infinite shadow in the abyss <note>original: *abysso*; the primordial deep or void before creation</note>, and water above it; and a subtle, intellectual spirit <term>intellectual spirit: the *spiritus intellectualis* or divine breath that contains the blueprints of the cosmos</term> existed within the chaos by divine power. Then a holy splendor flourished, which led forth the elements from beneath the sand and the moist nature; and all the gods <note>In this context, "gods" often refers to the planetary powers or celestial administrators of the universe</note> chose a seminal nature. When all things were yet indistinct, the light elements eventually flew up into the high region, while the heavy elements settled beneath the moist sand. Once all things were distinguished and balanced, being carried by a fiery spirit, the heaven shone forth in seven circles <note>The "seven circles" refer to the ancient geocentric model of the universe, consisting of the orbits of the Moon, Mercury, Venus, the Sun, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</note>. The gods appeared in the forms of stars, along with all their signs...

### Hermes to Tat: The Mixing Bowl, or the Monad
### IV.

The Creator fashioned the entire universe by the Word <note>original: *verbo*; translating the Greek *Logos*, implying both speech and divine reason</note>, not with hands. You should think of Him in this way: as always present, acting in all things, the one God establishing all things by His will. For this is His "body"—not something tangible, nor visible, not measurable, nor distant, nor like any other thing. For He is neither fire, nor water, nor air, nor spirit; rather, all these things depend on Him. He is Goodness itself, so much so that it belongs to Him alone. He also willed to adorn the Earth with the beauty of divine craftsmanship. Therefore, He sent down Man, a mortal creature among living things. And while the world is filled with living beings through intellect and reason, Man was made to be a spectator <note>original: *contemplator*; a witness or observer who learns through sight</note> of the divine work; indeed, while he was admiring it, he came to recognize its Author. Speech, indeed, O Tat...

O Tat, God shared speech <note>original: *sermonem*; while the text here starts with "shared," the context of the Greek original and the following paragraphs implies the sharing of basic human reason or language with all, contrasted with the higher Mind</note> with every individual person, but Mind <note>original: *mentem*; translating the Greek *nous*, which refers to a higher, divine faculty of intuition and understanding</note> by no means to everyone. Therefore, as many as listened to the herald and immersed themselves in Mind, these became partakers of knowledge <note>original: *cognitionis*; meaning *gnosis*, or direct spiritual insight</note>; and receiving Mind, they turned out to be perfect men. But those who neglected the herald’s proclamation, they indeed partake in speech <note>original: *sermonis*; the basic human capacity for language and logic</note>, but are devoid of Mind, and are left in ignorance of why and by whom they were brought into being. Furthermore, the senses of these people are like those of irrational animals; thus, being entangled in desire, they do not admire those things worthy of contemplation. For, enslaved to the lusts of the body, they believe [that Man was] born for these things...

...threeness <note>original: *τριότητα*; likely referring to a "triad" or the Trinity, reflecting a Christianized interpretation of the Hermetic text common during the Renaissance</note>. Toward all divination, toward idolatry, the rites of the gods, initiations—or more accurately, "will-worship" <note>original: *thelothrescias*; a term meaning self-imposed or artificial religiosity</note>—magic arts, theurgy <note>original: *theurgias*; rituals meant to invoke divine presence</note>, fate, the demiurgic gods <note>original: *opifices deos*; the lesser gods or forces that physically craft the world</note>, and many such impure and wicked things. <margin>IV</margin>

## Hermes to Tat: The Mixing Bowl, or the Monad <note>original: *Crater, siue Monas*; the "Mixing Bowl" is a central Hermetic metaphor for a vessel of divine Mind</note>

The Creator <note>original: *opifex*; the divine craftsman or demiurge</note> fashioned the entire world by a word, not by hands. Think of Him in this way: as one present and always acting in all things, the unique God establishing all things by His will. For this is His body: not tangible, not visible, not measurable, not distant, nor like anything else. For it is neither fire, nor water, nor air, nor spirit; truly, all these things depend on Him. But the Good is such that it belongs to Him alone. He willed also to adorn the earth with the decoration of a divine work. Therefore, He sent down Man—a mortal creature to inhabit the divine creation <note>the Latin *mortalis animantis, mortale animal* emphasizes the human role as a mortal observer in an immortal cosmos</note>. And the world indeed is filled with the living creatures of a world that lives through intellect and reason. For man was made a contemplator of the divine work; and truly, while he wondered at it, he came to know its author. Speech indeed, O Tat...

<header>PIMANDER <note>While "Pimander" is the title of the first book, it was often used as a general header for the entire Hermetic collection in early modern editions.</note></header>

... O Tat, God imparted speech <note>original: *sermonem*; likely translating the Greek *logos*, here referring to human reason or language</note> to every individual person, but the Mind <note>original: *mentem*; the Greek *Nous*, or divine intellect</note> He did not. Not because He felt envy toward any, for envy does not proceed from Him, but rather from those who dwell with the souls of men who lack Mind. **TAT.** Why, O father, did God not share the Mind with everyone? **TR.** <note>Abbreviation for Trismegistus (Hermes)</note> Because, O son, He willed to set it in the middle as a prize and a reward for souls to strive for. **TAT.** Where then did He place it? **TR.** When He had filled a wide bowl <note>original: *craterem*; a large vessel used for mixing wine and water, here symbolizing a font of divine essence</note> with this Mind, He sent a herald, commanding him to announce such things as these to the souls of men: "Let whatever soul that is able dip itself into this vessel, the one which believes it will return to Him who sent it down, and which knows for what purpose it was born." Whosoever therefore listened to the herald and cast themselves into the Mind, they became partakers of true knowledge <note>original: *cognitionis*; likely referring to *Gnosis*, or spiritual insight</note>, and having received the Mind, they emerged as perfect men. But those who ignored the proclamation remained partakers of speech indeed, but devoid of Mind; they were left ignorant of why they were created and by whom. Furthermore, the senses of these people are like the senses of irrational animals; and so, being entangled in desire, they by no means admire those things worthy of contemplation. For, enslaved to the lusts of the body, [they believe man was] born for these things...

...consider him merely a man. But whoever are supported by the nature of God, O Tat, through the comparison of their works, are regarded as immortals rather than mortals. They embrace all things with their intellect <note>original: *intelligentia*; referring to the higher faculty of divine understanding</note>—everything on earth, in the sea, and whatever might exist beyond the heavens. And so they raise themselves up to behold the Good itself. Indeed, when they perceive it, they consider this life we lead here to be a kind of misery. Despising all corporeal things, they are drawn toward the One alone.

This, O Tat, is what it means to have earned the knowledge <note>original: *scientiam*; here implying *Gnosis*, or direct spiritual insight</note> of divine things: it is the contemplation of the intellect of God through the existence of the divine vessel <note>original: *cratere*; the "Mixing Bowl" or vessel of Divine Mind mentioned on the previous page</note>.

**TAT.** Father, I truly desire to be washed in the waters of this vessel.

**TR.** <note>Abbreviation for Trismegistus</note> Unless you first hate your body, O son, you will not be able to love yourself. But once you love not yourself, but God Himself, you will immediately attain the Mind <note>original: *mentem*; the *Nous*, or Divine Intellect</note>. And having finally obtained this, you will immediately possess true knowledge.

**TAT.** How can you say this, O father?

**TR.** It is impossible, O son, to focus on both at once—that is, on the mortal and the divine. For since there are only two things in the order of reality, the corporeal and the incorporeal—the former being called mortal and the latter divine—by the choice of one, we lose the other. Whenever our care for one is relaxed, the activity of the other is intensified. Therefore, the choice of the better...

Yet such knowledge is not the beginning of the Good itself, but it provides for us the beginning of that which is known. Therefore, let us embrace this Beginning. ->### MERCVRII TRISM.<-

...higher things and to turn oneself toward more powerful things. For those things which we perceive with our eyes delight us excessively, while hidden things produce distrust. Moreover, manifest things are surely evils, while the Good is hidden from those who devote themselves to things that are apparent. For it <note>Referring to the "Good" or the Divine essence</note> has neither form nor figure. For this reason, it is like only to itself, and unlike all other things. Indeed, the incorporeal cannot appear to the body; such is the difference between the similar and the dissimilar, and the inferiority of the dissimilar to that which is similar.

The <term>Monad</term> <note>original: *Monas*; in Hermetic philosophy, this refers to the 'One' or the absolute unity that precedes all multiplicity</note>, that is, Unity, is the principle, root, and origin of all things; but without a principle, there is nothing. A beginning <note>original: *initium*</note>, however, is not the principle of itself, but of something else. The Monad, therefore, is the principle; it contains every number while being contained by none, and it begets every number while being begotten by no number. Whatever is begotten is surely imperfect, divisible, subject to growth and to decay. To that which is perfect, however, none of these things happen. Indeed, that which increases, increases by the power of the Monad; but it fades away through its own weakness when it can no longer contain the Monad.

Let this, O Tat, be a sketch <note>original: *subscripta*; literally an outline or description written down</note> of the image of God for you, as far as I am able. If you consider it diligently and come to know it with your internal eyes, believe me, my son, you will find the way of ascent to the heights. Moreover, the image itself will lead you; for the act of vision has a certain power of its own, and it <insert>seizes</insert> those who burn with the desire to behold it,

# PIMANDER

...will take hold of you, and draw you in the same way as the stone called a magnet <note>original: *magnes*; a common Renaissance metaphor for spiritual attraction or "sympathy" between the divine and the soul</note> draws iron.

### COMMENTARIES.

The fourth discourse exhorts us to lay hold of wisdom, which is the open mixing-bowl <term>Crater</term> <note>original: *crater*; in Hermetic thought, this is a vessel filled with Mind (Nous) sent down by God for souls to dip into to attain enlightenment</note> of the divine mind. Whichever soul immerses itself into this, being made a partaker of knowledge, looks up toward the Mind. But truly, so that the soul may raise itself to it, it is necessary for it to transcend the heavens themselves, to overcome the circuit of the stars and their movements, and to leave the choirs of the blessed far below. Then it stretches toward the one and only God, the unsurpassable and infinite Good without end; when the soul beholds this, it looks down upon all bodies and considers the life we live here to be misery, its desires intent only upon the incorporeal Good. Yet no one is able to immerse themselves in the divine mixing-bowl who has not hated their own body, and who has not loved God himself rather than themselves, and who, neglecting mortal things, has not clung to divine things alone, remained present with them alone, meditated upon them alone, and burned for them alone. Presently, through the analogy of unity and numbers, the discourse raises us to contemplate the true <term>Monad</term> <note>The 'One' or absolute unity that precedes all plurality</note> and the true numbers of nature. This is "The Mixing-Bowl."

### MERCURY TRISMEGISTUS

...be lacking to you, nor should you be ignorant of that which, although hidden to many, appears to be clear. For if it were manifest nowhere, it would certainly be nothing. Whatever offers itself to the sight is begotten <note>original: *genitum*; referring to things that have a beginning in time or are created in the physical world</note>. But that which is hidden is eternal. Nor is there a need for it to appear, since it never ceases to be. Indeed, it places all other things before our eyes, while it itself remains secret, as one that enjoys eternal life. For imagination <term>phantasia</term> <note>original: *phantasia*; in this context, the mental faculty that processes sensory images of the material world</note> is concerned only with things that are begotten, in which nothing exists beyond the process of generation. But that unique, unbegotten <term>ingenitum</term> thing is incomprehensible to the imagination. 

Since, however, all things are made clear through Him, He shines again through all things and in all things. And He appears especially to those to whom He has chosen to communicate knowledge. You therefore, O my son Tat, first of all entreat with pious prayers the Lord and Father—the only one, the One, and the source from whom the One comes—that you may be worthy of His mercy. Thus at last you will be able to perceive so great a God, if even just one ray of His light shines kindly upon your understanding. For only hidden understanding <term>intellectio</term> <note>original: *intellectio*; the higher intuitive grasp of the mind rather than mere logical reasoning</note> perceives hidden things; therefore, if you look with the eyes of the mind, O Tat, He will be manifest to you (believe me). Indeed God, being entirely free from envy <note>The author uses a common Platonic idea that God, being perfectly good, lacks "envy" and therefore does not hide Himself out of spite, but desires to be known</note>, shines everywhere through every individual part of the world, and shows Himself to be so known that you may not only understand Him, but even—so to speak—[handle Him] with your very hands... <note>The text breaks off here; the catchword "ceat" suggests the next word is *liceat*, meaning "it may be permitted" to handle or perceive Him freely</note>

...is permitted <note>The text likely begins with a completion of the phrase "free from envy, so that it is permitted"</note> to touch Him. For from all sides His image is observed by our eyes; it presents itself and impresses itself upon us. But if even what is lowest is hidden from you, how will you find either yourself or Him? Finally, when you wish to see God, look up at the order of the other stars; tell me, who preserves the perpetual order of these things? Indeed, every order is bounded by the limits of number and place. The Sun is the most excellent of the celestial gods. The rest of the heavenly beings <note>original: *coelites*; inhabitants of heaven</note> obey the Sun as if he were their prince and king. The Sun, so great—being larger than both the earth and the sea at once—nevertheless allows the countless smaller stars above him to revolve. Whom does he fear? Whom does he respect? O son, the movements of the stars are diverse. Who assigns the measure of movement to each one?

**T A T .** Arcturus <note>The brightest star in the northern constellation of Boötes, used here to represent the turning of the celestial sphere</note> perpetually turning around the same point, and pulling the entire machinery of the world <note>original: *mundi machinam*; a common metaphor for the universe as a complex, ordered system</note> along with it.

**T R I S .** Who uses this instrument? Who has enclosed the sea within its borders? Who halts the weight of the earth and balances it in the center? Surely, O Tat, there is some author and lord of these things. For indeed, to maintain place, or number, or measure without the power of an author is impossible. Order cannot arise from shapelessness <term>deformitas</term> <note>original: *deformitas*; here meaning chaos or a lack of formative structure</note>. For shapelessness lacks a master who may provide order. If only the ability were given to you, O son, that with the help of wings you might fly into the lofty region of the air, and having attained <note>original: *fortitus*; the text breaks here at the catchword "titus"</note> the region between heaven and earth...

...Titus, <note>In this Latin translation, the son of Hermes, usually called "Tat," is referred to as "Titus."</note> you would behold the solidity of the earth, the spreading out of the sea, the flow of rivers, the vastness of the air, and the swift intensity of fire. O most happy spectacle, my son! O most blessed vision! If indeed by one movement of your eyes <note>original: *luminum motu*; literally "the movement of the lights," referring to the eyes as the source of sight.</note> you could grasp the sequence of the entire world, and you would perceive the unmoved Maker as he moves, both hidden and yet clearly visible. 

But if you also wish to investigate God the craftsman through those things sustained by the earth—things which are fragile or hidden in the depths of the waters—come, my son, look around at the construction of the human body. Through its instruction, learn thoroughly: who is the founder of so beautiful an image? Who is the painter of the eyes? Who fashioned <note>original: *tornauit*; to turn on a lathe, implying precise craftsmanship.</note> the nose and the ears? Who stretched the lips of the mouth? Who tightened and bound the nerves? Who irrigated the veins? Who assembled the solid bones? Who covered the flesh with a thin skin? Who separated the fingers and the joints? Who extended the foundations of the feet? Who pierced the pores and opened the passages? Who gathered and compressed the spleen? Who impressed the pyramid shape upon the heart? <note>The pyramid or cone was a common classical description for the anatomical shape of the heart.</note> Who further wove the fibers of the liver? Who carved the pipes of the lungs? Who gave the belly its capacious breadth? Who shaped the honorable members of the body in the open, and who hid the private <note>original: *obscœna*; literally "unclean" or "shameful," referring here to the reproductive organs in accordance with the modesty of the period.</note> parts entirely in darkness, and willed that they lie secret from the sight of those looking on?

See how many works of divine art are demonstrated in a single substance, each one beautiful, rightly measured, and differing from one another by their own specific functions. Who then fashioned these individual things? What kind of mother, what kind of father? Was it not the invisible God himself alone, who labored over all of them by his own will? And since no one would dare to assert that a statue or a painting <note>original: *imaginẽ*; literally "an image," but in this context referring to a portrait or artistic representation.</note> could be made without a craftsman or a painter, shall we think that this wondrous constitution of the world was established without a Founder? 

O blind little man! <note>original: *homunculũ*; a diminutive, often used here to emphasize the insignificance or ignorance of humans compared to the divine.</note> O too impious! O one overwhelmed by the deep darkness of ignorance! Beware, I say, O my son Tat, <note>Latin: *Tati*; the vocative form of Tat, the son of Hermes. The previous page translated this name as Titus.</note> lest you ever strip the craftsmanship of its craftsman; rather, having called upon God by his fitting name, consider him to be its true father. 

But if you force me to put forward something bolder, I would say his essence is to conceive and to make all things. Just as nothing can be made without a maker, so it is impossible for God to exist always unless he always acts upon all things—namely, in the heavens, the air, the earth, the sea, in the whole world, in any small part of the world, both in that which exists and in that which does not yet stand forth. <note>original: *non extat*; referring to things that have not yet been manifested or created.</note> There is nothing in all of nature which he himself is not. For he is indeed those things that are. He is even those things that are not. <note>This reflects the Hermetic "Panentheism," the idea that God is both the creator of the world and the world itself.</note> Those things that are, he has brought into the light; those things that are not, he hides within himself. This God, in name [greater?]...

### C O M M E N T A R I E S .

*The fifth lesson teaches that God is equally hidden and yet shines through every single particle of the world. All things that present themselves to us are His images, so that the wonderful and very beautiful order of things clearly declares the One who orders them. Individual things, circumscribed by their certain limits, declare their Lord and Author, whom the sun—the king and prince of the stars—obeys and serves, whom it fears and reveres; in short, the entire structure of the world declares its craftsman. Soon, the author offers a more confident judgment regarding the divine internal generation: that it is the essence of God to conceive and to make all things, so that it would be impossible for God to exist unless He is always acting upon all things. For the divine <term>Logos: the "Word" or "Reason" that acts as the blueprint and animating force of the universe</term> is thus all things, yet also none of them; in Him, the corporeal and incorporeal being, as well as nothingness, harmonize and coincide. Finally, Mercury <note>original: *Mercurius*; the Latin name for Hermes Trismegistus.</note> finishes and ends the dialogue in songs of divine praise.*

<page-num>404</page-num>

O Aesculapius <note>The legendary Greek god of medicine, portrayed here as a student of Hermes.</note>, the Good is found in nothing except in the one God; rather, God himself is always the Good itself. For this reason, it is necessary that God be the essence of all motion and of all knowledge. Nothing is deprived of this essence. This essence possesses within itself a stable power <note>original: "actum"; in a philosophical sense, this refers to 'actuality' or 'realized power' rather than a single deed.</note> that lacks for nothing, extending an infinite abundance. This is the one principle of all things, extending the good and pouring forth the good. Whenever I speak of the Good, understand it to mean that which contains all good things and which is always good. This belongs to the one God alone.

For He is not in need of anything, such that He might become evil by desiring to acquire it; nor can the loss of anything ever happen to Him, such that He would be afflicted by grief following a loss. For He is greater than any portion of evil, nor is there anything stronger than Him by which He might be conquered. No injury can fall upon Him by which He might be provoked or incited to rage. Nothing escapes His yoke <note>A metaphor for divine authority or the natural laws governing the universe.</note> whereby, being held in contempt, He would feel indignation or anger; nor is there anything wiser than Him that might provoke Him to envy <note>original: "aemulationem"; suggesting a sense of rivalry or jealous competition.</note>. Thus, since these things do not happen to Him, nothing remained of His nature except the Good itself. 

But just as none of those things which are evil exist within this essence, so also the Good is found in nothing else. For in all other individual things, various other qualities are present, both in the small and in the great, and also in...

Thus it happens that our "good" is nothing else than the smallest portion of evil. From this it also follows that a good of this kind cannot be separated from evil.

## C O M M E N T A R I E S

*Sextus <note>Likely referring to the sixth book or a specific commentator</note> contends this: that in God alone the Good and the nature of the Good is found—that is, goodness itself—along with the nature of beauty, power, and wisdom. Thus says Sextus.*

### That the greatest evil for men is to be ignorant of God.

<margin>VII.</margin>
Where are you rushing, drunken mortals, you who have drunk deep the unmixed wine of ignorance? Since you cannot bear it, vomit it up! Live soberly; look upward with the eyes of the mind. Even if all of you cannot do so, at least let those who are able do it. This plague of ignorance subverts the whole earth and corrupts the soul imprisoned in the chains of the body, nor does it allow it to take up the path of salvation. Do not permit yourselves to be submerged in the lake of corruption and death. Breathe now, breathe! Return to the fountain of life, and take hold of Him <note>original: "capessite"; meaning to seize or grasp eagerly</note> who will lead you into the inner sanctuary of truth.

Above all, however, it is necessary to strip off the garment you wear—the cloak of ignorance, the foundation of wickedness, the chain of corruption, the dark veil, a living death, a sentient corpse, a portable tomb, and finally, a thief in the house who hates while he flatters, and envies while he hates. Of such a kind is the hostile shadow in which you are wrapped. It drags you down to itself, lest by chance, beholding the beauty of truth and the nearby Good, you might hate its own wickedness; or lest you should ever perceive the snares it constantly plots against you. This dulls and blunts the edge of the internal senses; it chokes them with thick matter and intoxicates them with abominable and loathsome pleasure, so that you may never hear or see those things which by right ought to be heard and, above all, to be gazed upon.

### COMMENTARY

The eighth tractate teaches first that the celestial bodies constantly maintain one and the same course, which they initially received from their Father. It also teaches that death and destruction appear first among the living bodies of the earth, but that the name of "death" and the "destruction" of bodies is almost a hollow term; for indeed, the bodies themselves are merely changed, they do not perish. Rather, God exchanges those very qualities—the images and likenesses of the <term>Ideas</term><note>In Hermetic and Platonic philosophy, "Ideas" are the perfect, eternal archetypes of which physical things are mere copies.</note> with which he wished to adorn matter—with immortal matter. 

And man is an immortal <term>living being</term><note>original: "animal"; here meaning a being endowed with "anima" or soul.</note>, yet dissoluble; he is the bond and the knot of all nature, being partly bodily and partly incorporeal. He was created in the likeness of the world and is capable of higher intellect, so that he might understand the sensible world <note>The physical world that can be perceived by the senses.</note> and, through his mind, rise toward the Supreme Mind in joyful contemplation. Thus ends the eighth tractate.

In Hermetic philosophy, these are not necessarily "devils" in the modern sense, but intermediary spirits that can influence human thoughts and impulses, often associated with the lower material world.</note>; their light descends entirely from God himself. When a demon is poured into a man, it scatters the seeds of its own nature. The mind, having been sown with these seeds and made pregnant, then gives birth to adultery, debauchery, homicide, parricide, sacrilege, contempt for divine things, throat-cuttings, the overthrowing of cities, the plagues of mankind, and all other such things which are the works of evil demons. 

Clearly, God’s seeds are few, but they are truly great, beautiful, and good: namely virtue, self-control, and **piety**. <term>Piety</term><note>original: "pietas."</note>, moreover, is the **knowledge of God**. He who recognizes God, being filled with all good things, attains divine conceptions—conceptions, I say, that are not like those of the many. 

For this reason, if any dedicate themselves to this <term>knowledge</term><note>original: "cognitio"; often used to translate the Greek "gnosis," implying a direct, experiential understanding of the divine.</note>, they neither please the common people, nor does the crowd please them. Indeed, they are ultimately thought to be insane and are mocked; sometimes they are even hated, subjected to insults, and deprived of life. For we have said that wickedness dwells here, and that the earth is its province—I say the **earth**, not the **entire world**<note>original: "non mundum totum"; the author distinguishes between the physical Earth (the realm of change and decay) and the "Cosmos" or Universe, which he considers a divine and harmonious creation.</note>, as some impious people wrongly claim. 

Nevertheless, a man devoted to God, as soon as he has tasted the divine vision, consigns all other things to oblivion. And also, those things which are evils to other men happen to him as goods, as he considers them wisely.

In Hermetic philosophy, "sense" or "perception" is the gateway through which the mind receives information from the material world.</note>. However, some things that are born good become sterile in the practical use of their activity. For the revolution of the world, which drives the cycles of birth, produces certain qualities—staining and defiling some with evil, while protecting and purifying others with good.

For the perception and intelligence of the world is this one thing: namely, to create all things and to dissolve them again. It is the instrument of the divine will, constructed for this primary purpose: that receiving all seeds from God and hiding them within its vast bosom, it might produce all things by joining them together, and again take them all away by dividing them.

### ->MERCURY TRISMEGISTUS<-

...it received its origin from God, and preserves it perpetually.

God is certainly not, as it seems to some, deprived of sense and mind. For those people, oppressed by their own misery, speak wrongly and slanderously. Whatever things exist, O Asclepius, are simultaneously in God and dependent upon God—some acting through the body, some moving through the <term>vital essence</term><note>original: "essentiam animalis." In this context, it refers to the soul-force or the animating principle that distinguishes living things from inanimate matter.</note>, others giving life through the spirit, and others serving as the <term>receptacles of the dead</term><note>original: "receptacula defunctorum." This likely refers to physical matter or the earth itself, which receives the remains of living things once the vital spirit has departed.</note>.

We would say more correctly, however, that God does not merely "possess" such things, but rather, to express the clear truth, we shall confess that he **is** all things. Nor does he receive these qualities from the outside, for he stretches nothing toward the outside <note>This suggests God is all-encompassing; there is no "outside" for him to reach into or receive from.</note>; that is the very sense and understanding of God. Hence, there will never be a time in which anything that exists vanishes into nothingness. Whenever I say "existing things," I am speaking of God’s **treasure**; for God himself embraces all of existence. Outside of Him there is nothing, and outside of "nothing," he is himself.

These things, O Asclepius, will seem true to one who understands; but to the ignorant, they will seem unbelievable. For to understand is itself to believe; but not to believe is, without doubt, to be ignorant. Indeed, my discourse has run all the way to the truth. A mind that is spacious, and led by discourse to a certain certainty, has reached the truth. Finally, when the mind comprehends all things and finds them to be in harmony with those things it was interpreting, it believes immediately, and in that very faith...

## COMMENTARIES.

*The <term>Mind</term><note>original: "Nous." In the Hermetic tradition, Nous refers to the Divine Intellect or the higher faculty of human reason that connects a person to God.</note> instructs humanity. While all people possess the faculty of understanding, those who are material-minded conceive their thoughts from the seeds of <term>daemons</term><note>original: "daemonum." In this historical context, daemons were viewed as intermediary spirits—neither strictly good nor evil—that could influence human impulses and the physical world.</note>. No part of the world is free from their presence. Once pregnant with these influences, such people eventually give birth to adultery, debauchery, murder, parricide, and every kind of shameful crime. In contrast, those who are spiritual and focused on the true essence of things conceive every adornment of virtue with God as their sower, and they bring forth every good and virtuous deed.*

*For the seeds of God are few, yet they are great, beautiful, and good—far superior to the countless multitude of vices. However, those who follow these seeds do not please the common crowd, nor does the crowd please them. They are ultimately thought to be insane and are mocked, for the earth is the very seat and province of wickedness. Yet the world was formed by this law: that by receiving all seeds from God, it might become an instrument worthy of divinity. Thus, all things would proceed toward their birth in a wonderful beauty of orderly arrangement, persevere in that state, and finally reach their natural end. This would certainly be the case, were it not for the Enemy coming into the midst of...*

### The Key of Hermes Trismegistus to
### Tat.

I dedicated yesterday’s discourse to you, O Asclepius; therefore, it is right to dedicate today’s to Tat, and all the more so because the present discussion will be a concise summary of all the things we have spoken to him previously. God, and the Father, and <term>the Good</term><note>original: "bonum." In Hermetic philosophy, "The Good" is not just a moral quality but the ultimate source and essence of reality.</note>, O Tat, possess the same nature, or rather, the same activity. For "Nature" is a name for growth and <term>divine providence</term><note>original: "divinationis." Here meaning the foresight or administrative power of the divine over the world.</note> which concerns things both changeable and unchangeable—that is, the human and the divine—every one of which He wills to exist. 

Elsewhere, however, His activity <note>original: "actum." Referring to the "actualization" or the way God's power manifests in the world.</note> (as we have shown in other places) concerns both divine and human things, which must indeed be understood in this context. The will is the expression of this activity, and His essence is to will that all things exist. What is God, and the Father, and the Good, if not the very being of all these things that do not yet exist? Moreover, the very existence of these same things is exactly that: it is God, it is the Father, it is the Good, to whom nothing else from all existing things is joined. For the world and the sun [are] of those things which [follow]...

...according to <term>participation</term><note>original: "participationem." A philosophical concept where lower beings share in the qualities or essence of a higher source without diminishing that source.</note> He is the Father, yet not for the living is He the cause of life and goodness. For if this is the case, the living being is moved by being encompassed by the will of the Good, without which it is impossible for anything ever to be or to become. And because He receives nothing, He wills that all things exist. I do not say, O Tat, that He *makes* all things; for the one who makes, failing over a long period of time, is unworthy of the task. For sometimes such a maker works, and sometimes he ceases, being in need of both quantity and quality—sometimes arranging things of such a quality and such a quantity, and at other times their opposites. But God is both Father and the Good, by the very fact that He is all things. Therefore, such a being is able to command these things; for He wills them to be, and they are. And this is especially true for Himself, for all other things exist because of Him. Indeed, it is the property of the Good, O Tat, to make itself known. That is the Good, O Tat.

But if a soul has fallen into a human body and persists in evil, it tastes nothing of immortality, nor does it enjoy the Good. Instead, its journey is reversed, and it is cast headlong back into reptiles. This is surely the judgment and the punishment of an evil soul: the depravity of the soul is <term>ignorance</term>.<note>original: "ignorantia." In Hermeticism, spiritual ignorance—forgetting one's divine origin—is considered the greatest vice and the source of all evil.</note> A soul that is ignorant of the nature of things and of the Good, blinded in its eyes, entangles itself in the passions of the body. Such a soul...

### PIMANDER

D 5

...the second of those things that exist. Lacking, moreover, by its very nature, having been made at some point, yet always existing in <term>becoming</term><note>original: "generatione." In this philosophical context, it refers to the state of "coming-to-be"—the constant flux of the physical world compared to the stillness of the divine.</note>, and being the offspring of all qualities and quantities. For it is mobile. Indeed, every material motion ought to be called becoming. The <term>intelligible</term><note>original: "intelligibilis." Refers to the realm of pure thought or spirit, which can be understood by the mind but not seen with the eyes.</note> state also drives material motion in this manner.

Since the world is a sphere—that is, a head—there is nothing material above it; just as there is nothing intelligible beneath its feet, but all things are material. Mind, indeed, drives the head in a circle—that is, a movement according to the nature of the head. Therefore, all those things that are contiguous to the membranes of that head—which is truly the soul—are born immortal, as if the body were established within the soul; and those things having a soul are full of body. 

But whatever is far from the membrane—in which those things exist that participate more fully in the soul—exists as body. The whole, however, is a living being. Thus, the world is composed of something material and something intelligible.

The world is the first living being; man is the second after the world. Man is the first, however, among all other living creatures. Whatever function of the soul is granted to others, man also possesses. And he is weighed as being not only "not good," but even "evil," insofar as he is mortal. For the world is not good, because it is in motion; yet it is not evil, because it is immortal.

...two, and immortal: whereas on earth they are changeable and subject to corruption. God is the soul of Eternity; eternity is the soul of the world; and heaven is the soul of the earth. God is in the mind, the mind is in the soul, and the soul is in matter. All these things exist through the age <note>original: "æuum" (Aion). In this philosophy, the Aion is a middle state of duration—more than human time but less than God’s absolute eternity—that keeps the universe stable.</note>, throughout this entire body which contains all other bodies. The soul, being full of mind and of God, fills the inner parts of the world and encompasses its outer boundaries, providing life to all things. It provides this life outwardly to the world itself—which is a vast and perfect living being <note>The Hermetic tradition views the entire universe as a "perfect animal" or living organism animated by a world-soul.</note>—and inwardly to all the other living creatures that dwell within the world. Above in the heavens, which remain ever the same, the soul holds all things steady; but below on the earth, it sets the process of generation <note>The cycle of birth, growth, and death.</note> in motion.

Truly, the age contains the world, whether through necessity, providence, or nature; and whatever else a person thinks of, or will ever think of, it is God who performs it all. The activity of God is an insuperable power, with which no one would dare compare any human power, nor even any other divine power. Therefore, take care, O Mercury, that you do not consider anything in the lower realms, or even in the higher realms, to be like God; for if you did, you would wander far from the truth. Indeed, nothing is like Him, for He is unique, alone, and One. Nor should you think that any other being possesses the same power that belongs to God; for what else after Him is capable of both immortality and the transformation of qualities? <note>This refers to the ability to change the very essence or "quality" of a thing while maintaining its existence.</note> What else besides this...

To even suspect such a thing is a sacrilege <note>original: "nefas." An act against divine law or a moral impossibility.</note>. 

But if it is granted that nothing in the nature of things exists which does not possess a certain natural vigor for acting, as well as the execution of a specific task, how much more must it be asserted that God lacks neither the power nor the effect of all things? For whatever is idle is imperfect. And to call God imperfect is a sacrilege. Therefore, God makes all things.

And that work, O my sweetest Mercury, is life; it is truly beauty, it is goodness, and finally, it is God.

### C O M M E N T A R I E S.

The eleventh [discourse] concerning the mind, a divine sermon, fully declares that eternity depends on God, the world depends on eternity, time on the world, and change <note>original: "transmutationem," referring to the constant shifting and flux of the material world.</note> on time; and from change, both death and life depend. It weightily demonstrates through both reason and analogy that no power—neither divine, nor human, nor of the beings above, nor of those below—is comparable to the insuperable power of God. He is the only One. Since He cannot be idle, He is always making all things; you may rightly understand this as what is said regarding the eternal generation of the Word <note>The commentator here links the Hermetic text to Christian theology, specifically the "Logos" or eternal Word mentioned in the Gospel of John.</note>. For it says that the divine work was necessary for existence, so that those things which are being made, those which were made, and those which will be made in the future might exist. That work is life, it is the beautiful, it is the good, and it is, finally, God and the life of all. But what is this except that which the most high—

The Evangelist sounded the trumpet like a herald when he said: *In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. This was in the beginning with God; all things were made through Him, and without Him nothing was made that was made; in Him was life.* <note>original: "In principio erat verbum..." — This is a direct citation of the opening of the Gospel of John, which the commentator uses to bridge Hermetic philosophy with Christian scripture.</note> Therefore, the life of all things flows from God, and that life itself is God. From this it follows that what is commonly thought to be death is not a true death or a real destruction of things, but rather that life, withdrawing itself into a hidden place, deserts the living thing. Indeed, he uses a wonderful proportion <note>In this context, "proportion" refers to a rational or mathematical relationship used to describe the nature of the divine.</note> to grasp Him who escapes all proportion—He who, though grasped, remains incomprehensible, and who, though unknown to all, makes Himself known in all things. Therefore, all you who are pious, attend now with your whole being and incline your own minds to the discourses of the Mind, so that you may finally know Him who fashioned all things for this reason: so that you might perceive Him through each individual thing. 
This concludes the discourse of the Mind.

### Mercury to Tat: On the common Mind. XII. <note>The twelfth book of the *Corpus Hermeticum* traditionally discusses how the "Mind" (Mens) is distributed among humans and its role in the cosmos.</note>

The Mind, O Tat, is born from the very essence of God—if indeed He has an essence <note>The author uses "if indeed" to suggest that God is "trans-essential," meaning His nature is so high that even the word "essence" (what a thing is) might not be grand enough to describe Him.</note>. Whatever its nature may be, the Mind alone purely understands itself. Therefore, the Mind is by no means divided from the essence of God, but is rather connected to it in the same way that light <note>original: "lumen"</note> is connected to the body of the Sun.

...are the passions of irrational things (as I think): therefore the mind is a kind of <term>passion</term> <note>Latin: *passio*. In this philosophical context, a "passion" is not just an emotion, but any state of being "acted upon" or affected by an external force or internal movement.</note>, for it is shaped by passions. 

**T R I S:** <note>Abbreviation for Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage and "father" in this dialogue.</note> 
Well said, my good son; how nobly you ask! It is right that I should answer you. All things that are <term>incorporeal</term> <note>Non-physical or spiritual entities.</note> within bodies are susceptible to being affected; indeed, they are properly called passions. Every bodily movement, even within the bodies themselves, is moved by the mind. Moreover, motion is a passion. Therefore both—that which is moved, and that which moves—undergo an effect: the latter as the ruler, the former as the subject. 

When, however, the mind is separated from the body, it is freed from these passions. Yet truly, nothing anywhere is entirely incapable of being affected, my son, for all things are susceptible. But "passion" and "that which is susceptible" differ most in this: that one acts and the other is acted upon. 

Bodies also act according to their own nature; for they are either immobile or they are moved; whichever of these it may be, it is a passion. Incorporeal things, however, are always active, and for that reason, they are susceptible to being affected. Let not these names trouble you. For <term>operation</term> <note>Latin: *operatio*. Here meaning "action" or "activity."</note> and "passion" are the same thing; nevertheless, there is no harm in using a more honorable word. 

**T A T.** 
You have given a clear account of these matters, O father. 

**T R.**

God, however, is around all things and simultaneously through all things; the mind is around the soul, the soul is around the air, and the air...

->### MERCURIUS TRISMEGISTUS<-

In other bodies which are composite, there is a specific number for each body. Without number, it is impossible for constitution, composition, or dissolution to occur; for units indeed beget and increase the number, and when they are dissolved again, they draw the number back into themselves.

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Hermes Trismegistus and his son Tat. They are discussing the nature of life and death, arguing that nothing truly perishes in a divinely animated universe, but rather changes form through dissolution and motion.</meta>

# PIMANDER

...is the corruption of life, and corruption is indeed destruction. <note>original: "vitæ corruptio est, corruptio verò pernicies"</note> By what means, therefore, can any part of that which is incorruptible be corrupted, or anything of God be destroyed?

**TAT.** Oh father, do not the animals which are in the world, being parts of the world, perish?

**TRISMEGISTUS.** Speak more correctly, my son. For you err in the term used: nothing in the world dies, but composite bodies <note>Bodies made of multiple elements, such as the four elements of earth, air, fire, and water.</note> are dissolved. <term>Dissolution</term> <note>Latin: *dissolutio*. In Hermetic philosophy, this refers to the breaking apart of a physical form into its component parts, rather than the total end of existence.</note> is not death, but a certain breaking down of the mixture. The union is dissolved, not so that those things which exist might perish, but so that old things might become young again. <note>original: "vetera iuuenescãt". This suggests a cyclical view of nature where matter is recycled into new life.</note>

**TAT.** Since there is a certain operation of life, is this not a certain motion? And therefore, what in the world is immobile?

**TRISMEGISTUS.** Nothing, my son.

**TAT.** Does the earth not seem immobile to you?

**TRISMEGISTUS.** Not at all; rather, it is agitated by many motions, though it alone is in a certain way stable. For would it not be ridiculous if the very nurse of all things, conceiving and bringing forth each thing, were to lack motion? For it is impossible for anything to give birth without motion. That is no less ridiculous than to call that body sterile; for the name "immobile" signifies nothing other than something sterile.

Consider this whole matter generally, my son: everything that is in the world moves either by increasing or by decreasing. But that which moves also lives; however, not all living things are necessarily the same...

->### MERCURY TRISMEGISTUS<-

...must be so. For at the same time, while the entire universe exists, it is indeed immobile as a whole, but its parts are moveable on all sides; yet nothing is subject to corruption, though certain false names trouble men. For generation is not the creation of life, but the unfolding of a hidden life <note>original: "latentis explicatio vitæ". Hermes argues that "birth" is simply life revealing itself, not starting from nothing.</note>; nor is change death, but rather a concealment. Since these things are so, all things are immortal. The matter of life is spirit, and the matter of the soul is mind. <note>In Hermetic thought, "Spirit" (*spiritus*) is often the vital breath or pneuma that connects the physical and the divine, while "Mind" (*mens*) is the highest faculty of the soul.</note> Everything living flows forth from the mind. Therefore, every living thing, through the mind, remains immortal. 

But most immortal of all is man, who receives God <note>original: "Deum capit". For this reason, it is truly said that man knows "those things which are, those which have been, and those which are soon to be brought to pass."

He looks up to heaven and reaches it with his sense; he reaches God...

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Hermes Trismegistus and his son Tat. Hermes is expanding on the idea that the divine is present throughout the universe and that what we perceive as the "world" is actually the visible manifestation of God’s own "members" or attributes.</meta>

->### PIMANDER<-

...indeed, He is around all things at once and through all things; for He is the activity <note>original: "actus". And the participation in all these is the Good itself; nor does anything else happen anywhere, nor has anything been made, where God himself is not present.

**TAT.** Is He therefore in matter, father?

**TRISMEGISTUS.** Matter, my son, is separate from God <note>Hermes is making a distinction between God’s essence and the physical "stuff" of the universe, though God still acts upon it.</note>, so that a proper place may be assigned to it. But if it is formed, it is surely formed by someone; for we have said that the operations of forming are parts of God. From whom...

He clarifies the relationship between God and matter, stating that while God forms matter, matter itself is a separate, originally unformed substance.</summary>

# MERCURY TRISMEGISTUS <note>The Latin text uses "Mercurius Trismegistus," the Roman name for Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage to whom these mystical writings are attributed.</note>

Therefore, individual living beings are granted life, by which they become immortal—at least those who enjoy the gift of immortality; and by which those things that are changeable change—whether you call it <term>matter</term> <note>the physical substance of the universe</note> or the body—remember that these are the activities <note>original: "actus". In this philosophy, God is "pure act," meaning His existence is identical to His doing/creating.</note> of God.

And the activity of matter is the <term>reason</term> <note>original: "rationem". Here meaning the governing principle or logical structure.</note> of matter; the activity of the body is the reason of bodies; the activity of <term>essence</term> <note>the fundamental "being" or soul of a thing</note> is the reason of essence. All of this, in its entirety, exists; nor is there anything in the whole of existence that is not God himself. 

Therefore, neither magnitude <note>size or greatness</note>, nor place, nor quality, nor figure <note>outward shape</note>, nor even time exist around God; for He is the All. And the All is around all things and through all things. Contemplate <note>The Latin "co-" is likely a fragment of "contemplare".</note> this word, O son, and adore it. For the worship of God is but one thing: to not be evil.

->### COMMENTARY<-

*This twelfth section concerns the lower mind, which is an image or a certain footprint of the primary mind. Following the precise definition of the primary mind, this lower mind associates with individual souls. In irrational animals, this mind manifests simply as "nature," but in humans it manifests as reason. Those humans who are deprived of the benefit of reason are carried away, like wild beasts, by a flaming impulse toward the fulfillment of their desires. They set no limit to their lust, nor do they find an end to their own evils and passions...*

<summary>Hermes explains that God is the essential "activity" within matter, bodies, and souls, concluding that true worship is the rejection of evil. The commentary distinguishes between the divine "Reason" in humans and the "Nature" that governs animals.</summary>
<keywords>Hermes Trismegistus, Divine Activity, Pantheism, Essence, Reason vs Nature, Ethics, Immortality</keywords>

# PIMANDER

...the boundary, those who suffer by fate and divine decree, and pay the deserved penalties for their ignorance. Good men, on the contrary, over whom the **Mind** <note>original: "mens". In this context, it refers to the divine intellect or higher consciousness.</note> presides as an image of the good and the beautiful, look up toward the good things that fate has established for them. You shall by no means escape fate; for fate is the divine law itself. However, you are able to escape evils and the punishments that follow as the attendants of wickedness. 

Mercury, full of oracular wisdom, discusses many things; he often heard the oracle pouring forth <note>original: "infundentem". Suggesting a divine flow of knowledge.</note>. He commends two divine gifts in men: **Mind** and **Speech** <note>original: "mentem, atque sermonem". In Greek philosophy, these represent "Nous" and "Logos."</note>. He reveals the oracles of the Good Spirit <note>original: "boni dæmonis". In the ancient world, a 'daemon' was a guiding spirit or lesser deity, not an evil 'demon.'</note>—or if you prefer, of the heavenly spirit breathing with divine inspiration—concerning God, the Word, the world, and matter. He explains that nothing in the world is devoid of life, and nothing should be called "mortal," but rather "dissoluble" <note>meaning something that can be broken down or transformed rather than truly ceasing to exist</note>. He teaches what should be thought: that nothing is immobile. He also teaches that among all dissoluble things, God meets with man alone in various ways, and by what means man can rise from the things of the senses to the perception of God. 

This concludes the twelfth book.

# HERMES TRISMEGISTUS

Then I stood by, pleading that you would finally reveal the nature of <term>regeneration</term> <note>original: "regenerationis"; in this context, it refers to a spiritual rebirth or "being born again" into a divine state of consciousness</note> to me; for that was the only thing then remaining for me to learn. ...[that which is] not colored, not figured, not <note>The OCR text "nõ conc" likely refers to *non concreptum* (not tangible) or *non conclusum* (not enclosed).</note> contained, but naked, clear, understood by itself, the unchangeable good, and the <term>incorporeal</term> <note>original: "incorporeum"; that which lacks a physical body or material substance</note>.

### COMMENTARIES.

*The thirteenth [book] concerns the hidden mystery of regeneration* <note>original: "arcano regenerationis mysterio." In the Hermetic tradition, regeneration is a spiritual rebirth where the soul is purified of earthly vices.</note>, *before which no one was saved; the author of this regeneration is the Son of God [made] man, by the will of the one God. This is a mystery that is not taught, but is hidden in silence, and is worshipped in silence by the holy ones. You, O Christian, read the rest; and if you have been reshaped by a new regeneration in God through the Son of God, having driven away ignorance, sadness, greed, injustice, lust, deceit, envy, fraud, anger, recklessness, and malice—those twelve horrible avengers of darkness* <note>The "twelve avengers" (vltricibus) are the twelve zodiacal vices that, in Hermetic thought, torment the soul until they are expelled by the ten divine virtues.</note>: *exult with your whole mind, having attained the ten opposing powers through the piety of God. Remember to give thanks to God the Reformer with all the strength of your mind; burn entirely with His love. Having become entirely spirit and reborn from the spirit, sing the hymn of piety and hold fast to the spotless piety of regeneration. Turning entirely toward God the Parent and the author of regeneration, His Son, you have attained this fruit from this thirteenth book—or at least you have been stirred by the kindness of His mind to think so piously.*

### MERCURY TRISMEGISTUS.

Since my son Tatius <note>Tatius, often called Tat, is the son and disciple of Hermes Trismegistus in the Hermetic dialogues.</note> (while you were away) wished to learn the nature of all things, and since he himself, being younger and newly approaching the knowledge of each matter, did not want me to delay, I was forced to say a great deal—so that his view of them might be easy and ready. I have therefore judged it worthwhile to choose the more important points from many things and now summarize the preceding discussion for you. For it is permitted to run through certain <term>mysteries|sacred secrets or hidden spiritual truths intended for the initiated</term> with you, since you are one skilled in the nature of things.

All things that are perceived by the senses have been made, and are made daily. These <term>begotten things|genita; in this context, everything in the physical world that has a beginning or is created</term> are not made by themselves, but by another. There are many begotten things, each visible to the senses, and they are different and not entirely alike; yet whatever is begotten proceeds from another.

There is, therefore, some Maker <note>original: "factor"</note> of these things, and he is <term>unbegotten|ingenitus; eternal, having no beginning, and not created by any other power</term>, so that he is older than the things he has made. For we have said that begotten things flow from another. Nothing, however, except for the unbegotten, can be older than the begotten. Indeed, the Maker is more powerful, and unique, and alone truly wise in all things, since nothing at all precedes him. He also rules over the multitude, the size, the action, the continuity, and the differences of all created things. Furthermore, created things are visible; but he is invisible. For this reason he acts: so that he might become visible. Therefore, he always acts. It is worthy to understand, to wonder through understanding, and in wondering...

...and he is the same to himself, both in existing and in acting. Nothing, however, which is <term>begotten|genitum; that which is created or brought into being</term>, is begotten of itself; therefore, it is not made separately from the one who makes it. Whoever removes one of these, loses the other. For by its very nature, each one always looks toward the other nature.

If, therefore, two things are granted—the <term>efficient cause|efficiens; the active force or agent that produces an effect</term> and the effect—they are indeed united to one another, yet in such a way that one precedes and the other follows. The preceding is surely God, the active cause, while the following is that which is produced as the effect. Whatever that may be, let no one distrust what we have said, being intimidated by the sheer variety of things, as if the construction of such diverse objects were either too difficult or unworthy of the divine majesty. 

For the only glory of God is the constitution of all things; and this is, as it were, the body of God the <term>maker|effector; the one who brings form and reality into being</term>. From the maker himself, truly, comes nothing that is evil and nothing that is shameful. For these <term>passions|passiones; in this philosophical context, "passions" refers to accidental defects or "accidents" that happen to matter, rather than human emotions</term> are things that follow after created works, just as rust follows brass or grime follows living bodies. 

But just as the blacksmith did not introduce the rust, nor did the parent of a living body introduce the mud and filth; in the same way, God did not create evil. However, the continuous process of <term>generation|generatio; the constant cycle of things being born and coming into existence</term> causes evil to creep in. For this reason, God established "change" within things, as if it were a kind of purification for the process of creation itself. Furthermore, just as the same painter is permitted to depict the heaven, the earth, the sea,

### COMMENTARIES.

*The fourteenth book asserts these things: that all things which are perceived by the senses have been made, and are continually being made. For just as they flow from another—the one who rules over all things as the Almighty—so also He continually sustains them, lest by their own downward-tending nature they should fall and rush into nothingness. The knowledge of this God alone makes a person happy and blessed; He is the maker of all things, certainly the Father, and He alone is the Creator, and so forth. All things are created, and between the Creator and the created no middle ground can be placed. By this division, the universe is defined: for all things are two—the Creator and the created. Furthermore, he asserts this: that evil does not depend on God (just as the rust on iron does not depend on the blacksmith) but rather follows the works that have been created <note>This is a classic philosophical argument explaining that "evil" is a byproduct of material existence, like rust is an accidental byproduct of metal, rather than an intentional creation of the craftsman.</note>. And he raises us from the contemplation of human art to the understanding of divine art, showing that God Himself sows immortality in heaven, change on earth, and life and motion in the whole world. This is the Epilogue. We have added these few points by way of summary arguments.*
