**TRISMEGISTUS**: O Asclepius, how quickly you have learned the true essence of reason! <note>The "essence of reason" here refers to the *ratio*, or the underlying logic of the universe.</note> For I did not say that "all things are one and one is all things" in a simple sense, but rather that all things existed within the creator before he had created them all. Nor is he undeservedly called "all things," since all things are his members <note>original: "membra". In Hermetic philosophy, the universe is often viewed as a "Great Body" of which all created things are parts or limbs.</note>. Therefore, throughout this entire discussion, take care to remember him who is the "one-all," or the creator of all things himself. 

All things descend from heaven into the earth, and into the water, and into the air. Fire alone, because it is carried upwards, is life-giving <term>vivificum: that which bestows life</term>; that which moves downwards is subservient to it. But indeed, whatever descends from on high is generative <term>generans: the procreative or active force</term>, while that which emanates upwards is nourishing <term>nutriens: the sustaining force</term>. The earth alone, standing firm within itself, is the receiver of all things, and the restorer of all the various kinds of things that it receives. 

Therefore, in this whole system (as you remember) which belongs to all things or *is* all things, the soul and the world are moved, being encompassed by nature. All things are varied by a multiform equality of images in such a way that infinite species of qualities are recognized at intervals, yet they are joined together for this purpose: so that the whole may be seen as one, and all things may be seen to come from the one. Therefore, the elements by which the whole world is formed are

For the logic of divinity <note>original: "divinitatis ratio". Because of this, it outruns the attention not only of the listeners, but even of those who are discussing it, with its swift velocity.

->### COMMENTARY ###<-

*The first chapter teaches that all things belong to the One, and all things are the One: belonging to the One as the source from which all things come, and being the One insofar as all effects are united in their cause. It explains that every human soul is immortal, though their fates may perhaps differ. All things descend from heaven; that which descends provides the power of generation <term>generationem: the active force of procreation or bringing things into existence</term>, while that which ascends and reaches upward provides life itself. This very One—to whom all things belong and who is all things—moves the world and all the world's forms. These forms from which the world was composed are fire, air, water, and earth. Just as all individual bodies make up the single body of the world, the author also argues that all the forms of things create a single, "all-form" <term>omniformem: a form that contains or can take on all possible shapes</term> of the world, which he calls the Soul of the World <note>original: "anima mundi". A central Hermetic concept where the universe is viewed as a single, living, breathing organism.</note>. Therefore, the world possesses every body and every form; and these constitute one body, one soul, and the world*

# ASCLEPIUS #

one, one God, from whom the divine reason <note>original: "divina ratio"</note> and the divine word <note>original: "divinum verbum"</note>—very much like a torrential river rushing down from the heights with headlong speed—permeates all things, glides into all things, and flows into all things. And what else, I ask, is this divine reason and divine word but divine wisdom, the artisan of all things? This wisdom (as the wise man sings) <note>This is a reference to the biblical Book of Wisdom 7:24–27, which describes Wisdom as "more mobile than any motion."</note> is more mobile than all moving things; and though she is one, she can do all things, and remaining within herself, she makes all things new. This concludes the first small part.

->### CHAPTER II. ###<-

The Heaven, therefore, is a sensible god <note>original: "sensibilis deus." In Hermetic philosophy, the physical universe and the heavens were considered "sensible" (perceivable by the senses) deities, distinct from the invisible, supreme God.</note>, the administrator of all bodies, whose growth and decay are allotted to the Sun and Moon. But of heaven itself, and of the soul itself, and of all things that are in the world, God himself—who is the maker of all—is the governor. There is also another genus of living being <term>animalis: used here in the classical sense of "having an anima" or soul; in this context, it refers to plants</term>; a genus indeed without senses, yet not lacking a soul. Because of this, it rejoices in benefits and is diminished and corrupted by adversity—I speak of all those things which live through the health of their roots and stems in the earth, whose species are scattered across the whole world. 

Heaven itself is full of God. The aforementioned genera inhabit it right down to the locations of their species—those things of which all species are immortal. For a species is a part of a genus, just as a man is a part of humanity <note>original: "humanitatis"</note>; it must necessarily follow the quality of its own genus from which it is made. Thus, although all genera are immortal, not all species are immortal. 

In the case of the genus of Divinity, both the genus itself and its species are immortal. Out of necessity, humanity creates many connections with almost all other species. Because of this, the human who joins himself to the gods through divine religion—using the mind <note>original: "mente"</note> by which he is linked to the divine—approaches close to the gods. He who joins himself to the demons, approaches them. But those humans who are content with the middle-state <term>mediocritate: a "middle way" or average state, neither rising to the divine nor descending to the demonic</term> of their own genus, and all other types of men, will be like the species of those genera to which they have attached themselves.

### COMMENTARIES

#### *Chapter Two.*

To help understand the present matters and those that follow, one should not be unaware that **Hermes** <note>original: "Mercurium"</note> uses the word **living being** <term>living being: translated from the Latin "animal," which in this context means any entity endowed with a soul, including the stars and plants</term> and the word **soul** with a far different meaning than we are accustomed to. For in the second dialogue of the *Poimandres* <note>original: "Pimandri"; the first and most famous book of the Corpus Hermeticum</note>, he defines **soul** by **motion**. However, in the following chapter, he defines a **living being** as that which consists of **soul** and **body**.

Therefore, according to his specific way of speaking, whatever possesses a motive power <note>a power that causes movement</note> possesses a soul; and whatever possesses both a soul and a body is a **living being**. Consequently, the **heaven**, the **world**, **plants**, and the **elements** are all "living beings." In our common usage, however, it is customary to only call something a "living being" <note>original: "animal"</note> if it is an animated body endowed with **sensation**; and we define "soul" not by motion alone, but by life, sensation, voluntary movement, or intellect. Therefore, when we hear the term "living being" in this text, let us understand it in his way, not ours.

But now, let us return to the dialogue. He contends that **heaven** and the **celestial body** relate to other sensible things <note>things that can be perceived by the senses</note> in the same way that **man** relates to other **animals**. Furthermore, **man** is to other animals as an **animal god** <term>animal god: "animalis deus," a divine being existing within a living, physical form</term>, while **heaven** is to other sensible things as a **sensible god** <term>sensible god: "sensibilis deus," a divinity that can be seen and perceived, such as the stars or the cosmos itself</term>. I would believe that for God to be the ruler and governor of all things means nothing other than that God provides for all things and dispenses all things through

Because this [creation] was so great and so good, God willed that there be another who could contemplate the one he had made from himself. For the will of God is itself the highest perfection, seeing as he wills and perfects in one and the same moment.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the "Asclepius," specifically concluding the discussion on the dual nature of humanity (mortal and immortal) and the relationship between God and the created world as a "second God."</meta>

->ASCLEPIUS<-

...established, and the discussion is clear. It also explains why He tempered man from both natures—mortal and immortal—and why He clothed the mind (which He created in His own likeness and image, as the form of the vision of divine similarity) with a worldly and bodily covering. It further explains that the will of God is the highest perfection of all things, which necessity follows, and the result accompanies that necessity. For God completes both the willing and the perfecting at one and the same point in time. 

The fact that he calls the world a "second God" <note>original: "mundum secundum Deum"</note> both here and in chapter six, is just as if you were to call "duality" a "second unity." For duality is one, and a binary is one, but the <term>monad<note>original: "monas." A term from Greek philosophy referring to the "One" or the indivisible source of all numbers and existence.</note></term> is absolutely one, whereas the binary is not absolutely one, but one by participation and contraction—a "second one." In this same way, God is one, absolutely God; but the world is not God [in itself], but is God by participation, and is the most beautiful "footprint" <note>original: "vestigium." This suggests that the physical world is a visible trace or reflection of the divine creator's power.</note> of God among sensible things.

## COMMENTARY

*The sixth chapter discusses how God is absolutely the first God; the world is the second God, not absolutely but through participation <note>In Platonic and Hermetic thought, "participation" (participatio) refers to the way created things share in the qualities of their divine source without being equal to it.</note>, as it is the first image of the absolute God. Through the soul, the senses, the spirit, and reason—as if by superior elements—man is able to ascend into heaven. Yet, because he is also composed of fire, air, water, and earth <note>The four classical elements that make up the physical, "lower" world.</note>, he is subject to death, and must leave all worldly things to the earth when they are stripped of that divine part. The measure according to which man ought to live is religion, which is followed by goodness; this religion is seen to be perfect when, fortified by virtue, it despises the desire for all external things: possessions, the body, and everything we crave—including, finally, the very sense of craving itself. For man should only be called a man, in his own estimation, insofar as the focus of reason guides his mind. Thus, through the contemplation of divinity, he has joined to himself that part which is mortal by the necessity of preserving the lower world...*

God, therefore, is everlasting, God is eternal, and He cannot be born, nor could He have been; He is, He was, He shall be always. This, therefore, is the nature of God, which is entirely of itself. Matter <note>original: "hyle"</note>, however, or the nature of the world, and spirit, although they seem born from the beginning, nevertheless possess within themselves the power of being born and procreating, and the nature of fertility; for the beginning is in the quality of nature, which possesses within itself both the power and nature of conception and birth. ## COMMENTARIES.

The seventh chapter contains a veiled philosophy concerning the <term>genesis of the world<note>The origins or creation of the cosmos.</note></term>, <term>Hyle<note>A Greek term (*ὕλη*) used in ancient philosophy to describe primordial, unformed matter.</note></term>, the matter of the world, the accompanying spirit, and "place." Therefore, he does not suggest that the "place" of the world was "born" <note>The author argues that "Place" or the void is eternal, whereas the physical objects within it are "born" or created.</note>; however, he claims the world is both born and not born: it is born if you consider the physical crafting of creatures, but not born if you consider the essential truth of that crafting. For Hyle and the spirit—that is, the world and a certain divine force flowing through and diffused across all things—were not yet in the world's physical structure when they were not yet "born," but (as he says) they were already present then in the source from which they had to be born. But in what were they present, if not in that divine <term>Word<note>Latin: *verbum*. ...it was made, it was life, and from where at last whatever was made came forth. [The author argues] that <term>Hyle<note>A Greek term (*ὕλη*) referring to the primordial, unformed matter of the universe.</note></term> is fertile with the quality of water, which has the character of the good, and is equally fertile with malice, because it is equally capable of both good and evil; just as the same earth is fertile with both healing and harmful herbs, and the earth possesses this as an inherent part of its own property, so also does Hyle. Yet, he notes that God has provided for humans (as much as was reasonably fitting) with <term>sense<note>Latin: *sensus*. In Hermetic philosophy, this refers to a higher spiritual perception or divine intelligence rather than mere physical sensation.</note></term>, as well as with learning and intelligence, against this kind of material property, so that malice might not occupy our own "matter" like a harmful weed in a deserted, neglected, and uncultivated field. Furthermore, in this seventh part, he discusses a few things regarding the spirit diffused through all things, the underworld, and sense—which is the flowing of higher minds into human minds, like rays of light into the eyes.

When joined together, however, they are one—or rather two—from which all things are made and by which they are made: that is, from <term>Matter<note>original: *materia*, the raw substance of the universe.</note></term>, out of which they are made, and by His will, at whose nod all other things are brought into being.

God recognized that of all the animals, humans alone possess reason and discipline. Through these tools, humans are able to turn away from and distance themselves from the vices of their bodies, and God held out to them the pursuit of, and the hope for, immortality.

In the end, God fashioned the "good man"—the kind of person capable of becoming immortal—from both natures: the divine and the mortal. Because man was composed in this way by the will of God, it was decreed that such a man is even superior to the gods (who are formed only from an immortal nature) as well as to all other mortal creatures.

For this reason, because man is joined to the gods by a shared kinship, he worships them with religious devotion and a holy mind. The gods, in turn, look upon and protect all human affairs with a sense of pious affection. However, this is said only of those few men who are endowed with a pious mind...

### COMMENTARY

The eighth chapter covers the <term>usiarchs</term><note>Latin: *usiarchae*, derived from the Greek *ousia* (essence/substance) and *archon* (ruler). These are primordial powers that govern the essential nature of different realms of existence.</note> and substantial princes, whom he calls gods: he calls Jupiter the usiarch of heaven. [He calls] Light the usiarch of the sun. He establishes thirty-six <term>horoscopes</term><note>Latin: *horoscopios*. In this context, these are the "Decans," 36 celestial spirits who each govern ten degrees of the zodiac and monitor the hours and the fixed stars.</note>, that is, observers of the hours, among the stars always fixed in the same place; and he calls their leader <term>Pantomorphos</term><note>Greek/Latin: *Pantomorphon*, meaning "The All-Shaped" or "The Omniform."</note>, that is, the "all-formed." As the princes of the seven wandering spheres <note>The seven "wandering spheres" are the planets known in antiquity: Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, the Sun, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon.</note>, he names Fortune and Fate. He also establishes a usiarch of the air. 

But these appear to be the fabrications of demons and certain empty veils leading toward <term>pagan</term><note>Latin: *gentilitios*. Literally "of the gentiles," used here by the commentator to label non-Christian or Hermetic beliefs as errors.</note> errors; things which, rather than bringing perfection, cause those who linger on them too long to waste away. From here, he returns to the contemplation of the supreme God—the ineffable and unnameable, or he who is named by the names of all things—who is most full of <term>fecundity</term><note>Latin: *foecunditate*. This refers to God's infinite creative power and ability to generate life.</note>. From him, all things possess the quality that nothing can be barren. From this comes that love of procreating and nature’s vast drive—having nothing at all foul or shameful in itself, provided it is considered religiously, and discourse concerning it is held in such a way, and handled with no less devotion. There is...

->ASCLEPIUS. 511<-

For this has been granted as an imitation of divine fruitfulness <note>original: "fæcunditatis"</note>. But because the majority of men are ignorant of the <term>mysteries<note>In the Hermetic tradition, 'mysteries' refer to the hidden spiritual truths about the universe and the soul that are only revealed to the initiated.</note></term>, they profane divine laws; in the manner of beasts, they handle these things insanely, irreverently, and as if they were raving and mad. Therefore, concerning such matters, one should hardly dare to think or speak anything out of shame, because that disorder and that irreverence of men toward the venerable ordination of God thrusts itself into our senses and thoughts—rather than that beautiful, holy, and uncontaminated arrangement of God. And because it is granted to only a few to have pure senses, I believe that only a few should think and speak of such things.

Soon he adds that God has imparted understanding and discipline to humans alone, so that his immortal and divine <term>particle<note>The 'divine particle' refers to the human soul or intellect, viewed as a spark of the divine essence residing within a mortal frame.</note></term> might avoid the vices it would otherwise easily encounter through its mixture with the physical mass. For by reason of the body and its dissolvable part, it is inevitable that the cravings of desire and other mental vices fall upon the souls of men.

This is the eighth part.

### HERMES TRISMEGISTUS

Asclepius, recognize this power. Just as the Lord and Father, or (that which is highest) God, is the creator <note>original: "effector"</note> of the celestial gods, so too is man the creator of the gods who are in the temples, satisfied with human proximity. These gods not only receive light but also give it; not only does man benefit from them, but he even sustains <note>original: "confirmat," suggesting the strengthening or animation of these divine images through ritual</note> the gods. Do you wonder at this, O Asclepius, or do you perhaps distrust it, as many do?

**ASCLEPIUS.** I am confounded, O Trismegistus, but having freely assented to your words, I judge man to be most happy, having attained such great happiness.

**TRISMEGISTUS.** And not without merit is he worthy of wonder, who is the greatest of all gods. For the nature of all the celestial gods is manifest and distinct, propagated from the purest part of nature; their signs are, as it were, only the heads standing for the whole. But the types of gods which <term>humanity<note>Here "humanitas" refers to the collective creative capacity of the human race.</term> fashions are formed from both natures: from the divine nature, which is prior and much more divine, and from that nature which is within humans—that is, from the <term>matter<note>In Hermetic philosophy, "matter" (materia) is the physical substance used to create temple statues, which humans then animate with divine power.</note></term> with which they were fabricated. These are shaped not only with heads alone, but with all their limbs and their whole bodies.

Thus humanity, mindful of its nature and its origin, perseveres in that imitation of divinity. Just as the Father and Lord made the eternal gods so that they might be like Himself, so humanity fashions its own gods [in its own image].

### COMMENTARY

This entire ninth chapter is profane, which Augustine <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), who critiqued the "Asclepius" in his work "The City of God" for its defense of animating statues</note> also rightly refutes in his book *On the City of God* <note>original: "de Ciuitate Dei"</note>. It approves of idolatry, extols it with wondrous praises, preaches it, and deplores its fall. It places a certain god above the peak of heaven looking around at all things, but within that space contained by heaven and earth, it places Jupiter as the dispenser. However, it makes Plutonic Jupiter the dispenser of the earth and sea, as if there were one God in heaven, another in the air, and another on the earth and sea—all of which contain a vast [mass] of errors... <note>The Latin text "im-" is a truncated word, likely "immensitatem" (immensity) or "impetum" (force), continuing on the next page.</note>

The Prophet says with a truthful mouth: *All the gods of the nations are demons.* <note>original: "Omnes dij gentium daemonia" — a common patristic citation of Psalm 96:5 (95:5 in the Vulgate) used to argue that pagan deities were actually fallen angels or malevolent spirits.</note> Let these few points suffice against the impurity of Mercury <note>The author refers to Hermes Trismegistus by his Latin name, Mercurius.</note> and this ninth part of the work. Lazzarelli <note>Ludovico Lazzarelli (1440–1500), a Renaissance scholar and Hermeticist who attempted to reconcile the "Hermetica" with Christian doctrine through allegorical interpretation.</note> pulls this passage toward an analogy, as if the "idols" were actually the apostles; the "man-maker" is Christ; the "power instilled from above" is the Holy Spirit; "Egypt" represents the darkness of the nations and the persecution of the disciples, apostles, and martyrs. These things are piously imagined, but they are perhaps a forced <note>original: "violenta" — meaning an interpretation that does violence to the literal sense of the text.</note> reading of the literal letter. 

Along with Augustine, I perceive the error of Hermes both in this chapter and in the thirteenth. For the seers of the Gentiles (such as Balaam or the Sibyls) <note>Balaam was a non-Israelite prophet in the Bible; the Sibyls were ancient Greek and Roman prophetesses. Both were often cited by Christians as having genuine but flawed or "shadowy" glimpses of divine truth.</note> seem to possess this quality: they endure both light and darkness, experiencing bright and shadowy intervals in their prophecies—sometimes pure, and at other times impure.

I believe this Sun to be the <term>second god</term> <note>In Hermetic philosophy, the 'Second God' is the visible governor of the universe, often identified with the Sun or the Demiurge, who carries out the will of the supreme, invisible God.</note>, O Asclepius, governing all other things and illuminating all the creatures of the world, whether they possess souls <note>original: 'animantia'</note> or are inanimate.

Therefore, the world must be completely full of life and eternity, if it is necessary for it to live forever.

The world is the <term>receptacle of time</term> <note>In Hermetic philosophy, the physical world is seen as a vessel or container where the abstract flow of time manifests as growth, change, and decay.</note>, by whose course and movement the world is nourished. Time, however, is maintained by order. Order and time, through their alternation, bring about the renewal of all things that exist within the world.

## COMMENTARY.

The tenth partition concerns death and the examination of the soul when it has departed from the body, and how those whose lives are justly taken by human laws on account of the magnitude of their crimes are punished more severely after death. It also discusses how God serves as a protection for the righteous, and addresses the divinity of the sun and the world. Hermes posits that the world is the first <term>sensible god</term> <note>original: 'sensibilem deum'; a deity that can be perceived through the physical senses, like the sun or the cosmos, as opposed to an abstract or invisible intellect.</note> and that the sun is a "second world" which will never rest and will never be destroyed. We, however, do not attribute the <term>incommunicable name</term> <note>original: 'nomen dei incommunicabile'; a theological concept referring to the name of God (often the Tetragrammaton) that cannot be applied to any created thing.</note> of God to either the sun or the world, and we believe the world will eventually be dissolved. Therefore, if these things are understood exactly as the simple words of Hermes sound, they manifest the error of the pagans <note>original: 'gentilium'; the author is likely a Christian commentator reconciling these Hermetic texts with Christian doctrine.</note>. Nevertheless, we do attribute a kind of divinity to them by way of participation, viewing them as the excellent works of God. This concludes the tenth partition.

## CHAPTER XI.

Since all things are situated in this manner, nothing is stable, nothing is fixed, and nothing is immobile—neither among things being born, nor celestial things, nor earthly things. For God alone—and deservedly He alone—is entirely full and perfect in Himself, from Himself, and around Himself. He is His own firm stability, and He cannot be moved by the impulse of any other nor by any change of place, since all things are in Him and He alone is in all things. This is true unless one should dare to say that His own motion exists within eternity; but...

--- Page 556 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of Chapter XI from the previous page, moving from the assertion that God alone is truly stable to a complex philosophical exploration of how eternity, time, and God’s own "immobile movement" relate to one another.</meta>

-> MERCURY TRISMEGISTUS <-

...even more so than that, immobile eternity itself, into which the movement <note>original: 'agitatio'; refers to the active, shifting nature of time and change as opposed to the stillness of eternity.</note> of all ages returns, and from which the movement of all ages takes its beginning. God, therefore, was stable, and eternity always existed together with him in the same way, holding within itself the unborn world—which we rightly call <term>sensible</term> <note>original: 'sensibilem'; here meaning the physical cosmos that can be perceived by the five senses.</note>—as the image of this God. From this, the world was made an imitator of eternity.

Time, however, possesses the force and nature of its own stability, even though it is always in motion, due to that very necessity of returning back into itself. Therefore, although eternity is stable, immobile, and fixed, because it is always drawn back into eternity by the mobility of time—and that mobility is directed by the logic of time—it results that eternity itself, while truly immobile, seems to be moved only through time, in which eternity exists and in which all movement is contained. 

Thus it happens that both eternity, as stability, is moved, and the mobility of time becomes stable by the fixed law of its course. In this way, it is also believable that God is moved within himself by that same immobility; for within the very magnitude of his stability, there is an immobile movement. Indeed, there is an immobile law governing his very magnitude.

And you, O Tat, and Asclepius, and Hammon, cover these divine mysteries with silence within the secrets of your hearts, and hide them in stillness.

## COMMENTARIES.

*This thirteenth chapter suffers from a similar impurity as the ninth chapter, and while Hermes wishes for man to be most divine and most worthy of admiration, in this matter man is surely most impious and profane. This is because he discovered idolatry <note>original: "idololatriam"</note>, because he placed summoned demonic spirits into images, and added rites and sacrifices concerning Asclepius, Hermes, Isis, and Osiris, who were worshiped by the Egyptians. He also included the animals which the Egyptians held sacred, as well as the herbs, stones, aromatics, harmonies, and hymns with which they might appease those spirits placed within the statues and images. There are some "pythonic" people <note>original: "pythonici"; a term referring to those possessed by a divining spirit or practicing necromancy, derived from the Delphic Python</note> who still tend to do this (O, unhappy age!) who think they hold spirits enclosed in either rings or small vessels—a most impure race of men, hostile to God and men alike, established as enemies on the opposing side. Against this profane error of impiety, the blessed Augustine <note>St. Augustine (354–430 AD) was a fierce critic of this specific passage of the *Asclepius* in his work *The City of God*, arguing that the "gods" Hermes claimed to create were actually demons.</note> argues, and rightly so, in his book **The City of God**, where he convicts them in the name of truth. So much for the thirteenth chapter.*

**ASCLEPIUS.** What part of reason, therefore, do <term>destiny: translated from the Greek "heimarmene" (εἱμαρμένη), referring to the fixed lot or fate of a person</term> or the fates inhabit, O Tris-

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Hermes Trismegistus and Asclepius regarding the nature of the cosmos. Having previously discussed the "making of gods" (idolatry), the conversation now shifts to the governing forces of the universe: Fate, Necessity, and Order.</meta>

->ASCLEPIUS.<-

...megistus, if the celestial gods rule universally, and the earthly gods inhabit specific things, what is this that we call **Fate** <note>original: "εἱμαρμένην" (eimarmene), a Greek term for the lot or destiny assigned to a person</note>? **TRIS.** O Asclepius, it is the necessity of all things that occur, always joined to itself by interlinked chains. This is either the creator of all things, or it is the highest God, or it proceeds from God himself—the God who is the second-made effect <note>In Hermetic philosophy, the "second god" often refers to the Cosmos or the Sun, acting as an intermediary between the supreme Mind and the world.</note>—or it is the discipline of all celestial and earthly things, firmly established by divine laws. 

This **Fate** and **Necessity** are both joined to one another by an inseparable bond. Of these, the first—Fate—gives birth to the beginnings of all things, while Necessity drives them toward their completion <note>original: "effectum"</note>, depending on those original seeds. Following these is **Order**, which is the sequence and arrangement of time for the fulfillment of things. For nothing exists without the structure of order. 

In all these, this world is perfect. For the world itself is carried by order, or rather, it consists entirely of order. Therefore, these three—**Fate**, **Necessity**, and **Order**—are primarily brought about by the will of God, who governs the world by His law and divine reason. From these powers, all "wanting" or "not wanting" is entirely absent by divine decree. They are not moved by anger, nor are they swayed by favor, but instead they serve the necessity of eternal reason. This eternity is unchangeable, immovable, and indissoluble. First, therefore...

<meta>catchword: Fate (εἱμαρ)</meta>

<summary>Hermes Trismegistus defines Fate, Necessity, and Order as the three divine mechanisms that govern the universe under God's law. He explains that while Fate initiates events, Necessity ensures their completion, and Order organizes them within time.</summary>

<keywords>Fate, Necessity, Order, Hermes Trismegistus, Asclepius, Divine Law, Eternal Reason, Eimarmene, Hermeticism</keywords>

This page defines how these three interact with Eternity and the cyclical nature of time.</meta>

<page-num>540</page-num>
# HERMES TRISMEGISTUS.

**Fate** <note>original: "εἱμαρμένη" (heimarmene)</note> is that which, like a sown seed, takes up the offspring of all future things. **Necessity** follows, by which all things are compelled by force toward their completion. The third is **Order**, which preserves the weaving <note>original: "textum", implying a fabric or interconnected sequence of events</note> of those things which Fate and Necessity arrange. 

This, therefore, is **Eternity**, which neither began to be nor shall cease; it is fixed by an immutable law of progress and preserved by everlasting motion. It rises and falls through various parts <note>original: "membra", literally 'limbs', referring here to the constituent parts or cycles of the universe</note> such that as times change, it rises again with the very same parts through which it had fallen. For such is the nature <note>original: "ratio"</note> of this revolving sphere <note>original: "rotunditas"</note> that all things are so tightly bound together that you cannot tell where the rotation begins, since all things always seem both to precede and to follow one another. **Outcome** and **Chance**, however, are present, mixed into all worldly things.

### CHAPTER XV.

We have spoken of these individual matters as far as humanity was able, as far as the Divinity willed, and as far as it permitted. This alone remains for us: that having blessed God and prayed, we should return to the care of the body. For in treating sufficiently of divine matters, we have saturated our minds as if with the food of the soul <note>original: "animi pabulis", a metaphor for intellectual or spiritual nourishment</note>. 

Indeed, having stepped out from the inner sanctum <term>adyton: the most sacred, restricted area of a temple where the public was not allowed</term>, when they began to pray to God, they were looking toward the South. For when the sun is setting, anyone who wishes to pray to God ought to direct themselves there, just as at sunrise one should face toward that which is called the East-dweller <term>Subsolanus: the Latin name for the East wind, here used to denote the direction of the rising sun</term>. 

As they were already beginning to speak the prayer, Asclepius said in a low voice, "O Tat, let us suggest to your father <note>referring to Hermes Trismegistus, who acts as a spiritual father to Tat</note> that he command us to say the prayer to God with the addition of incense and perfumes." Moved [by this suggestion], <note>Hermes is responding to Asclepius's suggestion—from the previous page—to burn incense.</note> he said, "Speak better, speak better omens, O Asclepius! For it is similar to sacrilege when you ask to burn incense and other such things for God. For nothing is lacking to Him, who is Himself all things, or in whom all things are; but rather, let us adore Him by giving thanks. For these are the highest 'incenses' of God: when thanks are offered by mortals. 

We give thanks to You, O highest and most excellent one. For by Your grace, we have attained so great a light of Your kinship <note>original: "cognationis tuæ," referring to the divine spark or relation between the human soul and God</note>: holy and honorable name, the one name by which alone God is to be blessed according to the religion of our fathers. 

For You deign to provide to all people paternal piety, and religion, and love, and whatever sweet efficacy there may be, when You gift us with **sense**, **reason**, and **intelligence**: 

**sense**, so that we may know You; 
**reason**, so that we may seek You out through our suspicions <note>original: "suspicionibus," meaning through indirect hints, conjectures, or investigative reasoning</note>; 
**intelligence**, so that in knowing You through such cognition, we may rejoice. 

And saved by Your divine power, let us rejoice that You have shown Yourself to us in Your fullness. Let us rejoice that You have deigned to consecrate us to eternity while we are still situated in our bodies. For this is the only human thanksgiving: the knowledge of Your majesty. 

We have known You; and we have understood You, the greatest light, perceptible only by the intellect <note>original: "solo intellectu sensibile," meaning that which is "sensed" or perceived by the mind rather than the physical eyes</note>. O true way of life! O fertile pregnancy of all natures! We have known You, [as the fullness] of all nature...

### COMMENTARY.

*The fifteenth chapter concludes the dialogue in a religious manner with thanksgivings. With the adoration finished and thanks rendered to God, the four men who had filled the sacred sanctuary—Mercury <note>The Latin text uses "Mercurius" for the speaker Hermes Trismegistus</note>, Asclepius, Hammon <note>original: "Amnon"</note>, and Tat <note>original: "Tatius," the son of Hermes</note>—turn themselves toward a pure meal without animal flesh, according to the religious rite of the Egyptians. And here ends the little book of Hermes regarding the will of God.*

->THE END.<-

### THE STABILITY OF THE SOUL

*The image of the pyramid provides a final meditation for the reader. Just as the four men in the preceding text sought "eternal endurance" through divine knowledge, the pyramid represents that which is permanent and unaffected by the "slips" or "falls" of the material world. Shaded to show its three-dimensional form, the pyramid catches the light of truth, standing firm as a monument to the spiritual life described by Hermes Trismegistus.*
